items.title: R-Type
items.text:
A networked remake of the classic horizontal shoot'em up, built on our own C++ game engine.

Up to four players connect to an authoritative server and fight the Bydos together. The project is split into a graphical client, a multithreaded server, and the engine they both rely on.

Project status

Early skeleton: the client opens a window and the server starts. The pages below describe the target design and are filled in as the engine takes shape.

  • Getting started

    Build the client and the server on Linux or Windows, and run them.

    Build and run

  • Architecture

    How the engine is organised: rendering, networking and game logic as decoupled layers.

    Architecture

  • Network protocol

    The binary UDP protocol between clients and server, precise enough to write your own client.

    Protocol specification

  • Technical decisions

    Why we chose each library and tool, compared with the alternatives.

    Decision records

  • Accessibility

    What the game and its documentation offer to players with disabilities.

    Accessibility

  • Contributing

    Git workflow, coding conventions, and how to add a page to this documentation.

    Contributing

items.title: Accessibility
items.text:
Draft

This page lists the accessibility goals of the project. Each item is updated with what is actually implemented.

items.title: In the game
items.text: Category Planned features Physical and motor Remappable controls, gamepad support, adjustable game speed, auto-fire option Visual Colour-blind friendly palettes, player ships distinguishable by shape and not only by colour, scalable UI text, high-contrast mode Audio Visual cues for important sounds, separate volume controls for music and effects Mental and cognitive Difficulty levels, pause at any time, short and clear menus, tutorial

items.title: Implemented so far
items.text: Category Feature Where Physical and motor Every action can be bound to any key or gamepad input, with several inputs per action. The engine supports it; the menu to change the controls is still to be done. Input Physical and motor Gamepad support, with analog sticks and an adjustable dead zone for worn sticks. Input Physical and motor Controls work on any keyboard layout: keys are physical positions, so WASD is ZQSD on AZERTY. Input Audio Separate volumes for the music and the sound effects, on top of a master volume. The options menu sets the effects volume; the music and master volumes are still to be added to it. Audio Visual The game keeps its aspect ratio and scales to any window size, without being cropped or stretched. Rendering Visual Colour filters for the three kinds of colour blindness (protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia), applied to the whole image, chosen in the options menu. Rendering Visual High-contrast filter for players with low vision. Rendering Visual Simulation filters showing the game as colour-blind players see it, for the team to check that sprites stay distinguishable. Rendering Physical and motor Every menu can be used with the keyboard only, a gamepad only, or the mouse; holding a direction repeats it. Scenes and interface Visual The focused widget is shown three ways: a frame, another colour, and a bigger size, so that it is not told by colour only. Scenes and interface

items.title: In this documentation
items.text:
• Light and dark themes, both with sufficient contrast.
  • Full keyboard navigation and built-in search.
  • A heading structure that screen readers can follow.
  • Every image has an alternative text, and every diagram is followed by a sentence summarising it.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
Draft

This page describes the target architecture. It is updated as each subsystem is implemented.

R-Type follows a client/server model with an authoritative server: clients only send player inputs and render what the server tells them; every gameplay decision (spawns, collisions, deaths) is taken by the server.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Client["r-type_client"]
        direction TB
        CInput[Input] --> CNet[Networking]
        CNet --> CWorld[Local world state]
        CWorld --> CRender[Rendering & audio]
    end

    subgraph Server["r-type_server"]
        direction TB
        SNet[Networking] --> SLogic[Game logic]
        SLogic --> SWorld[Authoritative world state]
    end

    Client -- "player inputs (UDP)" --> Server
    Server -- "world updates (UDP)" --> Client

Clients send their inputs to the server over UDP; the server simulates the game and sends world updates back to every client.

items.title: Server processes
items.text:
The server hosts several games at once. The r-type_server you start is the master: it runs the lobby and starts one process per game (ADR 0013). The client talks to the master over TCP until it joins a game, then to the game over UDP (ADR 0012). Both are encrypted (ADR 0014).

flowchart LR
    Client["r-type_client"]
    subgraph Host["Server host"]
        Master["Master<br/>r-type_server<br/>lobby"]
        G1["Game 1<br/>r-type_server --instance"]
        G2["Game 2<br/>r-type_server --instance"]
        Master -- "starts, local TCP" --> G1
        Master -- "starts, local TCP" --> G2
    end
    Client -- "TLS over TCP 4242: lobby" --> Master
    Client -- "encrypted UDP: inputs and world" --> G1

The client joins a game through the master, then exchanges the game traffic directly with that game's process.

How the server starts, what it is given and how it stops: Server.

New to networking? Start with Networking concepts.

items.title: Layers
items.text:
The engine is split into decoupled subsystems, shared by the client and the server where it makes sense.

Layer Responsibility Used by Core Entities, components, systems (libs/ecs), physics (libs/physics), logging (libs/log), timing Client, server Networking Sockets (Asio), binary serialization, reliability over UDP, encryption, the protocol Client, server Game logic Players, Bydos, missiles, waves, collisions (libs/game, ADR 0015, Game) Server, client offline Rendering Window, textures, drawing, built on raylib Client Interface Menus, options and HUD, made of entities like the world (libs/engine) Client Audio Music and sound effects, built on raylib (libs/audio) Client Input Keyboard / gamepad mapping to player actions Client

items.title: World and interface
items.text:
Everything the client draws is an entity of the ECS, as decided in ADR 0007: the world (ships, Bydos, missiles, star-field), the HUD and the menus. Each drawn entity belongs to a layer, and the layers are drawn one after the other:

flowchart TB
    subgraph Frame["One frame of the client"]
        direction TB
        Update["ecs.update(elapsed)<br/>scenes, interface, game, layout"]
        World["1. World layer<br/>ships, Bydos, star-field"]
        UI["2. Interface layer<br/>HUD and menus"]
    end
    Update --> World --> UI --> Renderer["Renderer<br/>(the only one drawing)"]

Each frame updates the ECS, then draws the world layer and the interface layer on top of it.

  • Only the Renderer draws: the systems never call raylib.
  • The interface layer is always drawn after the world. In VR, the world layer is drawn on the board and the interface layer on a floating panel.
  • Phases of the game (home screen, game, pause menu) are scenes: groups of entities opened and closed together. See Scenes and interface.

items.title: Libraries
items.text:
The programs are built on twelve libraries:

Library Role Page libs/render Window, textures and fonts, drawing at a fixed logical resolution. Wraps raylib. Rendering libs/input Keyboard and gamepads turned into game actions, with rebindable controls. Wraps raylib. Input libs/ecs Entities, components and systems, with a hierarchy. Shared with the server, so it never depends on raylib. ECS libs/log Messages with a level and a subsystem name, coloured in a terminal. Shared with the server. Logging libs/network Addresses, UDP and TCP sockets, the event loop that runs them, TCP framing, TLS and the binary serialization. Wraps Asio and Mbed TLS. Shared with the server. Networking libs/physics Movement and collisions as components and systems on the ECS. Knows no game: each game names its collision layers and reacts to the collisions. Shared with the server. — libs/game The rules of the R-Type: a Simulation that takes the inputs of the players and steps the world one tick at a time. Shared by the server and the client offline; no raylib, no network. Game libs/lobby The messages of the lobby protocol, between a client and the master: hello, list, create and join games. Shared by the client and the server. Server libs/engine Client systems on the ECS: scenes, drawing, animations, menus as entities, navigation. Scenes and interface libs/audio Sound effects and streamed music, with separate volumes. Wraps raylib. Audio libs/core Building blocks shared by the other libraries: resource handles and caches. Header-only, no dependency. — libs/shaders GLSL shaders (colour filters, lighting of the 3D models), one file per stage in glsl/, embedded at build time as C++ strings and compiled by render. Header-only, no dependency. Rendering

Their public headers contain no raylib type: raylib is a private dependency of render, input and audio, and the client code only uses our own classes. The server only links the libraries that do not depend on raylib: the ECS, the physics, the game, the lobby, the log, the core and the network libraries. Likewise, Asio and Mbed TLS are private dependencies of network, and reproc, which starts the instances of the server, a private dependency of r-type_server.

items.title: Repository layout
items.text:
apps/       executables, one subdirectory per program
  client/   graphical client (r-type_client)
    assets/ sprites, fonts and sounds, copied next to the executable
  server/   game server (r-type_server)
  keygen/   generates the keys of the server (r-type_keygen)
libs/       libraries shared by the programs, one subdirectory per library
  audio/    sound effects and music (client)
  core/     handles and resource caches (all)
  ecs/      entity component system, hierarchy (client and server)
  engine/   client systems: drawing, animations, menus (client)
  game/     rules of the R-Type, the Simulation (server and client offline)
  input/    keyboard and gamepad input (client)
  lobby/    messages between a client and the master (client and server)
  log/      logging (client and server)
  network/  addresses, sockets and event loop (client and server)
  render/   window, resources and drawing (client)
  shaders/  GLSL shaders, embedded in the binaries at build time (client)
tests/      unit and smoke tests (Catch2)
cmake/      CMake helpers (CPM bootstrap)
docs/       this documentation (Zensical)
doxygen/    API reference configuration
scripts/    developer and CI scripts

Each library keeps its public headers apart from its implementation, so that the libraries it depends on (raylib, for instance) stay out of its interface:

libs/<name>/
  CMakeLists.txt
  include/rtype/<name>/   public headers, included as <rtype/<name>/Header.hpp>
  src/                    implementation

The client's assets live in apps/client/assets/. The build copies them next to the executable (build/bin/assets/) and the client package ships them in the same place, so the client loads them from rtype::render::applicationDirectory() / "assets" and finds them wherever it is started from. Paths given to the ResourceManager are relative to this directory, for instance "sprites/player.png".

items.title: Audio
items.text:
The audio library (libs/audio, namespace rtype::audio) plays the sound effects and the music of the client. Like the render library, it wraps raylib: its public headers contain no raylib type.

Class Role AudioDevice Opens the audio output and closes it when destroyed. Only one can exist. AudioPlayer Loads sounds and music once, plays them, and holds the music and effects volumes. 
Window window;
AudioDevice device;                                           // after the window, see below
AudioPlayer audio(device, applicationDirectory() / "assets");

const SoundId shot = audio.loadSound("sounds/shot.wav");
const MusicId stage = audio.loadMusic("music/stage1.ogg");
audio.playMusic(stage);

while (!window.shouldClose()) {
    audio.update();                                           // once per frame, for the music
    if (controls.wasPressed(Action::Shoot)) {
        audio.play(shot);
    }
}

items.title: The audio device
items.text:
AudioDevice opens the default audio output in its constructor and closes it in its destructor (RAII). The AudioPlayer takes it as a constructor parameter: declare the player after the device, so that sounds are freed before the output closes.

No sound is not an error. On a computer without sound card, in a virtual machine or in the CI, the output cannot be opened: a warning is logged and the game keeps running silently, with every sound ignored. Audio can also be disabled on purpose:

AudioDevice device({.enabled = false});   // tests, servers, or a "no sound" option

Create it after the window

raylib's messages are redirected to the log when the Window is created. An AudioDevice created before the window prints raylib's messages about the audio output directly to the console.

items.title: Sound effects and music
items.text:
Sound effects Music Typical use Shots, explosions, menu sounds Background music of a stage Loading Fully decoded in memory Streamed from the file while it plays At the same time Several sounds, and the same sound several times One music at a time Functions loadSound(), play() loadMusic(), playMusic(), stopMusic(), pauseMusic(), resumeMusic()

Each file is loaded once: loading the same path again returns the same handle (SoundId, MusicId), like textures in the render library. Both use the same ResourceCache, from the core library.

loadSoundAsync() and loadMusicAsync() return shared futures. Call finishPendingLoads() on the audio owner's thread each frame, then use the handle once its future is ready. Sound files are decoded on a worker; audio buffers are created on the owner thread. Pass engine.assetLoading().queue() to the player constructor to share the engine's worker with rendering. See ADR 0017.

items.title: Playing a sound several times at once
items.text:
With raylib, playing a sound that is already playing restarts it: fast shots would cut each other. Each sound effect therefore has 4 voices, which share the same samples in memory. play() uses a free voice, or restarts the oldest one if all four are busy.

play() takes optional settings:

audio.play(explosion, {.volume = 0.8f, .pitch = 0.9f, .pan = -0.5f});
Setting Effect volume Volume of this sound, between 0 and 1, multiplied by the effects volume. pitch Speed and pitch: 1 is unchanged, 2 is one octave higher. Small random variations (0.9 to 1.1) keep a repeated sound from being tiresome. pan Position from left (-1) to right (1), 0 being centred: an explosion on the left of the screen can be heard on the left.

items.title: Streaming the music
items.text: A music is too long to be decoded in memory at once: it is read from its file in small parts while it plays. update() reads the next part; it must be called once per frame, otherwise the music stutters, then stops.

items.title: Volumes
items.text:
Volume Set with Applies to Master AudioDevice::setMasterVolume() Everything Music AudioPlayer::setMusicVolume() The music, immediately Effects AudioPlayer::setEffectsVolume() The sound effects played from then on

All volumes are between 0 and 1, and clamped to this range. Separate music and effects volumes are one of the accessibility features: some players need the effects louder than the music to follow the game, others are disturbed by the music. In the options menu, Effects volume is changed with Left and Right.

items.title: Supported formats
items.text:
Format Supported WAV, OGG, MP3, QOA Yes XM, MOD (tracker music) Yes FLAC No: disabled in raylib's default build

WAV suits short sound effects (no decoding cost), OGG suits music (small files, good quality, free format).

items.title: Testing
items.text: tests/audio.cpp tests the library with audio disabled, so that the tests give the same result with or without a sound card: volumes, single device, handles of sounds loaded twice, missing files, and the state of the music. Missing files are reported even when audio is disabled, so that they are noticed on every computer.

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• No spatial sound beyond left-right panning. For VR, sounds positioned in 3D around the player would help; raylib does not provide it, so it would need another approach.
  • No fading between two musics: playMusic() switches at once.
  • The effects volume does not change the sounds already playing, which are short.

items.title: A game in the client
items.text:
How the client plays a game: one game scene, fed by a game session, offline or online (ADR 0015). Offline, the Simulation of libs/game runs in the client; online, it runs in a server instance, and the client receives its snapshots (the online session comes with client: networking).

To play: Play, then Solo, in the main menu. Arrows (or WASD, ZQSD) move the ship, Space fires, Escape opens the pause menu.

items.title: Code layout
items.text:
apps/client/src/Game/
  GameSession.hpp        what the scene knows of a game: inputs in, snapshots out
  LocalSession.cpp       a game offline: the Simulation, stepped 60 times per second
  RemoteSession.cpp      a game online: the UDP session with the instance (The client online)
  GameSessionSystem.cpp  controls → PlayerInput → session; snapshots → entities of the scene
  GameScenes.cpp         the game scene, its HUD, and the pause menu

The code of the client is the library r-type_client_core, and main.cpp the program, like the server: the tests use the library (tests/client_game.cpp).

items.title: A frame
items.text:
flowchart LR
    Controls["engine::Controls<br/>keyboard, gamepads"] --> System
    subgraph System["GameSessionSystem"]
        direction TB
        Input["inputFrom()<br/>PlayerInput"]
        Apply["apply()<br/>entities of the scene"]
    end
    Input --> Session{{"GameSession"}}
    Session -- "takeSnapshots()" --> Apply
    Apply --> Renderer["SceneRenderer<br/>boxes, HUD"]

Each frame, the input of the local player goes to the session, and the snapshots that come back become the entities the scene draws.

  1. The input. inputFrom() reads the virtual gamepad of the engine: the four directions, and FaceDown (Space, A on a gamepad) to fire. The bindings are those of Input: the game never reads a key. When a menu is over the scene (pause, console), the input is empty and the session is paused.
  2. The session. update(elapsed) lets the time go by. The LocalSession adds up the frame times and steps the simulation once per 1/60 s, whatever the frame rate, at most 5 times per frame: after a long frame (a loading, a debugger), the game slows down for a moment instead of freezing to catch up.
  3. The world. Each snapshot holds the whole world at its tick. An entity of the game gets an entity of the scene the first time it appears (Replicated with its id, Position, Drawable, and its look), is moved by the next ones, and is destroyed when a snapshot no longer has it.

The GameSessionSystem runs after the InterfaceSystem: Escape opens the pause menu before the game reads the input. When the game scene closes, the engine destroys its entities and the system forgets its session.

items.title: The scenes
items.text:
Scene What it holds game The starry sky, the world of the session, and the HUD: one line per player, in its colour, with its lives and score. Escape opens the pause menu. pause Over the game, dimmed: Resume, or Leave the game. Offline, the game stops while it is open.

GameScenes::play(session, onEnd) starts a game with a session: the game scene replaces every scene. "Solo" plays a LocalSession, and goes back to the main menu when it ends; the lobby plays a RemoteSession, and goes back to its list (The client online). The game ends when the player leaves it from the pause menu, or when its session is over (isOver()): game over, or the game lost online.

items.title: What it looks like
items.text:
For now each entity is a coloured box of the size of its collider in the rules, so that what is drawn is what collides:

Entity Look Ship 96 × 48, in the colour of its player: blue, red, green, yellow for the slots 0 to 3 Shot 24 × 8, in the colour of the player who fired Anything else (Bydos, later) A grey square

lookOf() decides it: sprites can replace the boxes there, without changing the rest.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
tests/client_game.cpp (tag [client]) runs without a window, with the FakeInput keyboard:

  • the LocalSession: 60 steps per second of game time with frames of any length, at most 5 per update, its player moved by its input, nothing while paused;
  • inputFrom() and lookOf(): the controls held become the bits of the input, the sizes are those of the rules, the four players have four colours;
  • the GameSessionSystem in an Engine: the ship drawn where the simulation puts it and moved by the keyboard, shots created when fired and destroyed once out of the area, the game stopped while a menu is over its scene, an empty input under a menu even for a session that goes on (as online), and the session forgotten when its scene closes.
./build/bin/rtype_tests "[client]"

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• No interpolation offline: the entities move 60 times per second, the rate of the simulation; online, they are interpolated between the snapshots (The client online).
  • Boxes instead of sprites, and no explosion when an entity is destroyed: the snapshots already say which ones were killed (DestroyCause::Killed).
  • No end of game: the rules have no lives to lose yet (server: gameplay).

items.title: The client online
items.text: How the client joins the lobby of a master and plays a game of it: the same game scene as offline, fed by a RemoteSession instead of a LocalSession (A game in the client, ADR 0015). To set up a server and play, see Play online.

items.title: Code layout
items.text:
apps/client/src/
  Online/
    LobbyClient.cpp    the connection to the lobby: TLS with the key pinned, HELLO, the requests
    OnlineScenes.cpp   the Online menu and the list of the games
  Game/
    RemoteSession.cpp  a game online: the UDP session with the instance, inputs out, world in
    Interpolation.cpp  the world drawn 100 ms in the past, between the snapshots around that time
    Prediction.cpp     the ship of the player, moved at once by its inputs, then reconciled with the game

The client has one EventLoop for its network, polled by the game loop once per frame before the engine updates: everything network runs on the thread of the game, without locks.

items.title: From the menu to the game
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant C as Client
    participant M as Master
    participant I as Instance
    P->>C: Online, server and name, Connect
    C->>M: TCP, TLS (key of server.pub pinned), HELLO
    M->>C: WELCOME
    C->>M: LIST_GAMES
    M->>C: GAME_LIST: the lobby is shown
    P->>C: Create a game, or Join
    C->>M: CREATE_GAME or JOIN_GAME
    M->>C: GAME_JOINED (UDP port, session, keys)
    C->>I: CONNECT, then INPUT 60 times per second
    I->>C: ACCEPTED, then SNAPSHOT 30 times per second

The client goes through the master to get a game, then talks to its instance directly.

  1. Online asks for the server (host:port, the port 4242 by default, [::1]:4242 for IPv6) and the name of the player. An IP address is used as it is; a host name is looked up when Connect is pressed.
  2. The key of the server is read from server.pub, next to the executable (Generate the server keys). A server that does not hold the matching private key is refused during the handshake: "This is not the expected server".
  3. The lobby lists the games of the server: Create a game (for 4 players, named after the player), Join one, Refresh, Disconnect. Escape disconnects too.
  4. The game plays a RemoteSession with what GAME_JOINED gave. When it ends, by the pause menu or because the game ended, the client leaves it (LEAVE_GAME) and shows the list again.

Everything that goes wrong is shown in a toast: a server unreachable or not the expected one, a game full, a game that crashed, the connection lost. A lobby connection lost brings the player back to the main menu.

items.title: LobbyClient
items.text:
rtype::client::LobbyClient lobby(loop, server, pinned, "Pavel",
    {.onWelcome = [&](std::uint32_t player) { lobby.listGames(showList); },
     .onLeftGame = [&](const rtype::lobby::LeftGameMessage &left) { /* game over, crash, timeout */ },
     .onClosed = [&](const std::string &reason) { /* toast it */ }});
lobby.joinGame(id, [&](const rtype::client::LobbyClient::JoinResult &result) { /* GAME_JOINED or an error */ });
  • One callback per request. The master answers in order (lobby protocol), so each reply goes to the oldest request waiting. An ERROR goes to the callback of its request: describe(code) gives the message for the player.
  • LEFT_GAME is the reply to LEAVE_GAME, or a notification when the player did not ask (game over, crash, timeout): the latter goes to onLeftGame.
  • PING is sent after 10 seconds without sending anything, so that the master, which closes a connection silent for 30 seconds, keeps it.
  • A name is checked before connecting (std::invalid_argument): HELLO is written in a handler of the loop, where nothing may throw.

items.title: RemoteSession
items.text:
Direction What How often Client → instance INPUT: the input of the player, stamped with a tick, with the inputs of the 7 ticks before 60 per second, whatever the frame rate Instance → client SNAPSHOT parts and ENTITIES_DESTROYED, into a RemoteWorld 30 and as they come Instance → client PLAYER_JOINED, PLAYER_LEFT: the names of the players When they join and leave Instance → client GAME_OVER, DISCONNECT, or nothing for 5 seconds: the end Once
  • The tick of an input is the one at which the game should apply it (section 9.2 of the game protocol): the tick of the latest snapshot, plus the time since it came, plus the round-trip time measured by the session, plus 2 ticks of margin. It never goes back: the game ignores an input older than the last one.
  • takeSnapshots() gives, at every frame, the world of the interpolation: the GameSessionSystem draws it as it draws the offline world, and the entities move at the frame rate.
  • Pausing does nothing online: the game goes on, and the input sent under the pause menu is empty.
  • Leaving sends DISCONNECT to the game, when the session is destroyed.

items.title: Interpolation
items.text:
The snapshots come 30 times per second, some late, some lost; the client draws 60, 144 times per second. Drawing the newest snapshot moves the entities in jumps: still for 33 ms, then 20 units at once. Interpolation draws the world 100 ms in the past instead, between the two snapshots around that time (game protocol, 9.3):

snapshots received:   tick 40 ──────────── tick 42 ──────────── tick 44 (newest)
                                   ▲
                       drawn tick 41.3 = newest − 6 ticks (100 ms): 65 % of the way from 40 to 42
What happens What is drawn Snapshots on time Each entity between its positions in the two snapshots around the drawn tick A snapshot lost The same, between the snapshots that arrived: 4 ticks apart instead of 2 No snapshot for a while Each entity goes on with its velocity for 250 ms at most, then waits An entity created It appears when the drawn tick reaches its first snapshot An entity destroyed It disappears when the drawn tick reaches its destruction, not when ENTITIES_DESTROYED arrives 100 ms earlier

The drawn tick advances with the time of the frames, 60 ticks per second, and is nudged towards its target (newest tick − 6): a little faster when it falls behind, a little slower when it gets ahead, never backwards. The jitter of the snapshots and the drift between the clocks of the client and of the server are absorbed without a jump; after a pause of more than half a second (a window dragged, a debugger), it jumps to its target.

Interpolation is pure, without a clock nor a network: the RemoteSession gives it each world received (receive()), the destructions (destroyed()) and the time of each frame (advance()), and draws view().

items.title: Prediction
items.text:
The interpolation draws the world 100 ms in the past, on top of the round trip: fine for the others, whose keys the player does not see, but the ship of the player itself would answer late. Prediction moves it at once instead, and the game stays the one that decides:

  1. Each input sent moves the predicted ship by one tick, with game::moveShip(), the movement of the game itself: speed, diagonals, walls. The inputs are kept with their tick.
  2. Each snapshot says where the game had the ship at its tick, every input up to that tick applied. The prediction starts again from there and replays the inputs sent for the later ticks (reconciliation). When nothing was lost, it lands exactly where it was: no correction at all.
  3. A wrong guess (an input lost without its copies, something the game saw first) moves the prediction: the ship is not teleported, the gap is drawn and fades out in a few frames. A gap of more than 120 units (the ship came back elsewhere) is applied at once.
  4. Without a ship (destroyed, waiting to come back), nothing is predicted: the game decides.
inputs sent:   12  13  14  15  16   ◄── applied at once: the ship is drawn there
snapshot of 13 from the game ──► start from its position, replay 14, 15, 16 ──► the same place, if nothing was lost

game::moveShip() (libs/game/include/rtype/game/ShipMovement.hpp) is shared with the systems of the game, and a test checks that both give the same position to the bit, over a minute of random inputs against the walls. A rule that changes how a ship moves must change there, or every snapshot would correct the prediction.

Only the movement of the ship is predicted: its shots, the hits and its destruction are drawn as the game sends them, through the interpolation.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
tests/client_online.cpp (tag [online]) runs the client against a real master in the same process: the Lobby and the Games of r-type_server, with real instances.

  • the address of a server, and a message for every error of the master;
  • two clients welcomed, a game created, listed and joined, an error given to its request, a player who leaves;
  • a server without the pinned key refused, a server unreachable, a name refused before connecting;
  • two clients playing the same game, each moving its own ship and seeing the other's, with the names of the players, the world drawn at every frame behind the newest one, and inputs stamped ahead of the world;
  • a game that crashes reported to its player, who can create another one, and a game that stops ending the session of its player.

tests/client_interpolation.cpp (tag [interpolation]) plays a server sending 30 snapshots per second to a client drawing 144 frames per second: the world drawn 100 ms behind, an entity moving a little at every frame, with snapshots on time, irregular or lost; extrapolation then waiting without snapshots; entities appearing and disappearing when the drawn tick reaches them; a server clock running faster; a pause; and the drawn tick never going back.

tests/client_prediction.cpp (tag [prediction]) plays the client against the real rules, a Simulation with the InputBuffer of the server, the inputs and the snapshots delayed: never corrected when nothing is lost, nor when an INPUT is lost (the next ones carry its inputs); the ship answering before the game; the game ending where the prediction was; the walls; without redundancy, a lost input corrected smoothly; no ship, then back elsewhere; a correction too large applied at once; and the ticks skipped when stamping.

./build/bin/rtype_tests "[online]"
./build/bin/rtype_tests "[interpolation]"
./build/bin/rtype_tests "[prediction]"

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• The shots are not predicted: they leave a round trip and 100 ms after Fire is pressed. Predicting them means drawing a shot before the game creates it, then matching it with the one it sends.
  • The player sees the others 100 ms in the past and its own ship in the present: a Bydo shot can seem to miss and still hit, as in every game that predicts.
  • The names of the players are known (RemoteSession::names()) but not shown in the HUD yet.
  • One server at a time, typed by hand: no list of servers, no address remembered.

items.title: ECS
items.text:
libs/ecs (rtype::ecs) is the Entity Component System everything else is built on: the client's world and interface (ADR 0007), the physics and the rules of the game. It is shared with the server, so it depends on nothing, not even raylib.

The ECS only knows entities, components and systems, plus a hierarchy between entities. Game notions (scenes, events, drawing, input) belong to the engine (libs/engine), built on top of it: see Scenes and interface. How the components are stored is decided in ADR 0006.

items.title: Where things are
items.text:
libs/ecs/include/rtype/ecs/
  Ecs.hpp                       Ecs: entities, components, systems, update, deferred actions
  Entity/Entity.hpp             entity_t, EntityRef
  Component/ComponentCache.hpp  ComponentCache<T>: the components of one type
  Component/ComponentCaches.hpp ComponentCaches: one cache per type
  Component/ICache.hpp          type-erased base of the caches
  System/System.hpp             System: base class of the systems
  Hierarchy.hpp                 Position, LocalPosition, Parent, Hidden, attach(), isHidden(), TransformSystem

Include "rtype/ecs/Ecs.hpp" for the core, and "rtype/ecs/Hierarchy.hpp" for the hierarchy.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Ecs
        direction TB
        Entities["Entities<br/>alive flags, generations, free ids"]
        Caches["ComponentCaches<br/>type → ComponentCache<T>"]
        Systems["Systems<br/>in registration order"]
        Deferred["Deferred actions"]
    end
    Caches --> Position["ComponentCache<Position><br/>slot per entity id"]
    Caches --> Velocity["ComponentCache<Velocity><br/>slot per entity id"]
    Systems -. "keep references to" .-> Position
    Systems -. "keep references to" .-> Velocity

An entity is an index: its components are the slots at that index in every cache. Systems hold references to the caches they use.

items.title: Entities
items.text:
An entity is only an id, entity_t (std::uint32_t): the index of its components in every cache.

Call Effect ecs.createEntity() A new entity, without components. Reuses the id of the last destroyed entity, if any. ecs.destroyEntity(entity) Removes all its components, destroys its children recursively (see Hierarchy) and frees its id. Does nothing on a dead entity. ecs.isAlive(entity) Whether the id currently designates an entity.

items.title: Entity references
items.text:
Because ids are reused, an entity_t kept somewhere may end up designating another entity. An EntityRef (ecs.ref(entity)) adds a generation, increased every time the id is freed: once the entity is destroyed, ecs.isAlive(reference) is false, even if its id was given to a new entity.

struct Target {
    EntityRef entity;   // not entity_t
};

const Target &target = ecs.getComponent<Target>(missile);
if (ecs.isAlive(target.entity)) {
    aimAt(target.entity.id);
}

Keep an EntityRef, never an entity_t, in a component or in any object that outlives the current update.

items.title: Components
items.text:
A component is plain data attached to an entity: a struct with default values, no logic, no pointer to another entity (use an EntityRef). An empty struct is a tag, such as Hidden.

Call Effect ecs.addComponent<T>(entity, args...) Builds a T from args in the entity's slot and returns it. Replaces the component the entity already has. ecs.removeComponent<T>(entity) Empties the slot. Does nothing if the entity has no T. ecs.hasComponent<T>(entity) Whether the entity has a T. ecs.getComponent<T>(entity) The entity's T. The entity must have one: check with hasComponent() first. ecs.cache<T>() The ComponentCache<T>, to go through every entity that has a T.

These calls look the type up in a hash map every time: they are meant for building entities and for tests. A system looks its caches up once, in its constructor (see Systems).

items.title: Caches
items.text:
ComponentCache<T> is a std::vector<std::optional<T>> indexed by the entity id. The cache of a type is created on first use; emplace, erase, has, get and size are what systems use.

  • size() is one past the highest id that ever had a T: it never shrinks, and slots below it may be empty.
  • A reference to a cache stays valid as long as the Ecs lives.
  • A reference to a component (T &) is invalidated when a T is added to an entity whose id is beyond size(): the vector grows and moves its slots. Do not keep one across an addComponent<T>().

items.title: Where to put them
items.text: Components used by the client and the server (positions, velocities, health) go in a library both link: libs/ecs for the hierarchy, libs/physics for movement and collisions, libs/game for the rules. Never in libs/engine, which depends on raylib and is not linked by the server.

items.title: Systems
items.text:
A system derives from rtype::ecs::System. It gets the caches of the components it uses with use<T>(caches) in its constructor and keeps the references, then goes through the entity ids in update():

class DamageSystem : public System
{
    ComponentCache<Health> &_health;
    ComponentCache<Hit> &_hits;

public:
    explicit DamageSystem(ComponentCaches &caches) : _health(use<Health>(caches)), _hits(use<Hit>(caches)) {}

    void update(float /*elapsed*/) override
    {
        for (entity_t entity = 0; entity < _hits.size(); ++entity) {
            if (_hits.has(entity) && _health.has(entity)) {
                _health.get(entity).points -= _hits.get(entity).damage;
            }
        }
    }
};
  • use<T>() also records the type: componentTypes() lists the components a system uses.
  • update(float elapsed) receives the time since the previous update, in seconds. Systems never read a clock, so that the tests and the server control time.
  • Iterate over the rarest component's cache, and test the others with has().
  • A system that needs something else (the Ecs to create entities, the scenes, the rules) takes it by reference in its constructor, after the caches.

ecs.registerSystem<S>(args...) builds S(caches, args...), keeps ownership of it and returns a reference. Systems are never removed: set enabled = false to skip one (the engine's events do this, see ADR 0008).

A step-by-step example, with a test: How to write a system.

items.title: An update
items.text:
ecs.update(elapsed) runs, in order:

  1. every enabled system, in registration order, with the same elapsed;
  2. the deferred actions, in the order they were deferred. An action may defer another one: they run until none is left.

The registration order is therefore the order of the frame: register the systems that move entities before the ones that read positions. The order of the client is in The systems and their order.

items.title: Deferred actions
items.text:
ecs.defer(action) runs action after the systems of the current update, or after those of the next update when called outside of one. It is how a system changes the world while it goes through it:

if (_health.get(entity).points <= 0) {
    _ecs.defer([this, entity] { spawnExplosion(_ecs, entity); });
}

items.title: What a system may do while it iterates
items.text: Change During the loop Read or write components of existing entities Safe. removeComponent(), destroyEntity() Safe: slots are only emptied, nothing moves. createEntity() then addComponent() Defer it: the caches may grow, which moves their components under the systems reading them. addComponent() of a type some system iterates or holds a reference to Defer it, for the same reason.

items.title: Hierarchy
items.text:
Hierarchy.hpp attaches entities to others: the Force to the ship, a turret to a boss, a button to its panel.

Component Meaning Position Position in the world, in game units. The physics and the game move it; for an entity with a parent, the TransformSystem computes it. Parent The entity is attached to another one (EntityRef). LocalPosition Position relative to the parent. Hidden Hides the entity and its children, without destroying them. 
attach(ecs, force, ship, {64.0f, 0.0f});   // the Force follows the ship, 64 units in front of it

attach() gives the child a Parent and a LocalPosition, and a Position if it has none.

  • Following: the TransformSystem sets Position = position of the parent + LocalPosition for every entity with the three components, parents first whatever their ids. Register it after the systems that move entities and before the ones that use positions (collisions, rendering). Move a child through its LocalPosition: its Position is overwritten.
  • Hiding: isHidden(ecs, entity) is true if the entity or one of its ancestors has Hidden. A closed dropdown can hide its options this way. Systems that draw or handle input check it; the ECS itself does not.
  • Destroying: ecs.destroyEntity(boss) also destroys its turrets, recursively. A child never outlives its parent with a dangling reference.
  • Detaching: remove the Parent (and the LocalPosition): the entity keeps its last Position and is moved like any other one from then on.
  • Loops: a hierarchy deeper than 64 levels is taken for a loop (an entity being its own ancestor) and its positions stop being computed there, instead of hanging the game.

The TransformSystem recomputes every chain from its root, and destroying an entity scans the Parent cache for its children. Both are cheap with the shallow hierarchies of the game.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
They follow from ADR 0006, and suit a few hundred entities:

  • Every system visits every slot up to the highest id of its cache, empty or not.
  • A rare component still takes one slot per entity id.
  • There are no queries over several components and no per-system entity lists: each system tests has().
  • There is no locking: an Ecs is used by one thread at a time. Each game on the server is its own process with its own Ecs (ADR 0013).

If profiling shows a problem, a sparse set for some types or per-system entity lists can be added behind the same cache interface, with a new ADR.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
File Tag Covers tests/ecs.cpp [ecs] Caches, recycled ids, systems (filtering, enabled, destroying while iterating, componentTypes()). tests/ecs_world.cpp [ecs][world] Elapsed time, entity references, deferred actions, hierarchy. 
./build/bin/rtype_tests "[ecs]"

items.title: Game
items.text:
The game library (libs/game, namespace rtype::game) holds the rules of the R-Type: the players, their ships and projectiles, and later the Bydos and the waves. It is used by the server instances, which run the games online, and by the client offline, in its LocalSession (A game in the client) (ADR 0015): the rules are written once, and a Bydo behaves the same offline and online.

The Simulation depends on the ECS, the physics and the log only: no window, no sound, no network. The messages of the game protocol are written with the serialization of libs/network (Writer, Reader), a private dependency: the rules never see it.

items.title: A game in three calls
items.text:
A Simulation is one game. It takes the inputs of the players, steps the world one tick at a time, and gives a snapshot of it:

#include "rtype/game/Game.hpp"

rtype::game::Simulation simulation;
simulation.addPlayer(0); // slots 0 to 3

// Every tick, 60 times per second
simulation.setInput(0, input);                               // the controls of player 0
simulation.step();                                           // exactly 1/60 s of game
const rtype::game::Snapshot &world = simulation.snapshot();  // what to draw

flowchart LR
    Inputs["PlayerInput<br/>per slot"] --> Sim
    subgraph Sim["Simulation"]
        direction TB
        Ecs["its own ECS<br/>ships, shots..."]
        Systems["the systems of the rules"]
    end
    Sim --> Snapshot["Snapshot<br/>players, entities, events"]

The simulation turns the inputs of the players into a snapshot of the world, one tick at a time.

items.title: Who calls step()
items.text:
The simulation never reads a clock: whoever uses it decides when a tick passes. That is what makes a game the same on every machine, and the tests exact.

Where Who calls step() Client offline LocalSession::update(elapsed) adds up the frame times and steps once per 1/60 s, like PhysicsStep Server instance The simulation thread, with a Timer at 60 Hz Tests A loop: 600 steps are 10 seconds of game, computed in a few milliseconds

The same inputs, in the same order, give the same snapshots, bit for bit: a test checks it over 20 seconds of a game with three players. Keep it that way: no clock, no std::rand(), no iteration over an std::unordered_map in the rules; a random generator, when the Bydos need one, is seeded by the game.

items.title: Inputs
items.text:
PlayerInput is the byte of the protocol (game protocol): one bit per control. It is data, not a device: libs/game does not use libs/input, which reads the keyboard and the gamepads through raylib and only exists in the client. The client makes the PlayerInput from the virtual gamepad of the engine (rtype::engine::Controls, fed by libs/input with the bindings of the player), once per tick; the server receives it in INPUT messages.

Keyboard, gamepads ─► libs/input ─► engine::Controls ─► GameSessionSystem ─► game::PlayerInput ─► Simulation
   (raylib)          (bindings)    (virtual gamepad)       (client)           (one byte)        (client or server)

rtype::game::PlayerInput input;
input.set(rtype::game::PlayerInput::Up, controls.isDown(rtype::engine::Control::Up));
input.set(rtype::game::PlayerInput::Fire, controls.isDown(rtype::engine::Control::FaceDown));

input.direction();                   // {x, y}, each -1, 0 or 1: up and down together cancel
rtype::game::PlayerInput::fromByte(b); // from the network: the reserved bits are dropped

An input stays until the next setInput(): a player who holds Right keeps moving.

items.title: Snapshots
items.text:
A Snapshot is the world at the end of a tick, with the fields of the SNAPSHOT message (game protocol), plus the events of the tick:

Field Content tick The tick it describes, 1 after the first step players Slot, lives and score of each player, by slot entities Each entity: id, kind, owner, position (its centre), velocity, health, flags, by id destroyed The entities destroyed since the previous snapshot, with the cause (removed, or killed: an explosion) waveStarted, gameOver A wave started, the game ended
  • Ids are never reused within a game (NetworkId, unlike the ids of the ECS): a client keeps them to recognize its entities from one snapshot to the next.
  • Positions are floats in game units; the network encodes them in eighths of a unit. Every entity stays in the area the protocol can encode (PositionLimit): what leaves the game area is removed.
  • An entity in destroyed is no longer in entities.

items.title: What the rules do now
items.text:
Rule Where Numbers (Rules) A ship appears on the left, one height per slot spawnPlayerShip() — It moves with the input, as fast in diagonal PlayerControlSystem, with shipVelocity() (ShipMovement.hpp, shared with the prediction of the client) shipSpeed 600 units/s It stays entirely in the 1920 × 1080 area physics::BoundsSystem, ConfinedToBounds shipHalfWidth, shipHalfHeight Fire held shoots from its nose PlayerControlSystem, spawnPlayerShot() fireInterval 10 ticks (6 per second), shotSpeed 1500 units/s What leaves the area is removed AreaSystem, LeavesArea areaMargin 128 units A player who leaves takes its ship away Simulation::removePlayer() — A Bydo shot that touches a ship destroys it, the player loses a life and gets a new ship, invulnerable for a while CombatSystem respawnDelay 90 ticks, invulnerableTicks 120 Every player out of lives ends the game (defeat) CombatSystem lives 3

The Bydos, the waves and the score come later. Nothing makes a Bydo shot yet: the hit is there for the projectiles to use.

A tick runs the systems in this order: PlayerControlSystem (inputs), WeaponSystem (the weapons), ProjectileSystem (the velocity of the projectiles), physics::MovementSystem (movement), physics::BoundsSystem (the walls), CombatSystem (the hits, the lives), AreaSystem (what left), then the snapshot is taken.

items.title: Projectiles
items.text:
A kind of projectile is data, a ProjectileDefinition, so that a new one is added without writing a system. A ProjectileRegistry keeps the definitions by id, and spawnProjectile() makes an entity from one.

flowchart LR
    Cat["ProjectileCategory"] --> Def["ProjectileDefinition<br/>id · model · category · collider"]
    Def -- "addDefinition()" --> Reg["ProjectileRegistry<br/>GameContext::projectiles"]
    Reg -- "getDefinition(id)" --> Spawn["spawnProjectile()"]
    Spawn --> Ent["entity: Projectile · Velocity · Collider<br/>LeavesArea · NetworkId · Kind · Owner · Position"]

The life of a projectile, from the shot to its disappearance:

sequenceDiagram
    participant Sys as A system (PlayerControlSystem...)
    participant Reg as ProjectileRegistry
    participant Ecs as ECS
    participant Tick as Systems of the tick
    participant Cli as Client

    Sys->>Ecs: defer(spawnProjectile(id, owner, position, velocity))
    Note over Sys,Ecs: after the systems of the tick, so the caches are not grown while read
    Ecs->>Reg: getDefinition(id)
    Reg-->>Ecs: model, category, collider
    Ecs->>Ecs: new entity (Projectile, Velocity, Collider, LeavesArea, NetworkId, Kind, Owner, Position)
    loop every tick
        Tick->>Ecs: MovementSystem moves it
        Tick->>Ecs: CombatSystem tests the hits
    end
    Tick->>Ecs: AreaSystem removes it once out of the area (DestroyCause::Removed)
    Ecs-->>Cli: Snapshot: its Kind, position and velocity; then `destroyed`

The data of a definition and where each one ends up:

classDiagram
    class ProjectileCategory {
        <<enum class>>
        Bullet
        Missile
        Laser
        Plasma
    }
    class ProjectileDefinition {
        string id
        string model
        ProjectileCategory category
        Collider collider
    }
    class ProjectileRegistry {
        addDefinition(definition)
        hasDefinition(id)
        getDefinition(id)
    }
    class Projectile {
        <<component>>
        ProjectileCategory category
        string model
    }
    ProjectileDefinition --> ProjectileCategory
    ProjectileRegistry "1" o-- "*" ProjectileDefinition
    ProjectileDefinition ..> Projectile : category and model copied
    ProjectileDefinition ..> Collider : collider copied to the entity
Attribute Type Role id std::string Unique name in the registry, how the systems and the configuration files designate it model std::string Path of the 3D model. The game only carries it: it has no raylib, the client loads it category ProjectileCategory Bullet, Missile, Laser, Plasma: what the rules that depend on the behavior key on collider physics::Collider The shape that hits what it meets, centred on the projectile 
simulation.context().projectiles.addDefinition(
    {"pulse", "models/pulse.glb", ProjectileCategory::Plasma,
     physics::Collider{physics::Aabb{{}, {8.0f, 4.0f, 0.0f}}, {}, false}});

spawnProjectile(ecs, context, "pulse", slot, x, y, 1500.0f, 0.0f); // from a system, through Ecs::defer()
  • The behavior of a category is in functions (Projectile/ProjectileBehavior.hpp), since a C++ enum class has no methods: one switch per question, so a new category is a new case in each.
Function Answers Bullet Missile Laser Plasma getProjectileVelocity(category, launch, age, rules) How it moves, each tick (ProjectileSystem) Straight Speeds up (missileBoostPerTick, missileMaxBoost) Straight Zigzags (plasmaZigzagSpeed, plasmaZigzagInterval) getProjectileSounds(category) The paths of its sounds: spawn, move, vanish (left the area), impact (hit). All empty: no sound file yet

The sounds are paths: the game has no audio, the client plays them. Nothing sends the events (spawn, vanish, impact) to the client yet, like the model, they wait for a decision on the protocol. - The velocity is not in the definition: the caller gives it at each shot, so that a weapon decides how fast its projectile goes; it is kept as Projectile::launch, and the category moves the projectile from it. spawnProjectile() throws std::out_of_range for an unknown id. - The registry is an std::unordered_map, only looked up by id, never iterated: this does not break the determinism above. Iterating it in the rules would. - The clients see an EntityKind only: a projectile with an owner is a PlayerShot, without one a BydoShot. The model and the category are not in the snapshot yet, so the client cannot draw them: it needs a decision on the protocol. - spawnPlayerShot() does not use this system yet.

ADR 0018 plans to load the definitions from Lua files; the registry is what the loader will fill.

items.title: Weapons
items.text:
A kind of weapon is data too, a WeaponDefinition, kept by id in a WeaponRegistry (GameContext::weapons). Durations are in ticks, distances in game units.

Field Type What it is projectile std::string The ammunition: the id of a ProjectileDefinition mechanic ProjectileCategory The firing mechanic: how its projectiles move (replaces the category of the projectile) projectileSpeed float Speed the projectiles leave with, to the right fireInterval ticks Between two shots while Fire is held (not 0) range float Distance a projectile flies before it vanishes, 0 for no limit magazineSize shots Ammunition capacity, InfiniteAmmo (0) for a weapon that never runs out reloadTicks ticks Reload time of an empty magazine 
flowchart LR
    Proj["ProjectileDefinition<br/>id · model · category · collider"] -- "projectile (id)" --> Def
    Cat["ProjectileCategory"] -- "mechanic" --> Def
    Def["WeaponDefinition<br/>id · projectile · mechanic · projectileSpeed<br/>fireInterval · range · magazineSize · reloadTicks"]
    Def -- "addDefinition()" --> Reg["WeaponRegistry<br/>GameContext::weapons"]
    Reg -- "equipWeapon()" --> Armed["Armed on the ship<br/>weapon · cooldown · ammo · reloadLeft"]
    Armed -- "WeaponSystem, Fire held" --> Shot["spawnWeaponShot()"]
    Reg -- "getDefinition(id)" --> Shot
    Proj -- "spawnProjectile()" --> Shot
    Shot --> Ent["Projectile entity<br/>category = mechanic · range · travelled"]
    Ent -- "ProjectileSystem: travelled ≥ range" --> Gone["removed (DestroyCause::Removed)"]

The state of the magazine, run by the WeaponSystem at each tick (with magazineSize not InfiniteAmmo):

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Ready: equipWeapon() (full magazine)
    Ready --> Cooldown: Fire held, one round spent<br/>cooldown = fireInterval
    Cooldown --> Ready: cooldown reaches 0
    Ready --> Reloading: last round spent<br/>reloadLeft = reloadTicks
    Reloading --> Ready: reloadLeft reaches 0<br/>ammo = magazineSize
simulation.context().weapons.addDefinition({"blaster", "pulse", ProjectileCategory::Laser, 1000.0f, 5, 600.0f, 8, 90});
equipWeapon(ecs, context, ship, "blaster"); // gives the ship an Armed component
  • WeaponSystem runs each Armed ship: it counts the cooldown down, spends a round per shot, reloads on its own when the magazine is empty (no shot meanwhile) and fires through spawnWeaponShot() (deferred).
  • A ship without Armed keeps the default shots of PlayerControlSystem (Rules::fireInterval).
  • The range is checked by ProjectileSystem on the distance flown (Projectile::travelled); a projectile past it is removed with DestroyCause::Removed.

items.title: Ships
items.text:
A kind of ship is data, a ShipDefinition, kept by id in a ShipRegistry (GameContext::ships): what a ship looks and sounds like, whoever flies it. The game only carries the paths of the model and of the sounds: it has no window and no audio, the client loads and plays them. An empty sound path means no sound.

Field Type What it is model std::string Path of the 3D model (required) sounds.move std::string Played while it moves sounds.destruction std::string Played when it is destroyed sounds.collision std::string Played when it collides with something 
simulation.context().ships.addDefinition({"bydo_scout", "models/bydo_scout.glb",
                                          {"sounds/scout_move.ogg", "sounds/scout_destruction.ogg",
                                           "sounds/scout_collision.ogg"}});

addDefinition() throws std::invalid_argument for an empty or taken id or no model; getDefinition() throws std::out_of_range for an unknown id.

items.title: Enemies
items.text:
A kind of enemy is data as well, an EnemyDefinition, kept by id in an EnemyRegistry (GameContext::enemies). Speeds are in game units per second. Nothing makes an enemy appear in a game yet: the registry is the base the spawning and the waves will read.

Field Type What it is ship std::string The id of a ShipDefinition: its model and its sounds health std::uint8_t Hit points it starts with, like the Health component (not 0) speed float Top speed (above 0) acceleration float Speed gained per second until the top speed, in units/s² (0 or more) weapon std::string The id of a WeaponDefinition 
flowchart LR
    Lua["Lua files<br/>(ADR 0018, later)"] -.-> Def
    Def["EnemyDefinition<br/>id · ship · health · speed · acceleration · weapon"]
    Def -- "addDefinition()<br/>checked: id, ship, health, speed, acceleration, weapon" --> Reg["EnemyRegistry<br/>GameContext::enemies"]
    Def -- "ship (id)" --> SDef["ShipDefinition<br/>id · model · sounds (move · destruction · collision)"]
    SDef -- "addDefinition()" --> SReg["ShipRegistry<br/>GameContext::ships"]
    Def -- "weapon (id)" --> WDef["WeaponDefinition"]
    WDef -- "addDefinition()" --> WReg["WeaponRegistry<br/>GameContext::weapons"]
    Reg -. "getDefinition(id)" .-> Spawn["spawning, waves<br/>(later)"]
    SReg -. "model, sounds" .-> Spawn
    WReg -. "equipWeapon()" .-> Spawn

Solid arrows exist today; dotted ones are what will come next.

simulation.context().enemies.addDefinition({"bydo_scout", "bydo_scout", 30, 240.0f, 720.0f, "blaster"});
  • addDefinition() throws std::invalid_argument for an empty or taken id, no ship, no health, no weapon, a speed not above 0 or a negative acceleration; getDefinition() throws std::out_of_range for an unknown id.
  • The ship and the weapon are not looked up when the enemy is added, so that the registries can be filled in any order; an unknown one fails when the enemy is made (getDefinition(), equipWeapon()).
  • ADR 0018 plans to load the definitions from Lua files, like the weapons.

items.title: Waves
items.text:
A wave is a group of enemies that appear one after the other. Like the enemies, it is data: a WaveDefinition, kept by name in a WaveRegistry (GameContext::waves). Nothing runs a wave yet: the registry is what the spawning will read.

Field Type What it is name std::string Unique name in the registry label std::string Short text shown to the players description std::string Longer text quantity std::uint16_t How many enemies (above 0) spawnInterval float Seconds between two enemies (0 or more; 0 = all at once) placement WavePlacement Manual or Random, one mode per wave spawns std::vector<WaveSpawn> Manual only: each enemy (enemy, x, y), in the order they appear enemy std::string Random only: the id of the EnemyDefinition of every enemy area WaveArea Random only: the rectangle (minX, maxX, minY, maxY) where they appear 
flowchart LR
    Def["WaveDefinition<br/>name · label · description · quantity · spawnInterval · placement"]
    Def -- "placement = Manual" --> Spawns["spawns: WaveSpawn[]<br/>enemy · x · y, one per enemy"]
    Def -- "placement = Random" --> Rand["enemy (id) + area: WaveArea<br/>minX · maxX · minY · maxY"]
    Def -- "addDefinition(wave, enemies)<br/>checked: name, quantity, interval, placement, area, known enemies" --> Reg["WaveRegistry<br/>GameContext::waves"]
    Spawns -- "enemy (id)" --> EDef["EnemyDefinition"]
    Rand -- "enemy (id)" --> EDef
    EDef -- "addDefinition()" --> EReg["EnemyRegistry<br/>GameContext::enemies"]
    EReg -. "hasDefinition(id)<br/>when the wave is added" .-> Reg
    Reg -. "getDefinition(name)" .-> Run["running a wave<br/>(later)"]

Solid arrows exist today; dotted ones are the checks made when a wave is added and what will come next.

The default area is a band just past the right edge of the game area (x from GameWidth to GameWidth + 100, the whole height), so that enemies come in from the side. A wave does not mix manual and random enemies: for that, play two waves one after the other.

auto &context = simulation.context();
context.waves.addDefinition(
    {"scouts_random", "Scouts", "Five scouts from the right", 5, 0.5f, WavePlacement::Random, {}, "bydo_scout"},
    context.enemies);
context.waves.addDefinition({"scouts_line", "Scout line", "", 2, 0.0f, WavePlacement::Manual,
                             {{"bydo_scout", 2000.0f, 200.0f}, {"bydo_scout", 2000.0f, 800.0f}}},
                            context.enemies);
  • addDefinition() needs the EnemyRegistry: unlike the enemies, the waves check that every enemy they name is known, so the enemies are filled first.
  • It throws std::invalid_argument for an empty or taken name, a quantity of 0, a negative interval, a Manual wave whose spawns do not number quantity or that sets enemy, a Random wave without enemy or with spawns, an unknown enemy, or an empty area (min above max). getDefinition() throws std::out_of_range for an unknown name.

items.title: Adding gameplay
items.text:
The rules are components and systems on the ECS, like the physics, so that anyone can add some:

  1. A component in Component/Components.hpp: plain data, struct Charge { std::uint32_t ticks = 0; };.
  2. A kind of entity, if the clients must draw it: a value in EntityKind (Snapshot.hpp) and in the table of the protocol, in the range of its family; then a spawn...() function in Entities.hpp, which gives it a NetworkId, its Kind, its Owner and its Position.
  3. A system in System/: it receives the caches, the Ecs and the GameContext (rules, tick, players and their inputs, events), and is registered in the constructor of Simulation, at its place in the tick.
  4. The numbers in Rules, so that they can be tuned in one place, and the tests use their own.
  5. A test in tests/game_simulation.cpp: inputs in, snapshot checked.

Inside a system, create and destroy entities through ecs.defer(): changing the world while a system goes through the caches is not safe. destroyEntity(ecs, context, entity, cause) destroys an entity and records it for the snapshot.

items.title: Messages
items.text:
Messages.hpp turns the messages of a game session into payloads and back, as the game protocol says. The sessions of libs/network (ClientSession, SessionHost) carry them with their type (message_type::Snapshot...); the server and the client share this one implementation.

Message Type Direction Struct ACCEPTED 0x02 Game → Client AcceptedMessage: slot, tick rate, tick PLAYER_JOINED 0x04 Game → Client PlayerJoinedMessage: slot, player id, name PLAYER_LEFT 0x05 Game → Client PlayerLeftMessage: slot, reason INPUT 0x40 Client → Game InputMessage: tick, inputs newest first SNAPSHOT 0x80 Game → Client SnapshotPart: tick, last input, part, players, entities ENTITIES_DESTROYED 0x81 Game → Client EntitiesDestroyedMessage: tick, ids and causes WAVE_STARTED 0x82 Game → Client WaveStartedMessage GAME_OVER 0x83 Game → Client GameOverMessage 
// Game, once per client, every 2 ticks
for (const rtype::game::SnapshotPart &part : rtype::game::splitSnapshot(simulation.snapshot(), lastInput)) {
    host.send(session, rtype::game::message_type::Snapshot, rtype::game::encode(part),
              rtype::network::Delivery::Unreliable);
}
for (const auto &message : rtype::game::destroyedMessages(simulation.snapshot())) {
    host.send(session, rtype::game::message_type::EntitiesDestroyed, rtype::game::encode(message),
              rtype::network::Delivery::Reliable);
}

// Client, in the message handler of its ClientSession
if (type == rtype::game::message_type::Snapshot) {
    if (const auto part = rtype::game::decodeSnapshotPart(payload)) {
        world.apply(*part);
    }
}
  • encode() has one overload per message. A value the protocol forbids (a slot above 3, no input, an id of 0, a part that does not fit in a datagram) is a bug of the sender: it throws.
  • decode...() never throws: it gives nothing for every case the protocol calls malformed, and for bytes left after the last field, and the receiver drops the message. Unknown reasons, causes and outcomes are read as the protocol says (Quit, Removed, Defeat), and reserved bits are dropped. The decoders are pure, with no state: they can be fuzzed.
  • Positions and velocities are floats in the structs, and eighths of a unit on the network: rounded to the nearest eighth, and kept within what an i16 holds (−4096 to 4095.875).
  • splitSnapshot() cuts a Snapshot in parts that fit in a datagram, each with the tick and the players: 69 entities per part with four players (maxEntitiesPerPart()), 16 parts at most. destroyedMessages() does the same for the destroyed entities: 228 per message.
  • Unknown kinds are decoded, so that a newer game can add some: isKnown() tells the client to skip them.

items.title: The world of a client
items.text:
RemoteWorld keeps the world as a client knows it from those messages, with the rules of the protocol: snapshots can be lost, late or out of order, and destructions are reliable.

rtype::game::RemoteWorld world;
world.apply(part);                                // a SNAPSHOT part
for (const auto &removed : world.apply(message)) { // an ENTITIES_DESTROYED
    // removed.last: where it was, for an explosion when removed.cause is Killed
}
for (const auto &[id, entity] : world.entities()) { /* draw it */ }
What arrives What the world does A part older than the latest applied Ignored (apply() gives false); the other parts of the latest tick still apply An entity in a part Created, or updated An entity missing from a part Kept: its part may have been lost ENTITIES_DESTROYED The entities are removed and given back with their last state; their ids are remembered until the snapshots reach the tick of their destruction, so that an older part cannot bring them back A kind it does not know Skipped

It keeps the latest state only; drawing 100 ms in the past and interpolating between snapshots come on top of it, in the client. Like the Simulation, it has no clock and no network.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
The tests in tests/game_simulation.cpp (tag [game]) step simulations and check their snapshots: the inputs, the players added and removed, the movement and its speed in diagonal, the walls, the shots and their interval, shots removed once out of the area with ids never given again, the same game twice with the same inputs, and an hour of random inputs with four players keeping every entity in the range of the protocol.

The tests in tests/game_messages.cpp (tags [messages] and [world]) check the bytes of the example of the specification, the round trip of every message, the rounding and the limits of positions, every malformed case, the encoders refusing forbidden values, random bytes that never crash a decoder, the splitting of snapshots and destructions into datagrams, the rules of RemoteWorld, and a whole game of four players sent through the messages, where the client ends with the world of the game.

./build/bin/rtype_tests "[game]"

items.title: Input
items.text:
The input library (libs/input, namespace rtype::input) turns the keyboard and gamepads into game actions. The game never asks whether a key is held, only whether an action is active:

if (controls.wasPressed(Action::Shoot)) { ... }

This keeps raylib out of the game code, lets players change their controls, makes the input logic testable without a keyboard, and gives the client exactly what it sends to the server: what the player wants to do, not which key they pressed.

items.title: Layers
items.text:
flowchart TB
    Game["Client code<br/>controls.isActive(Action::MoveUp)"] --> Map["ActionMap#lt;Action#gt;<br/>actions ↔ bindings"]
    Map --> Source["InputSource<br/>(interface)"]
    Source --> Devices["Devices<br/>keyboard and gamepads (raylib)"]
    Source --> Fake["FakeInput<br/>unit tests"]
    Source -.-> VR["VR controllers<br/>(planned)"]

The client reads actions from an ActionMap, which queries an InputSource; the real devices, the tests and future VR controllers are interchangeable sources.

Class / header Role Keys.hpp The Key, GamepadButton and GamepadAxis enums. InputSource Interface answering "is this key or button held, where is this stick?". Devices The InputSource reading the real keyboard and gamepads. The only file that uses raylib. Binding One physical input: a key, a gamepad button, or one direction of a stick or trigger. ActionMap<Action> Binds each action to its inputs, and updates the actions once per frame. TextInput The text of an input field, edited with the typed characters and Backspace.

The library does not know the actions of R-Type: the client defines them, in apps/client/src/Controls.hpp, and ActionMap is a template over their type.

items.title: Keys and buttons
items.text:
Keys are physical positions, named after a US (QWERTY) keyboard. Key::W is the key left of E, labelled Z on a French (AZERTY) keyboard: controls defined as WASD are ZQSD on AZERTY without any change.

Gamepad buttons are named after their position, so that they mean the same on every brand:

GamepadButton Xbox PlayStation FaceDown A Cross FaceRight B Circle FaceLeft X Square FaceUp Y Triangle LeftBumper / RightBumper LB / RB L1 / R1 LeftTrigger / RightTrigger LT / RT L2 / R2 Select / Start View / Menu Share / Options

Axes go from -1 to 1 for the sticks (left and up are negative, like screen coordinates) and from 0 to 1 for the triggers. A disconnected gamepad reads as released.

items.title: Bindings
items.text:
A Binding is created with one of four functions:

Binding::key(Key::Space)
Binding::gamepadButton(GamepadButton::FaceDown)                     // first gamepad by default
Binding::gamepadAxis(GamepadAxis::LeftY, AxisDirection::Negative)   // left stick pushed up
Binding::mouseButton(MouseButton::Left)

An axis binding only uses one half of the axis: the left stick pushed up triggers MoveUp, pushed down triggers MoveDown. Each binding gives a strength between 0 and 1:

  • a key, a gamepad button or a mouse button gives 0 or 1;
  • an axis gives 0 inside the dead zone, then grows progressively up to 1.

The dead zone (25% of the range by default, see ActionMap::setDeadZone()) ignores sticks that do not come back exactly to the centre. Outside of it, the remaining range is scaled back to 0..1, so that the movement starts smoothly instead of jumping when the stick leaves the dead zone:

Stick position Strength 0.2 0 (inside the dead zone) 0.625 0.5 1 1

items.title: Binding actions
items.text:
Each action can have any number of bindings; adding the same one twice has no effect.

enum class Action { MoveUp, Shoot };

ActionMap<Action> controls;
controls.bind(Action::Shoot, Binding::key(Key::Space));
controls.bind(Action::Shoot, Binding::gamepadButton(GamepadButton::FaceDown));

unbind(), clear() and bindings() change and list the bindings at any time, which is what an options menu needs to let players choose their own controls.

items.title: Reading actions
items.text:
update() reads the input source and updates every action. It is called once per frame, before reading the actions, which keep the state read there until the next update: all the code of a frame sees the same state. It also takes the time elapsed since the previous frame, used to repeat held actions and to measure how long they are held.

controls.update(devices, window.frameTime());

const float up = controls.strength(Action::MoveUp);   // 0..1, for analog movement
if (controls.wasPressed(Action::Shoot)) { fire(); }
Function True when Typical use isActive(action) The action is held. Moving, continuous fire. wasPressed(action) The action started at the last update (one frame only). Firing once per press, validating a menu. wasReleased(action) The action stopped at the last update (one frame only). Charged shot released. wasRepeated(action) The action was pressed, or is held and repeats (see below). Moving in a menu, auto-fire. strength(action) Returns 0..1: the strongest of its bindings. Analog movement. heldDuration(action) Returns how long the action has been held, in seconds. Charged shot.

The strength of an action is the maximum of its bindings, not their sum: holding the up arrow and the stick at the same time does not move faster.

items.title: Repeating and holding
items.text:
Holding Down in a menu should move the selection once, then keep moving it after a short delay, like in a text editor. wasRepeated() gives this behaviour: it is true when the action is pressed, then again after a delay, then at regular intervals while it is held.

flowchart LR
    Press["Pressed<br/>repeat"] -- "0.4 s" --> First["Repeat"]
    First -- "0.1 s" --> Second["Repeat"]
    Second -- "0.1 s" --> Third["..."]

A held action repeats when pressed, after 0.4 s, then every 0.1 s.

The delay and the interval are set with setRepeat(delay, interval), 0.4 s and 0.1 s by default. Repeating needs the elapsed time given to update(): without it, an action is only repeated when it is pressed.

heldDuration() gives how long an action has been held. On the update where the action is released, it still gives how long it was held, so that a shot charged while holding the button can be fired on release:

if (controls.wasReleased(Action::Shoot)) {
    const float charge = std::min(controls.heldDuration(Action::Shoot) / 2.0f, 1.0f);   // full after 2 s
    fire(charge);
}

items.title: Controls of R-Type
items.text:
apps/client/src/Controls.cpp defines the default controls:

Action Keyboard Gamepad (first one) MoveUp Up or W (Z on AZERTY) D-pad up, left stick up MoveDown Down or S D-pad down, left stick down MoveLeft Left or A (Q on AZERTY) D-pad left, left stick left MoveRight Right or D D-pad right, left stick right Shoot Space Bottom face button, right trigger Menu Esc Start ToggleFullscreen F11 —

items.title: Menu controls
items.text:
Menus have their own actions, separate from the game ones: engine::Navigation, with their own ActionMap (see Navigation). The same key can then mean something else in a menu: Esc opens the pause menu in game, and goes back in a menu. The interface reads the input before the game, and the game only reads its actions while its scene receives the input (see Scenes).

When moving, the client normalises the direction: pushing up and right at the same time must not move faster than pushing in one direction.

Vector2 direction{controls.strength(Action::MoveRight) - controls.strength(Action::MoveLeft),
                  controls.strength(Action::MoveDown) - controls.strength(Action::MoveUp)};
const float length = std::hypot(direction.x, direction.y);
if (length > 1.0f) {
    direction = {direction.x / length, direction.y / length};
}

To add an action, follow Add a player action.

items.title: Mouse
items.text:
The InputSource gives the state of the mouse:

Function Gives mousePosition() Position of the pointer in the window, in pixels. isMouseButtonDown(button) Whether a button (Left, Right, Middle, Back, Forward) is held. mouseWheel() How much the wheel turned since the previous frame, in notches: positive up, negative down.

Mouse buttons are usually read through actions, with Binding::mouseButton(), to get presses, releases and repeats like any other input.

items.title: Window pixels and game units
items.text:
The game is scaled to fit the window, which may show more than the game area around it: a position in window pixels is not a position in the game. The Renderer converts it, since it knows both sizes:

const MousePosition mouse = devices.mousePosition();
const Vector2 pointer = renderer.windowToGame({mouse.x, mouse.y});   // in game units, like everything drawn

Near the edges of a window of another shape than the game, the pointer can be outside of the game area: its coordinates are negative or larger than the game size. The conversion is the reverse of the view set by beginFrame() (computeVisibleArea()), and is unit tested (windowToGame() in Viewport.hpp).

Two vector types

The input library returns a MousePosition, not a rtype::render::Vector2: it does not depend on the render library. A small shared math library (Vector2, Rectangle) used by the ECS, the input and the render libraries would remove this conversion.

items.title: Mouse in menus
items.text: In menus, the widget under the pointer gets the focus when the mouse moves, and a click activates it. See Navigation.

items.title: Text entry
items.text:
A text field, such as a server address or a player name, reads characters, not keys. Characters follow the keyboard layout and its modifiers: Shift+A gives "A", and the accent keys of a French keyboard give "é". The InputSource gives the characters typed since the previous frame with takeTypedText(), and a TextInput turns them into the text of a field:

TextInput address;
address.setMaxLength(21);
address.setFilter([](char32_t c) { return (c >= U'0' && c <= U'9') || c == U'.' || c == U':'; });

// Once per frame, while the field has the focus
address.update(devices, window.frameTime());
renderer.drawText(font, address.text(), position, 48.0f, colors::White);
  • setMaxLength() limits the number of characters; setFilter() decides which characters are accepted, for instance only digits and dots for an address. Control characters (tabulation, line feed...) are always refused. Both also apply to pasted text.
  • The text is stored in UTF-8, ready to be drawn. length() counts characters, which can be less than the size in bytes: "é" takes two bytes.
  • wasChanged() tells whether the text changed at the last update, for instance to validate it while it is typed.

items.title: Editing
items.text:
A TextInput behaves like the text fields of common applications:

Keys Effect Typing Inserts at the cursor, replacing the selection if there is one. Left / Right Moves the cursor by one character. With a selection, goes to its start or its end. Ctrl+Left / Ctrl+Right Moves the cursor by one word. Home / End Moves the cursor to the start or the end of the text. Shift + any of the moves above Selects the text between the cursor and where it started. Backspace / Del Erases the selection, or the character before or after the cursor. Ctrl+Backspace / Ctrl+Del Erases the word before or after the cursor. Ctrl+A Selects the whole text. Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V Copies or cuts the selection, pastes the clipboard.

Moving the cursor and erasing repeat while the keys are held. The clipboard is the system one: text copied from a browser can be pasted in the game, and the other way around.

Control+A on AZERTY keyboards
