Keys are physical positions, and the A key of an AZERTY keyboard is where QWERTY keyboards have Q. Select all is bound to both positions, so Ctrl+A works on both keyboards; as a side effect, Ctrl+Q also selects everything on a QWERTY keyboard. C, X and V are at the same place on QWERTY, AZERTY and QWERTZ keyboards.

The cursor and the selection are given as byte offsets in text(). To draw them, measure the text before them:

const auto offsetOf = [&](std::size_t byte) {
    return position.x + renderer.measureText(font, field.text().substr(0, byte), size).x;
};

if (!field.selection().empty()) {   // selection, behind the text
    const float begin = offsetOf(field.selection().begin);
    renderer.drawRectangle({begin, position.y, offsetOf(field.selection().end) - begin, height}, selectionColor);
}
renderer.drawText(font, field.text(), position, size, colors::White);
const float cursorX = offsetOf(field.cursor());   // cursor, on top of the text
renderer.drawLine({cursorX, position.y}, {cursorX, position.y + height}, 3.0f, colors::White);

items.title: Reading characters once per frame
items.text:
Once per frame, while the field has the focus

Typed characters are consumed when they are read: a second call to takeTypedText() in the same frame returns nothing. Only the field that has the focus calls update(); characters typed while no field has the focus are lost, not delayed.

The fonts loaded by the ResourceManager include the accented Latin letters, so that typed names are drawn correctly (see Fonts).

items.title: Why not an existing library
items.text: Libraries such as Dear ImGui or RmlUi provide complete text fields. They also read the input and draw the interface themselves, outside of our Renderer and ActionMap, which would mean adapters for the rendering, the gamepad navigation and the VR panel, and would bypass the ECS in which the interface is built (ADR 0007). For the few text fields of the game (player name, server address), a small class built on our input is simpler. Dear ImGui remains a good candidate for development tools, such as an in-game console or an entity inspector, which do not need to look like the game.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
tests/action_map.cpp and tests/text_input.cpp test the ActionMap and the TextInput with a FakeInput (tests/FakeInput.hpp), an InputSource whose keys, buttons, axes, mouse, typed text and clipboard are set by the test. No window nor device is needed, so the tests run in the CI:

FakeInput input;
input.keys = {Key::Space};
actions.update(input);
REQUIRE(actions.wasPressed(Action::Shoot));

items.title: Adding an input source
items.text: Any class implementing InputSource works with ActionMap, without changing the game. This is how VR controllers are planned to be supported: a new source, and if needed new kinds of bindings for their buttons and gestures.

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• The pause menu does not pause the game, which is shared with the other players.
  • Text fields are single-line, without undo, mouse selection, nor scrolling: a text wider than its field overflows it. This is enough for a player name or a server address.
  • Bindings are not saved: the controls chosen by a player are lost when the game closes.
  • No mouse in text fields: clicking does not place the cursor, dragging does not select.
  • The actions are not sent to the server yet: they will be encoded in the INPUT message of the protocol, one bit per action.

items.title: Logging
items.text:
The log library (libs/log, namespace rtype::log) writes the messages of the client and the server. It is shared by both programs and, like the ECS, does not depend on raylib.

19:23:00.315 INFO  server   Server started on port 4242
19:23:00.315 DEBUG network  Packet INPUT #1532 from client 2
19:23:00.315 INFO  network  Client 2 connected from 127.0.0.1:51034
19:23:00.315 WARN  network  Client 3 has not answered for 2.5 s
19:23:00.315 ERROR network  Client 3 crashed: connection lost
                            Notifying the 2 other players

Each line shows the local time to the millisecond, the level, the name of the subsystem that sent the message, and the message. In a terminal, levels are coloured, warnings and errors stand out, and each subsystem keeps the same colour from one run to the next.

items.title: Writing messages
items.text:
Each subsystem creates a Logger with its name, and writes messages with the std::format syntax:

#include "rtype/log/Logger.hpp"

const rtype::log::Logger logger("network");

logger.info("Client {} connected from {}:{}", id, address, port);
logger.warning("Packet of {} bytes is too short, ignored", size);

The format string is checked at compile time: a missing or extra argument is a compilation error, not a crash. A logger only holds its name, so it is cheap to create; loggers can be used from several threads at the same time.

Do not use std::cout

Write messages with a logger rather than std::cout or std::cerr: they get a time, a level and a name, they can be filtered, and they do not get mixed up when several threads write at the same time.

items.title: Levels
items.text:
Level Use it for Shown by default trace Very detailed tracing, for instance every packet received. No debug Information useful when debugging. No info Normal events: a client connected, a wave started. Yes warning Something unexpected that the program recovers from. Yes error A failure: an operation could not be done. Yes

Messages below the current level are ignored before being formatted: disabled trace messages in a loop cost almost nothing. When computing a value only to log it is expensive, check logger.isEnabled(Level::Debug) first.

items.title: Naming loggers
items.text: Use short lower-case names for subsystems: client, server, network, game, render. The name column is 8 characters wide; longer names still work but shift their message to the right.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Setting How Minimum level Environment variable RTYPE_LOG_LEVEL (trace, debug, info, warning, error), or rtype::log::setLevel(). info by default. Colours On when the error output is a terminal, off when it is redirected to a file or when the NO_COLOR environment variable is set. rtype::log::setColors() forces them. Destination The error output by default. rtype::log::setSink() replaces it.

Both programs call rtype::log::configureFromEnvironment() at startup, so the level can be changed without recompiling:

LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
RTYPE_LOG_LEVEL=debug ./build/bin/r-type_server

$env:RTYPE_LOG_LEVEL = "debug"; .\build\bin\r-type_server.exe

An unknown level is reported with a warning, and the default level is kept.

items.title: raylib messages
items.text:
raylib prints its own messages: about thirty lines when the window opens, one more for every texture loaded. The render library redirects them to a logger named raylib, when the Window is created:

raylib level Our level TRACE trace DEBUG, INFO debug WARNING warning ERROR, FATAL error

raylib's INFO messages are details for us: they are hidden by default, and shown with RTYPE_LOG_LEVEL=debug. Its warnings, for instance a file that cannot be read, are always shown.

Fatal errors

raylib stops the program after a FATAL message, except when its messages are redirected. On desktop, its only fatal message is a failure to open the window, which Window reports with an exception: the error then goes through the normal error handling of the program.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
flowchart LR
    Logger["Logger<br/>(name)"] -- "level enabled?<br/>std::format" --> Output["Output<br/>(one at a time)"]
    Raylib["raylib<br/>messages"] -- "render library" --> Logger
    Output --> Sink["Sink"]
    Sink --> Console["Console<br/>(default)"]
    Sink -.-> Other["Test capture,<br/>file..."]

A logger checks the level and formats the message, then the message goes to the current sink, which writes it to the console by default.

  • Thread safety. The level is atomic, and messages go through the sink one at a time, protected by a mutex: lines written by different threads never get mixed up.
  • Sinks. A Sink receives each message as a Record (level, logger name, message, time). The console sink formats it with formatRecord() and writes it to the error output, which is not buffered: a message is visible even if the program crashes right after it.
  • Colours. Terminal colour codes; on Windows, the console is switched to the mode that understands them. Logger colours are chosen from a hash of the name that gives the same result on every platform.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
tests/log.cpp replaces the sink with one that captures the messages, then checks their level, logger name and formatted text. The tests also check formatRecord() directly: columns, colours only when asked, and alignment of multi-line messages.

A sink can be used the same way to check that some code logs what it should:

class CaptureSink : public rtype::log::Sink {
public:
    std::vector<std::string> messages;
    void write(const rtype::log::Record &record) override { messages.emplace_back(record.message); }
};

auto sink = std::make_shared<CaptureSink>();
rtype::log::setSink(sink);
// ... code under test ...
rtype::log::setSink(nullptr);   // back to the console

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• No log file yet. The server will probably need one; it is a new Sink, without changes elsewhere.
  • No thread name in the lines. It may be worth adding once the server runs several threads.

items.title: Networking concepts
items.text: This page explains the words used in the networking documentation, the protocol specification and the decision records 0011 to 0014. Read it first if you have not written networked games before: each term links the general idea to what R-Type does with it.

items.title: Addresses and ports
items.text: IP address Identifies a machine on a network: 203.0.113.7 (IPv4) or 2001:db8::7 (IPv6). Port A number from 1 to 65535 that identifies a program on a machine. An address and a port together (203.0.113.7:4242) identify one program. The R-Type master listens on TCP port 4242 by default, and each game on its own UDP port. Socket The object a program uses to send and receive on a port. libs/network wraps them in UdpSocket, TcpListener and TcpConnection. Loopback The address 127.0.0.1 (localhost): the machine itself. Traffic to it never leaves the machine. The master and its games talk over it.

items.title: TCP and UDP
items.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph TCP["TCP: a stream"]
        direction LR
        A1["H E L L O W O R L D"] --> B1["H E L L O W O R L D<br/>every byte, in order"]
    end
    subgraph UDP["UDP: datagrams"]
        direction LR
        A2["[1] [2] [3] [4]"] --> B2["[1] [3] [3] ... [2]<br/>lost, duplicated, reordered"]
    end

TCP delivers a continuous flow of bytes, complete and in order. UDP delivers separate messages that may be lost, duplicated or reordered.

TCP A connection between two programs that carries a stream of bytes. Every byte arrives, in order: the system resends what is lost. The cost: if one packet is lost, everything after it waits for it to be resent (head-of-line blocking). R-Type uses TCP for the lobby (ADR 0012). UDP No connection: a program sends datagrams, independent messages, to an address and a port. Each one arrives whole or not at all, but it may be lost, arrive twice, or arrive after a later one. Nothing waits for anything. R-Type uses UDP for everything inside a game. Datagram One UDP message. One datagram carries one R-Type message. Framing How a receiver finds where each message ends in a TCP stream, which has no boundaries. FTP ends each command with \r\n; R-Type starts each message with its size, and the receiver reads exactly that many bytes. MTU and fragmentation The largest packet a network link carries, often 1500 bytes. A larger datagram is split into fragments, and if one fragment is lost, the whole datagram is lost. R-Type datagrams are at most 1200 bytes, which fits every common path on the Internet.

items.title: Turning data into bytes
items.text: Serialization Writing a message as bytes (encoding), and reading it back (decoding). R-Type writes each field one by one with Writer and reads it with Reader, which refuses to read past the end of the data. A C++ struct is never sent as-is with memcpy: the compiler adds padding between fields, differently on each compiler. Endianness The order of the bytes of a number in memory. 0x1234 is 12 34 in big-endian and 34 12 in little-endian (x86 processors). The R-Type protocol always uses big-endian, also called network byte order. Malformed message A message too short, too long, of an unknown type or with out-of-range values. The receiver drops it without crashing and without allocating memory based on its content.

items.title: Living with an unreliable network
items.text: Packet loss, duplication, reordering What UDP lets happen. On the Internet, losing 1 to 2 % of the datagrams is common. Sequence number A number the sender writes in every datagram, increased by one each time. It lets the receiver detect duplicates, missing datagrams and old datagrams. Acknowledgement (ack) A message, or a field in one, that says "I received datagram n". R-Type puts in every datagram the last sequence number received and a bitmap of the ones before it, so one datagram acknowledges many. Reliable / unreliable message An unreliable message is sent once: losing it does not matter, because the next one replaces it (the positions of the entities). A reliable message is resent until it is acknowledged (a player dies, a player leaves). Heartbeat A small message sent regularly, even with nothing to say, to show the other side is alive. R-Type sends at least one datagram per second. Timeout How long without any message before the other side is considered dead. A client silent for a few seconds is removed from its game, and the other players are told.

items.title: Time and lag
items.text: Latency, round-trip time (RTT), ping Latency is the time a message takes to arrive. The round-trip time is the time for a message and its answer: what games display as ping. Typically 1 ms on a local network, 20–100 ms over the Internet. Jitter The variation of the latency from one message to the next. Bandwidth The amount of data sent per second, measured in kilobits per second (kbit/s). Tick, tick rate, fixed step A tick is one step of the simulation. The tick rate is the number of ticks per second (60 for the R-Type simulation). With a fixed step, each tick advances the world by the same duration (1/60 s), whatever the speed of the machine, so the server and the clients compute the same thing (ADR 0010).

items.title: Keeping the world in sync
items.text: Authoritative server The server decides everything that happens in the game; the clients display it. A client never says "I am at (120, 40)", only "the up key is pressed": the server moves the ship. Input What a client sends: the actions pressed at a given tick (move, shoot). Snapshot The state of the entities a client needs to see (position, velocity, type), sent by the server 20 to 30 times per second, unreliably. Event Something that happened once: an entity appears or is destroyed, a player dies, a player leaves. Sent reliably. Replication The whole mechanism that copies the server's world to the clients: snapshots and events. Network id The id the server gives to an entity for the network. The ECS entity_t of the same entity differs on the server and on each client, so the client keeps a table from network ids to its own entities. Interpolation Displaying the other entities slightly in the past (about 100 ms), between two snapshots already received, so that they move smoothly instead of jumping 20 times per second. Client-side prediction and reconciliation Prediction: the client moves its own ship immediately when a key is pressed, without waiting for the server. Reconciliation: when the server's answer arrives, the client corrects its ship if they disagree, and replays the inputs sent since. Delta compression Sending only what changed since a snapshot the client acknowledged, instead of the whole state.

items.title: The R-Type server
items.text: Master The r-type_server process you start. It runs the lobby: players connect to it over TCP, list the games, create or join one. It starts and watches the games (ADR 0013). Instance One game, in its own process (r-type_server --instance), with its own ECS world and its own UDP port. Lobby Everything before and around the games: the player's name, the list of games, creating and joining one. Session id The number that identifies a player inside a game, written in the header of each datagram so that the game knows which keys to use. Standalone mode An instance started without a master, with a fixed test key, in debug builds only. Used by the tests and the fuzzing.

items.title: Reaching a server over the Internet
items.text: NAT A home router shares one public IP address between all the machines of the home. It lets answers to outgoing traffic come back, and drops unsolicited incoming traffic. The client always speaks first, and its heartbeat keeps the way open, so players have nothing to configure. Port forwarding A rule on a router that sends incoming traffic on a port to one machine of the local network. Needed only if the server is hosted behind a home router. Firewall Filters traffic by port and protocol. The server's host must let in TCP 4242 and the UDP range of the games.

items.title: Security
items.text: Symmetric key A secret shared by both sides, used to encrypt and to decrypt. Fast. The keys of the datagrams are symmetric. Key pair: public and private key Two linked keys. The private key stays secret on its owner's machine; the public key can be given to everyone. Something signed with the private key can be checked with the public one. The server has a key pair. TLS The standard protocol that encrypts a TCP connection and proves the identity of the server: the "S" of HTTPS. R-Type uses TLS 1.3 on the lobby connection (ADR 0014). Certificate, fingerprint, pinning A certificate carries the server's public key. Its fingerprint is a short hash of it (SHA-256). Pinning means the client only accepts one known key, shipped with it, like SSH's known_hosts. AEAD, tag Authenticated encryption with associated data: one operation that encrypts the payload and computes a tag over the payload and some clear data (the header). Any change to either makes the tag wrong, and the datagram is dropped. R-Type uses ChaCha20-Poly1305. Nonce A number used once: each encryption with the same key needs a different nonce. R-Type uses the packet number of the datagram. Man-in-the-middle An attacker on the path who sets up encryption with each side and relays the traffic, reading everything. Prevented by checking the server's identity (pinning). Replay An attacker records a valid datagram and sends it again later. Prevented by refusing packet numbers already seen. Spoofing Sending datagrams with a fake source address. Spoofed datagrams are dropped, because they cannot carry a valid tag without the key. Amplification Using a server to flood a victim: send it a small request with the victim's address as source, and the server sends a large answer to the victim. A server must never answer an unknown address with more bytes than it received. Flooding, rate limiting Sending a huge number of messages to overload a server. Rate limiting caps the clients and the messages per second and per address. Fuzzing Feeding a program millions of random or mutated inputs to find crashes. The decoders are pure functions (bytes in, message or error out) so that a fuzzer can call them directly (ADR 0004).

items.title: Networking
items.text:
The network library (libs/network, namespace rtype::network) opens sockets and moves bytes between the client and the server. It is shared by both programs and, like the ECS, does not depend on raylib. It is built on Asio (ADR 0011) and encrypts with Mbed TLS (ADR 0014). Neither appears in its headers.

New to networking? Read Networking concepts first.

Class Role Address An IP address and a port, 127.0.0.1:4242 EventLoop Waits for the network and calls the handlers of the sockets UdpSocket Sends and receives datagrams TcpListener Listens on a TCP port and accepts connections TcpConnection Sends and receives a stream of bytes TlsConnection A TCP connection encrypted with TLS 1.3, on which the client is sure to talk to our server ServerIdentity The private key of the server, and the certificate it presents KeyFingerprint The SHA-256 of a public key, which the client pins DatagramKey, sealDatagram(), openDatagram() Encrypt a game datagram with a player's key, and check and decrypt it ReplayWindow, PacketCounter Drop the datagrams received twice, and number the ones sent MessageChannel Acknowledgements, resends and ordering of the messages of one session over UDP DatagramBody, encodeBody(), decodeBody() The decrypted body of a datagram: acknowledgements and messages Timer, StopSignals Call a function after a delay or every interval, and when the program is asked to stop ClientSession, SessionHost A client's session with its game, and the game's sessions with its players: connecting, heartbeats, timeouts, disconnecting FramedConnection A TCP or TLS connection that sends and receives whole messages (frames) FrameDecoder, makeFrame() Split a TCP stream into frames, and build a frame NetworkError, tlsCategory() The errors of the library and of TLS, as std::error_code Writer, Reader Turn the fields of a message into bytes and back, following the protocol isValidText() Checks a text before sending it as a str8

The lobby, the game instances and the protocol messages are built on top of these classes, in the next steps of the "Server & networking" work.

items.title: The event loop
items.text:
Sockets do not block: sending returns at once, and received data is given to a handler, a function the socket calls when data arrives. The EventLoop is what waits for the network and calls these handlers. Every socket belongs to a loop, and its handlers are only called on the thread that runs the loop.

There are two ways to run a loop:

A network thread (server)Once per frame (client) 
rtype::network::EventLoop loop;
// ... create the sockets ...

std::thread network([&loop] { loop.run(); }); // waits for events until stop()
// ... the simulation runs on this thread ...
loop.stop();
network.join();

rtype::network::EventLoop loop;
// ... create the sockets ...

while (!window.shouldClose()) {
    loop.poll(); // handles what is ready, returns at once
    // ... update and draw ...
}

flowchart LR
    Game["Any thread<br/>send(), close(), post()"] -- "queued" --> Loop["EventLoop<br/>run() or poll()"]
    OS["System sockets"] -- "data, connections" --> Loop
    Loop -- "calls" --> Handlers["Handlers<br/>(on the loop's thread)"]
    Loop -- "writes" --> OS

Calls from any thread are queued to the loop; the loop talks to the system and calls the handlers on its own thread.

Threads. Every function of the sockets can be called from any thread: the work is handed to the loop's thread, and done in the order of the calls. loop.post(function) does the same for any function, which is how another thread hands work to the network thread. The handlers are always called on the loop's thread, so the data they touch must be protected if another thread reads it.

Lifetime. Sockets must be destroyed before their loop. A socket can be destroyed at any time otherwise, including from inside one of its handlers: data that arrives afterwards is ignored.

Exceptions. An exception thrown by a handler leaves run() or poll(), which can be called again.

items.title: Timers and stop signals
items.text:
Two helpers call a function on the loop's thread, like the handlers of the sockets:

rtype::network::Timer tick(loop);
tick.startRepeating(std::chrono::milliseconds(16), [&] { host.update(Clock::now()); }); // every tick

rtype::network::Timer timeout(loop);
timeout.start(std::chrono::seconds(10), [&] { connection.close(); }); // once
timeout.cancel();                                                     // or not at all

rtype::network::StopSignals signals(loop, [&](const char *signal) { /* Ctrl+C, SIGTERM... */ });
  • A Timer started again forgets what it was doing; cancelled or destroyed on the loop's thread, it never calls its handler, even if it was already due. A repeating timer that falls behind skips the calls it missed rather than making them in a burst.
  • StopSignals catches Ctrl+C (SIGINT), SIGTERM, and on Windows SIGBREAK, while it exists: the program no longer ends at once, the handler decides. The server uses it to stop properly.

items.title: Addresses
items.text:
using rtype::network::Address;

Address::anyIpv4(4242);                   // 0.0.0.0:4242, every interface: for a server
Address::loopbackIpv4(4242);              // 127.0.0.1:4242, this machine only
Address::parse("192.168.1.10", 4242);     // std::optional<Address>: nothing if not an IP address
rtype::network::resolve("localhost", 4242); // std::vector<Address>, IPv4 first; looks up host names
  • parse() only reads IP addresses. resolve() also looks up host names, and blocks until the answer arrives, which can take seconds: call it at startup or from a thread that can wait, never in the game loop. It throws std::system_error if the name does not exist.
  • Port 0 means "any free port": a socket bound to it gets one from the system, given by localAddress().
  • An address can be logged directly, logger.info("Client connected from {}", address), and used as a key of an std::unordered_map.

items.title: UDP
items.text:
rtype::network::UdpSocket socket(loop, Address::anyIpv4(4243));

socket.startReceiving([&](const Address &from, std::span<const std::byte> datagram) {
    socket.send(from, datagram); // echo
});
  • The constructor binds the socket, and throws std::system_error if it cannot, for instance if the port is already in use.
  • send() copies the data: the buffer can be reused at once. A datagram the system cannot send (full buffer, unreachable network) is dropped and logged, like a datagram lost on the way: UDP never guarantees delivery.
  • The data given to the handler is only valid during the call: copy it to keep it.
  • Errors while receiving are logged, and the socket keeps receiving. On Windows, a datagram sent to a closed port makes the next receive fail: this does not stop the socket.

items.title: TCP
items.text:
A TCP connection is a stream: the bytes arrive complete and in order, but not in the pieces they were sent in. Two send() calls may arrive in one handler call, and one send() in several. The layer above splits the stream into messages (protocol framing).

ServerClient 
rtype::network::TcpListener listener(loop, Address::anyIpv4(4242));
std::vector<rtype::network::TcpConnection> clients;

listener.startAccepting([&](rtype::network::TcpConnection connection) {
    connection.start(
        [](std::span<const std::byte> bytes) { /* bytes received */ },
        [](std::error_code reason) { /* closed by the client, or lost */ });
    clients.push_back(std::move(connection)); // keep it, or it is closed
});

using rtype::network::TcpConnection;
std::optional<TcpConnection> server;

TcpConnection::connect(loop, address, [&](std::error_code error, std::optional<TcpConnection> connection) {
    if (error) {
        logger.error("Cannot reach the server: {}", error.message());
        return;
    }
    connection->start(onReceive, onClose);
    server = std::move(connection);
});
Event What happens connect() cannot reach the server The handler receives the error: refused, unreachable, or std::errc::timed_out after the timeout (10 s by default) The peer closes the connection The close handler is called once, with no error The connection fails (reset, network down) The close handler is called once, with the error close() is called, or the connection is destroyed The bytes already given to send() are sent, then the connection closes. The handlers are not called: the code that closed it already knows A listener is closed or destroyed No new connection is accepted. Connections already accepted stay open

Connections disable Nagle's algorithm, which would delay small messages to group them: lobby messages are sent at once.

A listener lets a restarted server listen again at once on its port on Linux. It does not on Windows, where the same option would let another program take a port in use.

items.title: TCP framing
items.text:
A TCP stream has no boundaries, so each message is sent as a frame: its size on two bytes, its type on one byte, then its payload (lobby, section 3). FramedConnection does it on top of a TcpConnection: the code above it only sees whole messages.

size (u16) | type (u8) | payload (size − 1 bytes)
00 09        01          00 01 05 50 61 76 65 6C      HELLO, version 1, "Pavel"

rtype::network::FramedConnection client(std::move(connection)); // a TcpConnection, not started yet

client.start(
    [](std::uint8_t type, std::span<const std::byte> payload) {
        rtype::network::Reader reader(payload); // one whole message: decode it according to its type
    },
    [](std::error_code reason) {
        if (reason == rtype::network::NetworkError::FrameTooLarge) { /* the peer broke the protocol */ }
    });

rtype::network::Writer hello;
hello.writeU16(1);
hello.writeString("Pavel");
client.send(0x01, hello.bytes()); // type, then payload: the size is added
  • Whole and in order. Each call to the frame handler is one frame, as it was sent, whatever the pieces TCP delivered.
  • Invalid frames close the connection. A size of 0, or above 16382, is refused as soon as its two bytes arrive, without waiting for the rest. The connection is closed, the close handler receives NetworkError::EmptyFrame or NetworkError::FrameTooLarge, and a warning is logged. The frames received before it are still handled.
  • Bounded memory. The connection keeps at most the frame being received: a peer announcing a frame of 16 KiB and sending it slowly holds 16 KiB, never more.
  • Payloads above MaxFramePayloadSize (16381 bytes) cannot be sent: send() throws std::length_error.
  • close() sends the frames already given to send(), then closes. It also stops the frames already received from being handled: after close(), even from inside the frame handler, no handler is called.

The splitting itself is done by FrameDecoder, which works on bytes only, without a socket, so that it can be tested and fuzzed alone:

rtype::network::FrameDecoder decoder;
decoder.feed(bytes);                       // bytes received, in any pieces
while (const auto frame = decoder.next()) { // each complete frame
    handle(frame->type, frame->payload);
}
if (decoder.failed()) { /* decoder.error(): EmptyFrame or FrameTooLarge */ }

items.title: TLS
items.text: The lobby connection is encrypted with TLS 1.3 (lobby, section 2): nobody on the path can read or change the bytes, and the client is sure to talk to our server, not to someone in the middle. TlsConnection adds it on top of a TcpConnection, and works the same way: start(), send(), close(), a receive handler and a close handler.

items.title: Keys
items.text:
The server has a key pair (ECDSA P-256). It keeps the private key secret, in a file given to it, and the clients know its public key. They do not compare the whole key, only its fingerprint: the SHA-256 of the key, 64 hexadecimal digits, like SSH's known_hosts (ADR 0014). The key pair is made with r-type_keygen: see Generate the server keys.

// Server: its private key, the --key option
const auto identity = rtype::network::ServerIdentity::load("server.key");
logger.info("Server key {}", identity.fingerprint().toHex());

// Client: the fingerprint of the server's public key, shipped next to the executable...
const auto pinned = rtype::network::KeyFingerprint::loadPublicKey("server.pub");
// ... or written in a configuration, as 64 hexadecimal digits
const std::optional<rtype::network::KeyFingerprint> fromText = rtype::network::KeyFingerprint::parse(text);
Function Gives Throws ServerIdentity::load(path), fromPrivateKey(pem) The identity of the server, from an ECDSA P-256 private key in PEM std::system_error (file), std::invalid_argument (not such a key) ServerIdentity::generate() A new key pair, for the tests and the key generation tool — identity.privateKeyPem(), publicKeyPem(), fingerprint() The keys in PEM, to write them to files, and the fingerprint — KeyFingerprint::loadPublicKey(path), ofPublicKey(pem) The fingerprint of a public key in PEM std::system_error (file), std::invalid_argument (not a key) KeyFingerprint::parse(hex), toHex() The fingerprint from and to 64 hexadecimal digits — (parse returns std::nullopt)

The fingerprint is the one OpenSSL computes, so it can be checked by hand:

openssl pkey -pubin -in server.pub -outform DER | sha256sum

The certificate a TLS server must present is made from the private key when the identity is created: it is self-signed, and the client only looks at the key it holds. No certificate authority, domain name or expiry date is involved.

items.title: Connecting
items.text:
Each side wraps its TCP connection, not started yet, then starts it:

ClientServer 
rtype::network::TcpConnection::connect(loop, server,
    [&](std::error_code error, std::optional<rtype::network::TcpConnection> connection) {
        if (error) { /* server unreachable */ return; }
        lobby.emplace(rtype::network::FramedConnection(
            rtype::network::TlsConnection::client(std::move(*connection), pinned)));
        lobby->start(onFrame, onClose);
        lobby->send(0x01, hello.bytes()); // waits for the end of the handshake
    });

listener.startAccepting([&](rtype::network::TcpConnection connection) {
    auto client = std::make_unique<rtype::network::FramedConnection>(
        rtype::network::TlsConnection::server(std::move(connection), identity));
    client->start(onFrame, onClose);
    clients.push_back(std::move(client));
});

FramedConnection takes a TlsConnection as well as a TcpConnection: the frames are then encrypted, and the code above does not change.

  • The handshake starts with start(). Both sides agree on keys, and the server proves it holds the private key of its certificate. It takes one round trip, a few milliseconds on a local network.
  • Bytes sent before its end wait for it, then leave encrypted. The client can send HELLO at once.
  • Its end can be known: start() takes a third handler, optional, called once when the handshake has ended, before the first bytes received. The lobby uses it to time the handshake and HELLO apart (start(onFrame, onClose, onSecured) on a FramedConnection over TLS; never called over plain TCP).
  • The client checks the key. If the server presents another key, the handshake fails, an error is logged with the fingerprint presented, and the close handler receives NetworkError::UntrustedServer. Nothing the client sent is ever delivered to that server.
  • TLS 1.3 only, with the algorithms of the specification: TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 (preferred) or TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, key exchange with x25519 or secp256r1, signatures with ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256. A peer offering only TLS 1.2 is refused. No session ticket, no resumption.
  • Everything received is authenticated. A changed byte, a record from someone else, or a peer that does not speak TLS ends the connection with an error of tlsCategory(), whose message() comes from Mbed TLS.
  • close() sends the bytes already given to send(), tells the peer that the connection ends (a TLS close_notify), then closes. Called during the handshake, it waits for its end if bytes are waiting to be sent. The peer's close handler is called without error.

The close handler of a TLS connection, or of a framed connection over TLS, can receive:

Reason Meaning No error The peer closed the connection NetworkError::UntrustedServer Client: the server does not have the pinned key. Tell the player the server is not the expected one. NetworkError::HandshakeInterrupted The TCP connection ended during the handshake: closed, or reset, by the peer reason.category() == tlsCategory() The TLS layer refused something: wrong version, invalid record, alert from the peer… NetworkError::EmptyFrame, FrameTooLarge Framed connections: the peer sent an invalid frame A system error The connection was lost

items.title: Threads
items.text: Mbed TLS is built without its own locks. Every call into it, from any connection or identity, holds one lock of the library, so identities can be loaded and connections used from any thread. A handshake holds it for about a millisecond: negligible at the scale of a lobby, and a reason to enable the locks of Mbed TLS (MBEDTLS_THREADING_C) if measurements ever show waiting.

items.title: Encrypted datagrams
items.text:
Every datagram of a game is encrypted and authenticated (game protocol, ADR 0014). UDP has no connection and no handshake, so TLS cannot be used: the master draws two keys per player, sends them to the client over TLS (GAME_JOINED) and to the game, and each side encrypts what it sends with its own key.

 0      2   3   4             8                       16                      16 + n         32 + n
 ┌──────┬───┬───┬─────────────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┬──────────────┐
 │ "RT" │ 1 │ 0 │ session id  │ packet number         │ body, encrypted       │ tag          │
 └──────┴───┴───┴─────────────┴───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┴──────────────┘
  header: in clear, but covered by the tag              ChaCha20                 Poly1305
  • The header stays in clear, so that the receiver knows the session, hence the key, before decrypting. The tag covers it as well: changing the session id or the packet number makes the datagram invalid.
  • The body is encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439). The nonce, a number that must never be used twice with the same key, is the packet number: that is why PacketCounter never gives a number twice, and stops instead of going back to 0.
  • The tag (16 bytes) proves that the datagram was made with the key and not changed on the way. Without the key, nobody can make a datagram that opens, nor change a byte of one, which also proves who sent it: only the player who received the key over TLS.

These functions only take bytes and give bytes, with no socket, like the frame decoder: the sessions of the next steps call them.

SendingReceiving 
// Once per session: the key of this side, and its packet numbers
rtype::network::DatagramKey ownKey(keyBytes);   // 32 bytes from GAME_JOINED
rtype::network::PacketCounter packets;

// For every datagram
const std::optional<std::uint64_t> number = packets.next();
if (!number) {
    // Every packet number was used (2^64 - 1 datagrams): the session must close
}
socket.send(peer, rtype::network::sealDatagram(ownKey, {sessionId, *number}, body));

// Once per session: the key of the peer, and the numbers already received
rtype::network::DatagramKey peerKey(peerKeyBytes);
rtype::network::ReplayWindow window;

// For every datagram, in this order, dropping it silently at the first failure
const auto header = rtype::network::parseDatagramHeader(datagram); // size, magic, version...
if (!header || header->session != sessionId) {
    return;
}
if (!window.accepts(header->packetNumber)) {
    return; // received already: duplicated by the network, or replayed by an attacker
}
const auto body = rtype::network::openDatagram(peerKey, datagram);
if (!body) {
    return; // forged, or changed on the way
}
window.mark(header->packetNumber); // only now: a forged datagram must not move the window
handle(*body);
Function Gives Refuses DatagramKey(bytes), DatagramKey::generate(), key.bytes() A key from its 32 bytes or drawn at random, and its bytes to send them over TLS — parseDatagramHeader(datagram) The session and the packet number, not authenticated yet Size outside 32–1200 bytes, wrong magic, version or reserved byte, session or number 0 (std::nullopt) sealDatagram(key, header, body) The datagram, body.size() + 32 bytes A body above 1168 bytes (std::length_error), a session or number 0 (std::invalid_argument) openDatagram(key, datagram) The body An invalid header, another key, any byte changed (std::nullopt) window.accepts(n), window.mark(n) Whether n may be new, and remembering it 0, a number received already, more than 256 below the highest one packets.next() 1, 2, 3… After 2^64 - 1 (std::nullopt)

Why a replay window. An attacker can record a valid datagram and send it again later: it still opens, since it was made with the key. The window remembers the numbers received, and drops the second copy. It only keeps the last 256: a datagram later than that is useless in a game anyway, and the window stays 40 bytes.

Keys are secret. A DatagramKey is never logged, its bytes are erased from memory when its last copy is destroyed, and copying it shares the same key. Like TLS, sealing and opening hold the lock of Mbed TLS (Threads), so keys can be used from any thread.

items.title: Reliability over UDP
items.text:
UDP loses, duplicates and reorders datagrams. Most game messages do not mind: a snapshot lost is replaced by the next one. Some must arrive, though: an entity destroyed, the end of the game. The MessageChannel gives each message the choice (game protocol):

Delivery::Unreliable Delivery::Reliable Sent Once Again and again, until the peer acknowledges it Arrives Maybe, in any order Exactly once, in the order it was sent For What the next message replaces: snapshots, inputs What must not be missed: destructions, waves, the end of the game

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Acknowledgements. Every datagram says which packets were received from the peer: the highest number (Ack) and 32 bits for the 32 before it (Ack bits), taken straight from the ReplayWindow. A datagram lost now is acknowledged, or not, by any of the next 33: one ack lost costs nothing.

Packets received by B:  … 37 38 __ 40 41          (39 was lost)
B tells A:               Ack = 41, Ack bits: bit 0 = 1 (40 ✓), bit 1 = 0 (39 ✗), bit 2 = 1 (38 ✓), bit 3 = 1 (37 ✓)

Resending. The sender remembers which packet carried each reliable message. When one of them is acknowledged, the message is forgotten; when none is after the resend delay, max(1.5 × RTT, 100 ms), the message goes again in the next datagram, which has a new packet number. A message may be sent several times; the receiver keeps the first copy only.

Ordering. Each reliable message has an id, 0, 1, 2… (wrapping from 65535 to 0). The receiver delivers id E, then E + 1, and so on: a message that arrives early waits until those before it are there, at most 256 ahead. An id already delivered is ignored.

Received:     2   0   3   1
Delivered:    –   0   –   1 2 3

Round-trip time. When a packet is acknowledged, the time since it was sent is a sample of the RTT, smoothed as 0.9 × rtt + 0.1 × sample. It sets the resend delay, and it is the ping shown to the player. Until the first sample, it is assumed to be 100 ms.

Failing. If the peer stops acknowledging, the reliable messages pile up: at 256 waiting, the channel fails and the session must close. Likewise once every packet number was used.

items.title: Using it
items.text:
The channel only builds and reads the bodies of the datagrams, and is given the time: the session around it seals and opens them (Encrypted datagrams), and owns the socket and the timers.

SendingReceiving 
rtype::network::MessageChannel channel;   // one per session

channel.send(0x80, snapshot, rtype::network::Delivery::Unreliable);
channel.send(0x81, destroyed, rtype::network::Delivery::Reliable);

// Once per tick, or at least once per second (a heartbeat then): as many datagrams as needed
const auto now = rtype::network::MessageChannel::Clock::now();
do {
    const auto datagram = channel.next(now);
    if (!datagram) {
        return closeSession(); // the channel failed
    }
    socket.send(peer, rtype::network::sealDatagram(ownKey, {sessionId, datagram->packetNumber},
                                                   datagram->body));
} while (channel.hasMessagesToSend(now));

const auto header = rtype::network::parseDatagramHeader(datagram);
if (!header || header->session != sessionId || !channel.accepts(header->packetNumber)) {
    return;
}
const auto body = rtype::network::openDatagram(peerKey, datagram);
if (!body) {
    return;
}
const auto messages = channel.receive(header->packetNumber, *body, now);
if (!messages) {
    return; // malformed body: dropped, and not acknowledged
}
for (const rtype::network::ReceivedMessage &message : *messages) {
    handle(message.type, message.payload);
}

next() puts the reliable messages due first, then the unreliable ones in order, as many as fit in 1200 bytes. A snapshot part that fills a datagram goes in its own: hasMessagesToSend() tells when another datagram is needed.

Function Gives Refuses or fails send(type, payload, delivery) Queues the message A payload above 1151 bytes (unreliable) or 1149 (reliable): std::length_error. Returns false if the channel failed next(now) The packet number and body of the next datagram std::nullopt once failed hasMessagesToSend(now) Whether another datagram is needed now — accepts(n), receive(n, body, now) Whether a packet may be new; the messages to handle std::nullopt for a packet already received or a malformed body rtt(), resendDelay(), pendingReliable(), failed() The measures, for the logs and the console —

encodeBody() and decodeBody() are the codec of the body alone, for the tests and the fuzzer.

items.title: Game sessions
items.text:
A session is the link between one client and its game, over UDP: everything above put together, plus what makes it a connection (game protocol). The master gives both sides the same session id and keys (GAME_JOINED to the client, ADD_PLAYER to the game); then:

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as ClientSession
    participant G as SessionHost (game)
    Note over G: add(session, keys): waits 10 s for its client
    C->>G: CONNECT (reliable, sent again until acknowledged)
    Note over G: onConnected(session, address)
    G->>C: ACCEPTED (made by the game: slot, tick rate, tick)
    Note over C: onAccepted(payload): State::Connected
    C-->>G: game messages, at least one datagram per second
    G-->>C: game messages, at least one datagram per second
    C->>G: DISCONNECT × 3, or 5 s of silence
    Note over G: onClosed(session, end)

A session connects with CONNECT and ACCEPTED, stays open with heartbeats, and ends with DISCONNECT or a timeout.

ClientSession (client) SessionHost (game) Sessions One: the one of GAME_JOINED One per player, added on ADD_PLAYER Sends to The game's address, through its send function The address each client sends from, learned from its first authentic datagram Handlers onAccepted, onMessage, onClose onConnected, onMessage, onClosed Before connecting send() refuses game messages until ACCEPTED Messages before CONNECT are ignored Gives up No ACCEPTED within 5 s: ConnectTimedOut (UDP is probably blocked) No CONNECT within 10 s: ConnectTimedOut

Like the channel, the sessions have no socket and no clock: they are given the datagrams received and the time, and send through a function. The application owns the UdpSocket and calls update() regularly:

Client (game loop)Game (network thread) 
rtype::network::UdpSocket socket(loop, rtype::network::Address::anyIpv4(0));
rtype::network::ClientSession session(joined.sessionId, joined.clientKey, joined.serverKey,
    [&](std::span<const std::byte> datagram) { socket.send(gameAddress, datagram); });

socket.startReceiving([&](const rtype::network::Address &from, std::span<const std::byte> datagram) {
    if (from == gameAddress) { // only the game's datagrams
        session.receive(datagram, Clock::now());
    }
});
session.start(onAccepted, onMessage, onClose, Clock::now());

// Every frame
loop.poll();
session.send(InputType, input, rtype::network::Delivery::Unreliable);
session.update(Clock::now()); // sends, resends, acknowledgements, heartbeat, timeouts

rtype::network::UdpSocket socket(loop, rtype::network::Address::anyIpv4(port));
rtype::network::SessionHost host(
    [&](const rtype::network::Address &to, std::span<const std::byte> datagram) { socket.send(to, datagram); },
    {
        .onConnected = [&](std::uint32_t session, const rtype::network::Address &) {
            host.send(session, rtype::network::session_message::Accepted, accepted,
                      rtype::network::Delivery::Reliable);
        },
        .onMessage = [&](std::uint32_t session, std::uint8_t type, std::span<const std::byte> payload) {},
        .onClosed = [&](std::uint32_t session, rtype::network::SessionEnd end) {},
    });
socket.startReceiving([&](const rtype::network::Address &from, std::span<const std::byte> datagram) {
    host.receive(from, datagram, Clock::now());
});

host.add(sessionId, clientKey, serverKey, Clock::now()); // on ADD_PLAYER
host.update(Clock::now());                                // every tick

The session layer handles CONNECT, ACCEPTED and DISCONNECT itself; every other message (PLAYER_JOINED, INPUT, SNAPSHOT…) goes to onMessage. The payload of ACCEPTED is made by the game and given as is to the client's onAccepted.

items.title: How a session ends
items.text:
SessionEnd::Cause When DISCONNECT sent Disconnected The peer sent DISCONNECT, with its reason (Quit, GameOver, Shutdown, ProtocolError) — TimedOut Nothing authentic received for 5 s: the peer crashed or lost the network No: the peer does not hear anyway ConnectTimedOut Never connected (5 s for the client, 10 s for the game) No Failed The peer stopped acknowledging: 256 reliable messages wait Yes, ProtocolError — The application called close(reason) Yes, with the reason; no handler is called

DISCONNECT is not reliable: it is sent in three datagrams in a row, and one of them is enough. If all three are lost, the peer closes after its 5 s timeout.

items.title: What the game protects itself against
items.text:
SessionHost::receive() follows the order of the protocol and drops silently at the first failure, without ever answering: an answer to a forged datagram could be used to flood someone else.

  1. Size and header (parseDatagramHeader()).
  2. A known session.
  3. At most 200 datagrams per second and per source address, counted before decrypting: a flood costs almost nothing.
  4. The replay window, then the tag, then the body.

A client whose port changes, which a home router may do, is followed: an authentic datagram from another address with a newer packet number moves the session there. An older one, arriving late, does not.

Handlers may call the host, including close() of the session they are called for: the messages that follow in the same datagram are then dropped.

items.title: Binary serialization
items.text:
A message is sent as bytes: each field written one after the other, as the protocol conventions define it: big-endian integers, no padding, str8 texts. Writer writes the fields, Reader reads them back. To add a message, follow Add a network message.

rtype::network::Writer writer;
writer.writeU8(0x01);        // type: HELLO
writer.writeU16(1);          // version
writer.writeString("Pavel"); // name: length on one byte, then the UTF-8 bytes
connection.send(writer.bytes());
Type of the specification Writer Reader u8, u16, u32, u64 writeU8() … writeU64() readU8() … readU64() i16, i32 writeI16(), writeI32() readI16(), readI32() bool writeBool() readBool(): a value other than 0 or 1 is an error bytes[N] writeBytes(span) readBytes(n) (a view into the data) or readBytes<N>() (a copy) str8 writeString(text) readString(min, max): length range of the field, text checked

Why not memcpy a struct? The compiler adds padding between fields, differently on GCC and MSVC, and an x86 processor stores integers little-endian. Writing each field explicitly gives the same bytes everywhere.

items.title: Reading safely
items.text:
The bytes come from the network: they may be cut, forged or random. Reader is built so that a decoder cannot go wrong:

  • It never reads past the end. A field that is not entirely there fails.

  • The first failure sticks. After a missing or invalid field, every later read returns 0, false or an empty value, and error() keeps the first problem. A decoder reads all its fields, then checks once:

    rtype::network::Reader reader(payload);
const std::uint16_t version = reader.readU16();
const std::string name = reader.readString(1, 16);
if (!reader.finish()) { // fails if a read failed, or if bytes are left
    logger.debug("HELLO dropped: {}", toString(reader.error()));
    return std::nullopt;
}

  • Texts are checked: valid UTF-8 (no cut or overlong characters, no surrogates), no ASCII control character, length within the range of the field. A name cannot carry a line break that would forge a line in the logs, nor terminal escape codes.

  • Decoders refuse values themselves with reader.fail(), for instance a number of players above 4.
  • Nothing is allocated from an unchecked length. A str8 is at most 255 bytes and only built once its bytes are there. For a list, never reserve(count) with a count read from the network: loop while reader.ok(), and the loop stops at the end of the data even if the count announces 65535 entries.
  • No side effect: a reader only reads its bytes. Decoders built on it are pure functions, bytes in and message or error out, which a fuzzer can call millions of times (testing policy).

Writer is used with values from our own code: a value the protocol forbids (a str8 over 255 bytes, a text with a control character) is a programming error, and throws an exception. Check a text typed by the player with isValidText() before sending it.

items.title: Logs
items.text:
The library writes with a logger named network (Logging):

Level Messages trace Every datagram and every piece of a stream received, with its size trace (TLS) Every piece of a TLS stream decrypted, with its size trace (datagrams) Every encrypted datagram dropped, with the reason: invalid header, or not authentic. Never the keys trace (reliability) Every malformed body dropped, every reliable message sent again debug (reliability) A channel that fails, and why; unreliable messages dropped because too many wait to be sent trace (sessions) Every datagram of an unknown session dropped debug (sessions) Sessions added, connecting, accepted, connected, moved to another address, closed and ended (with the cause), source addresses over 200 datagrams per second debug Sockets opened and closed, connections accepted, opened, closed and lost, datagrams dropped, TLS handshakes started and done (with the cipher suite) warning A listener that cannot accept connections (for instance, no file descriptor left), a peer sending an invalid frame, a TLS connection failing or closed during its handshake error A TLS server presenting a key other than the pinned one, with its fingerprint 
RTYPE_LOG_LEVEL=debug ./build/bin/r-type_server

items.title: Tests
items.text:
The tests in tests/network.cpp (tag [network]) run over the loopback, with ports chosen by the system so that they never conflict: datagrams in both directions and from another thread, ports in use, connections, large transfers, closing from either side, refused connections and timeouts.

The tests in tests/serialization.cpp (same tag) check the round trip of every type, the edge values, every rejection case, and the HELLO frame given as an example in the specification, byte for byte.

The tests in tests/framing.cpp (same tag) check the frame decoder with frames cut byte by byte, grouped, or cut at random places, the maximum size and the invalid sizes; then framed connections over the loopback: frames in both directions, a peer sending an invalid frame, and close() from inside the frame handler.

The tests in tests/tls.cpp (same tag) check the fingerprints against the one OpenSSL computes, the identities (generated, saved and read back, refused keys, files), then TLS connections over the loopback: large transfers in both directions, bytes sent before the handshake, a server with another key, a relay in the middle that reads nothing and whose changed byte is detected, peers that do not speak TLS, closing, frames over TLS, the end of the handshake reported once and never for a failed one, and Mbed TLS used from two threads at once.

The tests in tests/datagram.cpp (same tag) check two datagrams byte for byte against another implementation of RFC 8439 (Python's cryptography package), the round trip of bodies from 0 to 1168 bytes, that every bit changed anywhere makes a datagram invalid, other keys, random bytes, every invalid header, the edges of the replay window (256 and 257 numbers below, jumps, any order, the largest number) and the end of the packet numbers.

The tests in tests/reliability.cpp (same tag) check the body byte for byte, its round trip, every malformed case and random bodies; then a channel alone: acknowledgements, resends after the delay and not before, delivery in order whatever the order of the datagrams, ids wrapping from 65535 to 0, large messages in datagrams of their own, the RTT, and failing when the peer stops acknowledging. Last, two channels play 10 seconds of a game through a fake network that loses 30 % of the datagrams, duplicates 10 % and delays them by 20 to 120 ms, so that they arrive out of order: every reliable message arrives once and in order, no unreliable message arrives twice.

The tests in tests/session.cpp (same tag) run a ClientSession and a SessionHost through a fake network in memory, with the time given by the test: connecting, CONNECT sent again, both connect timeouts, heartbeats over 20 s of silence, the 5 s timeout on both sides, 30 % loss, DISCONNECT both ways and with two copies out of three lost, a game that stops acknowledging, a handler that closes its session, replayed, forged and unknown datagrams that get no answer, a client whose port changes, a late datagram from another address, and the limit of 200 datagrams per second. A last test runs a session over real UDP sockets on the loopback.

The tests in tests/timer.cpp (same tag) check timers once and repeating, cancelled and destroyed when already due, started again and from another thread, and the stop signals, raised in the test process itself.

Our client and server were also checked against OpenSSL, by hand (it is not installed on every CI runner):

# Our client against an OpenSSL server holding the test key of tests/tls.cpp
openssl req -new -x509 -key test.key -out test.crt -subj "/CN=test"
openssl s_server -accept 4433 -key test.key -cert test.crt -tls1_3 -www
# OpenSSL's client against our server: TLS 1.3 accepted, TLS 1.2 refused
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:4433 -tls1_3
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:4433 -tls1_2

./build/bin/rtype_tests "[network]"

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• No R-Type messages yet: the lobby and the game instances come next, following the protocol. The fuzzing of the decoders comes with them; parseDatagramHeader() and openDatagram() are ready for it.
  • No handshake timeout in the connection itself: a peer that opens a connection and never finishes the handshake keeps it open. The server closes such connections with the limits of the protocol (10 s for the handshake), in the lobby step.
  • One lock for all of Mbed TLS, see Threads.
  • One copy per send: send() copies the data into a new buffer, unless it is given a std::vector it can take (send(std::move(bytes))). Enough for now; a pool of buffers can replace it if measurements show the cost.
  • IPv4 or IPv6, not both on one socket: a socket bound to Address::anyIpv6() may or may not accept IPv4 depending on the system. The server listens on IPv4 for now.

items.title: Rendering
items.text:
The render library (libs/render, namespace rtype::render) is the only part of the client that talks to raylib for graphics. Its public headers contain no raylib type: the rest of the client draws through our own classes and types, and does not even link raylib.

Class / header Role Window Opens the game window and closes it when destroyed. ResourceManager Loads textures and fonts once, and hands out handles to refer to them. Renderer Draws textures, text and shapes at a fixed logical resolution. Types.hpp Vector2, Rectangle, Color and the colors:: constants. Paths.hpp applicationDirectory(), the directory of the running executable.

items.title: Lifetimes
items.text:
Graphics resources live in the window's graphics context: textures cannot exist without an open window, and must be freed before it closes. Each class enforces this with RAII (it acquires what it needs in its constructor and frees it in its destructor) and by taking the objects it depends on as constructor parameters:

const Window window;                                                   // 1. opens the window
ResourceManager resources(window, applicationDirectory() / "assets");  // 2. needs an open window
Renderer renderer(window, resources);                                  // 3. needs the window and the resources

C++ destroys local objects in the reverse order of their declaration, so this order is all it takes: the renderer and the resources are freed before the window closes.

Declaration order

Always declare the window first, then the resources, then the renderer. The constructors make it impossible to create the resources or the renderer without a window, but only the declaration order guarantees that they are destroyed before it.

items.title: Window
items.text:
Window opens the window in its constructor and closes it in its destructor. It cannot be copied nor moved, and only one can exist at a time, since raylib supports a single window: creating a second one throws std::logic_error.

Window window({.width = 1920, .height = 1080, .title = "R-Type", .targetFps = 144});

while (!window.shouldClose()) { ... }   // close button, system shortcut (Alt+F4), or requestClose()
const float dt = window.frameTime();    // duration of the last frame, in seconds

WindowSettings also sets whether the window is resizable, whether vertical synchronisation is on, and whether it opens in fullscreen.

items.title: Window options
items.text:
Most settings can be changed while the game runs, for instance from an options menu:

Function Effect setFullscreen(bool), isFullscreen() Switches between a window and fullscreen. setSize(width, height) Resizes the window, in pixels. Leaves fullscreen first. setTitle(title) Changes the title of the window. setCursorVisible(bool), isCursorVisible() Shows or hides the mouse pointer over the window. setVsync(bool) Turns vertical synchronisation on or off. setTargetFps(fps) Sets the maximum number of frames per second, 0 for no limit. requestClose() Asks the window to close, for instance from a Quit button: shouldClose() then returns true.

Fullscreen is a borderless window covering the screen it is on, at the resolution of that screen. raylib also has an exclusive fullscreen, which changes the video mode of the screen to match the window: it is slow to switch, can rearrange the other screens, and behaves badly when switching to another application. Since the game is already scaled to any window size, the borderless mode loses nothing. Leaving fullscreen restores the previous size and position of the window.

The client switches fullscreen with F11 (the ToggleFullscreen action) or from the menu, and hides the mouse pointer during the game, where it would hide part of the screen.

items.title: Escape key
items.text: raylib closes the window when Esc is pressed by default. Window disables this: in a game, Escape opens a menu rather than quitting without confirmation. The client binds it to the Menu action, see Controls of R-Type.

items.title: Handles
items.text:
The ResourceManager loads files from the assets directory and returns a handle for each one: TextureId for an image, FontId for a font. A handle is a small number that is cheap to copy and to store in an ECS component. Texture and font handles are different types, so one cannot be passed where the other is expected.

const TextureId ship = resources.loadTexture("sprites/ship.png");
const FontId font = resources.loadFont("fonts/FiraSans-Black.ttf", 48);

items.title: Each file is loaded once
items.text:
For nonblocking loading, call loadTextureAsync(), loadFontAsync() or loadModelAsync() and keep the returned std::shared_future. Call finishPendingLoads() once per frame on the render thread. Check future.wait_for(std::chrono::seconds(0)) before calling get(); draw a placeholder while it is pending. A failure is reported by get() as an exception. Requests for the same asset and options share one future. Pass engine.assetLoading().queue() to the manager constructor to share the engine's worker with audio. The client's startup displays a loading screen while its menu assets are prepared. See ADR 0017 for the thread boundaries and the model-loading limitation.

Loading the same path again returns the same handle without reading the file again: fifty enemies sharing one sprite share one texture in graphics memory. Fonts are identified by their path and their size, because a font is rendered to a texture at the size it is loaded with.

Internally, each kind of resource is stored in a ResourceCache, a generic container that maps a key (the path) to a handle and loads missing resources with a function given by the caller. It does not depend on raylib, which is why it is unit tested without a window (tests/resource_cache.cpp). It is part of the core library (libs/core), with the Handle type, so that the audio library uses it too.

items.title: Errors
items.text: raylib does not report loading errors: a missing file gives an empty texture and a warning in the console. The ResourceManager turns this into a std::runtime_error naming the file, so that a missing asset is noticed immediately.

items.title: Supported formats
items.text:
No JPEG

raylib is built with its default options: images must be PNG, BMP, QOI or another format enabled by default. JPEG is not supported, and is a poor choice for sprites anyway, since it has no transparency. Fonts are TTF or OTF files.

items.title: Fonts
items.text: By default, raylib only renders the ASCII characters of a font: any other character is drawn as "?". The ResourceManager also renders the Latin-1 characters, which cover the accented letters of most Western European languages ("é", "ç", "ü", "ß"...), plus "œ", "Œ" and "€". Characters outside of this set, for instance from Cyrillic or Asian scripts, are still drawn as "?".

items.title: Where assets are found
items.text: Assets live in apps/client/assets/. The build copies them next to the executable, and the client package ships them in the same place. The client loads them from applicationDirectory() / "assets", so it finds them wherever it is started from. See Draw a sprite for the full workflow.

items.title: Logical resolution
items.text:
The game has a fixed size, 1920x1080 game units by default, whatever the size of the window. Every position and size given to the renderer is in these game units: a ship at x = 1500 is at the same place on every screen, which is what lets the server and all the clients agree on coordinates.

The whole game area is always shown, scaled as much as the window allows. When the window has another shape than the game, the view extends around the game area, on both sides, instead of leaving black bars: a 16:10 screen shows the 1920x1080 game from y = -60 to y = 1140, a 21:9 screen from x = -320 to x = 2240. visibleArea() gives that part of the game, in game units; the interface is placed relative to it (the AnchorSystem uses it), so that it follows the edges of any screen, while the gameplay stays in the game area.

Positions coming from the window, such as the mouse pointer, are in window pixels. windowToGame() converts them into game units, taking the scaling into account (see Mouse).

items.title: A frame
items.text:
Everything is drawn between beginFrame() and endFrame(), in order: what is drawn last is on top.

renderer.beginFrame(colors::Black);
renderer.drawTexture(background, {0.0f, 0.0f});
renderer.drawTexture(ship, {100.0f, 540.0f});
renderer.drawText(font, "Score: 42", {20.0f, 20.0f}, 48.0f, colors::White);
renderer.endFrame();

The frame is not drawn directly in the window, but in an off-screen image of the size of the window:

flowchart LR
    Begin["beginFrame()"] --> Target["Off-screen image<br/>window resolution"]
    Draw["drawTexture()<br/>drawText()<br/>drawRectangle()"] --> Target
    Target -- "endFrame(): colour filter,<br/>copied as is" --> Window["Window<br/>(any size)"]

Drawing calls write in game units to an off-screen image at the resolution of the window; endFrame() copies it into the window.

  1. beginFrame() recreates the off-screen image if the window changed size, starts drawing into it, fills it with the background colour, and sets a 2D view that maps the visible area onto it.
  2. The drawing functions write into this image, in game units: the view scales them to pixels, so the image stays sharp on a large screen.
  3. endFrame() copies the image into the window, through the colour filter, then shows it.

The visible area is computed by computeVisibleArea() (Viewport.hpp), a pure function that is unit tested (tests/viewport.cpp).

items.title: Drawing functions
items.text:
Function Draws drawTexture(id, position, tint) A whole texture at its original size. drawTexture(id, source, destination, rotation, tint) Part of a texture (one frame of a sprite sheet), stretched to the destination and rotated around its centre, in degrees. drawRectangle(rectangle, color) A filled rectangle. drawCircle(center, radius, color) A filled circle, for instance a star or a round projectile. drawRectangleOutline(rectangle, thickness, color) The outline of a rectangle, for instance a hitbox or a button frame. drawCircleOutline(center, radius, thickness, color) The outline of a circle, for instance a round hitbox. drawLine(start, end, thickness, color) A straight line of any thickness, for instance a laser. drawTriangle(first, second, third, color) A filled triangle, for instance a placeholder ship. drawText(font, text, position, size, color) Text with a loaded font. drawText(text, position, size, color) Text with raylib's built-in font, for debugging. drawFps(position) The number of frames per second, for debugging.

Outlines are drawn inside the shape: the outer edge of the outline is the edge of the rectangle or circle. An outline drawn around a hitbox therefore shows exactly the area that collides.

textureSize() and measureText() give sizes without drawing, for instance to centre a text. The tint is multiplied with the texture: white keeps it unchanged, a lower alpha fades it.

items.title: Errors
items.text: Drawing outside of a frame, starting a frame twice or ending a frame that was not started throws std::logic_error, with a message telling how to fix the call. These are programming errors: raylib would otherwise draw to the wrong place without any warning.

items.title: Colour filters
items.text:
A colour filter changes the colours of the whole image, interface included, for colour-blind players or players with low vision:

renderer.setColorFilter(ColorFilter::Deuteranopia);
Filter For Effect Protanopia, Deuteranopia Players who do not perceive red or green (red-green colour blindness, about 8% of men) Shifts the colours they confuse towards colours they can tell apart. Tritanopia Players who do not perceive blue (blue-yellow colour blindness, rare) Same, for blue and yellow. SimulateProtanopia, SimulateDeuteranopia, SimulateTritanopia The team Shows the game as a colour-blind player sees it, to check that sprites stay distinguishable. HighContrast Players with low vision Stronger contrast and saturation.

The filter is a shader (a small program run by the graphics card on every pixel) applied in endFrame(), when the off-screen image is copied to the window: the game keeps drawing with its normal colours, and the filter costs one pass over the image. If the graphics card cannot compile it, a warning is logged and the game is shown unfiltered. Its GLSL code is in the shaders library (libs/shaders/glsl/), next to the lighting shader of the 3D models. At build time, each program becomes a generated header holding its code as strings (rtype/shaders/<Program>.hpp), so the game needs no shader file; the graphics driver compiles them when the game starts. If glslangValidator is installed, the build also checks their syntax.

How it works. Simulation uses the matrices of Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009), applied to linear colours (without the sRGB gamma curve). Correction, also called daltonisation, computes the difference between the original colour and the simulated one, which is what the player cannot see, and moves it to the channels they can see. For a player with deuteranopia, the perceived difference between the red and the green of the test palette goes from 60 to 129 (on a scale of 0 to 441) with the correction.

A help, not a substitute

Correction makes confused colours easier to tell apart, it does not restore them. The game must not rely on colour only: player ships, enemies and projectiles should also differ by shape, as planned in Accessibility. The simulation filters are the way to check it.

items.title: Implementation notes
items.text:
These details only matter when working inside libs/render:

  • Pimpl. ResourceManager and Renderer store their state in a struct Impl defined in their .cpp file. Their headers can then hold raylib objects without including raylib.h.
  • Private header. The RAII wrappers of raylib textures and fonts are in src/Resources.hpp, shared by the ResourceManager, which loads them, and the Renderer, which draws them. ResourceManager declares Renderer as a friend so that it can read them.
  • Name clashes. Our Vector2, Rectangle and Color have the same names as raylib's types. Inside the library, raylib's ones are written ::Rectangle, and raylib's colour macros (WHITE, BLACK...) cannot be used, as they expand to our Color.
  • Triangle winding. raylib only draws triangles whose corners are given counter-clockwise on screen: the others are culled without any warning. drawTriangle() reorders the corners, so they can be given in any order.
  • Upside-down render target. OpenGL stores off-screen images upside down: endFrame() copies the image with a negative source height to flip it back.

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• No sorting by layer: the drawing order is the call order. The ECS render system will sort entities by layer (background, enemies, players, interface) before drawing them.
  • No 3D yet. 3D models are planned: they will be drawn on the same plane and in the same game units as sprites, so that the server and the gameplay stay in 2D.

items.title: Scenes and interface
items.text: Everything the client draws is an entity of the ECS: the world, the HUD and the menus (ADR 0007). This page describes the client library built on the ECS (libs/engine): scenes, drawing, animations and menus.

items.title: Where things are
items.text:
The client library is organised like the ECS, with one file per system:

libs/engine/include/rtype/engine/
  Component/    the data attached to entities
    Drawing.hpp     Layer, Drawable, Text, BoundText, Sprite, Box, Scale, Opacity
    Animation.hpp   Easing, ease(), Tween, Spin, ModelAnimation, switchModelAnimation()
    Widget.hpp      Focusable, Focused, Hitbox, Button, Toggle, Slider, Choice, TextField
    Layout.hpp      Column, ColumnItem, AnchorPoint, Anchor
    Toast.hpp       ToastType, Toast
  System/       the systems, one per file
    InterfaceSystem.hpp  WidgetTextSystem.hpp  BoundTextSystem.hpp  TweenSystem.hpp  HitboxSystem.hpp
    ColumnLayoutSystem.hpp  AnchorSystem.hpp  ToastSystem.hpp  SpinSystem.hpp  ModelAnimationSystem.hpp
  Interface/    what the interface is built with
    MenuBuilder.hpp  InterfaceBuilder.hpp  Navigation.hpp  Style.hpp  Metrics.hpp
  Rendering/
    SceneRenderer.hpp  ColliderDebugRenderer.hpp
  Scene/
    Scenes.hpp      SceneId, SceneMember, SceneSettings, Scenes
  Engine.hpp    includes everything above

The sources in libs/engine/src/ follow the same folders. Every header compiles on its own: include the precise headers you need, or rtype/engine/Engine.hpp for everything.

items.title: The systems and their order
items.text:
Engine engine;
Ecs &ecs = engine.getEcs();
Scenes &scenes = engine.getScenes();
ecs.registerSystem<ConsoleSystem>(engine, devices);
ecs.registerSystem<InterfaceSystem>(ecs, scenes, devices, metrics, style);
ecs.registerSystem<GameSessionSystem>(ecs, scenes, engine.getControls());
ecs.registerSystem<WidgetTextSystem>();
ecs.registerSystem<BoundTextSystem>();
ecs.registerSystem<TweenSystem>();
ecs.registerSystem<SpinSystem>();
ecs.registerSystem<FlightSystem>();
ecs.registerSystem<IntroSystem>(scenes, devices);
ecs.registerSystem<ModelAnimationSystem>();
ecs.registerSystem<HitboxSystem>(metrics, style);
ecs.registerSystem<ColumnLayoutSystem>(ecs);
ecs.registerSystem<AnchorSystem>(metrics);
ecs.registerSystem<ToastSystem>(ecs, metrics, style);
ecs.registerSystem<TransformSystem>(ecs);
SceneRenderer sceneRenderer(ecs, scenes, style);

// Each frame
engine.update(window.frameTime());
renderer.beginFrame();
sceneRenderer.draw(renderer, Layer::World);
sceneRenderer.draw(renderer, Layer::Interface);
renderer.endFrame();
# System Role 1 Scenes Records which scene receives input for the whole update. 2 ConsoleSystem, InterfaceSystem Console commands, menu focus, and navigation; they read the input before the game. 3 GameSessionSystem The game: the input of the player to its session, the snapshots to the entities of the game scene (A game in the client). 4 WidgetTextSystem, BoundTextSystem, TweenSystem, SpinSystem Texts of the widgets and bound texts, tweens, spinning models. 5 FlightSystem, IntroSystem Client systems of the main menu: the ships flying around the station, the intro. 6 ModelAnimationSystem Animations of skinned models: the SceneRenderer poses each model before drawing it, fading from the previous animation after switchModelAnimation(). 7 HitboxSystem, ColumnLayoutSystem, AnchorSystem Sizes, then layout: columns, then anchors, which need the final sizes. 8 ToastSystem Places, fades and destroys the toasts. 9 TransformSystem Positions of the children from their parents, last.

The SceneRenderer is not a system: drawing happens after the update, between beginFrame() and endFrame(), and may happen several times per frame (once per eye in VR).

items.title: ECS features
items.text: The interface relies on features of the ECS described in ECS: the elapsed time given to systems, entity references (EntityRef), deferred actions (a button that opens a menu has its action deferred) and the hierarchy (attach(), isHidden()): the widgets of a menu are attached to its column, and nothing hidden is drawn or focused.

items.title: Scenes
items.text:
A scene groups the entities of a phase of the game: home screen, game, pause menu, options. Every entity of a scene has a SceneMember; when the scene closes, the Engine destroys them all at once, at the start of its next update (until then they are neither visible nor updated). Entities without it are persistent: a star-field shared by the menus and the game survives every scene change.
