Scenes are part of the engine (rtype::engine::Scenes, rtype/engine/Scene/Scenes.hpp), not of the ECS: the ECS only stores entities and components, and knows nothing about what a scene is. Scenes itself only keeps the stack and never touches the ECS: destroying the entities of a closed scene is the Engine's job.

const SceneId game = engine.getScenes().open({.updatesWhenCovered = true});
const entity_t ship = ecs.createEntity();
ecs.addComponent<SceneMember>(ship, game);

Scenes form a stack:

Setting Effect Example overlay The scenes below stay visible Pause menu over the game hidesInterfaceBelow With overlay, only the world of the scenes below stays visible, not their interface Submenu over the 3D background of the main menu updatesWhenCovered The scene keeps updating under others Network game under the pause menu onBack Called on Back instead of closing the scene Game: opens the pause menu

Systems ask Scenes what to do with an entity or a scene: receivesInput() (only the scene at the top), updates(), isVisible(), isInterfaceVisible().

The input owner is set at the start of the update

The scene that receives the input is recorded when the update starts, by the Scenes system. When Escape closes the pause menu, the game does not receive the input until the next update: it does not see the same Escape press and does not open the menu again.

items.title: Named scenes
items.text:
The Engine registers Scenes first and opens scenes by name (ADR 0009). A scene is declared once, with a function that builds its entities each time it opens:

engine.createScene("game", {.updatesWhenCovered = true}, [](Engine &engine, SceneId scene) {
    const entity_t ship = engine.getEcs().createEntity();
    engine.getEcs().addComponent<SceneMember>(ship, scene);
});
engine.subscribeToEvent("game:open", physics, Reaction::Enable);
engine.subscribeToEvent("game:close", physics, Reaction::Disable);

engine.switchScene("game"); // closes every open scene, then opens the game
engine.pushScene("pause");  // opens the pause menu over the game
engine.popScene();          // closes the scene at the top

These requests take effect at the start of the next Engine::update, then the events "<name>:open" and "<name>:close" of the scenes opened and closed are triggered, and their reactions applied in the same update.

items.title: Collider and grid debug overlay
items.text:
The client can draw visible physics colliders over the world layer. Press F3 to toggle the overlay, or start the client with RTYPE_DEBUG_COLLIDERS=1 to show it immediately. The overlay draws AABB outlines in green, sphere outlines in green, triggers in yellow, and the spatial grid in pale blue. Grid lines use the same cell size as CollisionSystem and game coordinates, so they stay aligned with the broad phase.

ColliderDebugRenderer lives in libs/engine, reads ECS Position and Collider, and skips hidden entities or entities in hidden scenes. It draws after the world and before the interface. The physics library still has no rendering dependency. The current game scene is empty; collider outlines appear as soon as the game creates entities with Position and Collider.

Component Draws Drawable Required: the layer (World or Interface) and the order inside it (higher on top). Text A text, centred on the position. Sprite A texture or a frame of a sprite sheet, centred on the position. Box A rectangle, filled or outlined, centred on the position. Scale, Opacity Size factor and transparency, animated by tweens.

The HUD is made of entities of the game scene in the Interface layer: it is drawn after the world.

items.title: Animations
items.text:
A Tween animates the Scale or the Opacity of an entity, then is removed, unless it goes back and forth:

ecs.addComponent<Tween>(enemy, Tween{.target = TweenTarget::Opacity, .from = 1.0f, .to = 0.2f,
                                     .duration = 0.1f, .pingPong = true});   // blinks when hit
Easing Shape Linear Constant speed EaseOut Fast, then slowing down EaseOutBack Goes slightly past the end, then comes back: a bounce

The focused widget of a menu bounces to InterfaceStyle::focusScale with EaseOutBack.

items.title: Menus
items.text:
MenuBuilder creates a background, a title and widgets stacked in a column, in a scene it opens:

MenuBuilder pause(ecs, scenes, metrics, style, "Pause", {.overlay = true});
const SceneId scene = pause.scene();
pause.button("Resume", [&scenes, scene] { scenes.close(scene); });
pause.toggle("Fullscreen", [&] { return window.isFullscreen(); }, [&](bool on) { window.setFullscreen(on); });

Or in a scene already open, such as a named scene in its build function:

engine.createScene("main_menu", {}, [&](Engine &engine, SceneId scene) {
    MenuBuilder menu(engine.getEcs(), scene, metrics, style, "R-Type");
    menu.button("Play", [&engine] { engine.switchScene("game"); });
    menu.button("Quit", [&window] { window.requestClose(); });
});

It only creates entities: an icon or an animation can be added to any of them afterwards.

Widget Shows Reacts to label A text that cannot get the focus — button Play Confirm, click toggle Fullscreen: On Confirm and click switch it; Right on, Left off slider Volume: 80% Left, Right and the wheel change it by steps choice Colour filter: None Left, Right, the wheel and a click go through the options textField Name: Player Typing edits it while focused, with cursor, selection and clipboard; Confirm submits it

Values are read and written through functions, not copied: a toggle for fullscreen always shows the real setting, even when it is changed by a shortcut key.

items.title: Elements placed anywhere
items.text:
InterfaceBuilder puts elements anywhere on the screen, in a scene already open: a HUD, a version number, a button in a corner. It draws no background. Each element gets an Anchor: its own point point is put on the same point of the screen, then moved by the offset (x to the right, y downwards). The AnchorSystem computes the position every frame from the size of the element: its hitbox at scale 1 for a widget, otherwise its text, sprite or box. An anchored entity must not have a Parent.

engine.createScene("game", {.updatesWhenCovered = true}, [&](Engine &engine, SceneId scene) {
    InterfaceBuilder hud(engine.getEcs(), scene, style);
    hud.boundText([&] { return "Score: " + std::to_string(score); }, {AnchorPoint::TopLeft, 20.0f, 20.0f});
    hud.text("v0.1", {AnchorPoint::BottomRight, -20.0f, -20.0f});
    hud.button("Pause", [&engine] { engine.pushScene("pause"); }, {AnchorPoint::TopRight, -20.0f, 20.0f});
});
Element Creates text A Text with the font, size and colour of the style boundText A Text rewritten every frame from a function by the BoundTextSystem (score, lives, ping) box A filled or outlined Box sprite A Sprite: a texture or a part of it button A focusable Button; the buttons of a builder get the focus in the order they are created backButton A small square Button with a leftwards arrow (←), as high as the other buttons, to go back header The top of a secondary screen: a backButton, then the title to its right on the same line

A BoundText can also be added to any entity with a Text, outside of the builders.

items.title: Toasts
items.text:
A toast is a short message shown in a corner of the screen for a few seconds, over every scene and across scene switches. Showing one takes only its text, and optionally its type, which sets the colour of its accent:

engine.showToast("Settings saved");
engine.showToast("Connection lost", ToastType::Error); // Info, Success, Warning or Error

The toast entity holds only a Toast (its text and type). Everything about its look lives in one place, InterfaceStyle::toast (ToastStyle): corner, margin, sizes, colours, accent of each type, durations, slide, maximum number shown. The SceneRenderer draws it from that style (drawToast), and the ToastSystem places, fades and destroys it. To change how every toast looks, change the style, or drawToast for its shape; the calls stay the same.

Toasts are stacked from the corner, the newest nearest to it; the others glide to their new place. Beyond maxVisible, the oldest fade out early. In the client, the console command toast [info|success|warning|error] <text> shows one.

items.title: Navigation
items.text:
Action Keyboard Gamepad (first one) Effect Up, Down Arrows D-pad, left stick Moves the focus, skipping labels, around at the ends Left, Right Arrows D-pad, left stick Changes the value of the focused widget Confirm Enter Bottom face button Activates the focused widget Back Esc Right face button, Start Goes back from the scene, even one without widgets: Escape in the game opens its pause menu Click Left mouse button — Activates the widget under the pointer
  • Only keys that do not type text are used, so that letters, Space and Backspace edit text fields.
  • Holding a direction repeats it; sticks have a larger dead zone (0.5) than in game.
  • The mouse focuses a widget only when it moves, so that a still pointer does not fight the keyboard.
  • A click activates the widget under the pointer, not the focused one.
  • Characters typed while no text field has the focus are dropped.

items.title: Testing
items.text: The ECS has its own tests (see ECS). tests/scenes.cpp tests the scenes, and tests/engine.cpp builds menus with MenuBuilder and drives them with the FakeInput and fake text measures, without a window: focus, every widget, layout, mouse, scenes, and the bounce of the focused widget.

items.title: Server
items.text:
r-type_server is one binary with two modes (ADR 0013): the master, started by whoever hosts the server, runs the lobby; each instance, started by the master with --instance, runs one game. This page describes how the program starts, what it is given, and how it stops. The lobby and the game come in the next steps of the "Server & networking" work.

To run a server, see Run a server.

items.title: Code layout
items.text:
apps/server/src/
  main.cpp                 reads the environment, then calls run()
  Server.cpp               run(): the options, then the master or an instance
  Common/                  what both modes share
    InstanceMessages.cpp   the messages between the master and its instances
    Options.cpp            the command line of both modes, the exit codes
    Lifecycle.cpp          runUntilStopped(): the event loop and the stop signals
    Secret.cpp             the secret the master gives to its instances
  Master/                  the master: the lobby, and the instances it starts
    Master.cpp             runMaster()
    Lobby.cpp              the lobby: the TLS connections of the clients and their requests
    Games.cpp              the games: one instance each, started, connected back, watched
    Process.cpp            Process: starts a program and stops it, on Linux and Windows
  Instance/                an instance: one game
    Instance.cpp           runInstance(): the life of the instance, with or without a master
    MasterLink.cpp         the connection to the master
    GameHost.cpp           the network side of the game: UDP, sessions, players, game messages
    GameThread.cpp         the simulation thread, at 60 ticks per second

Everything but main.cpp is the library r-type_server_core, so that the tests can call it (tests/server_options.cpp, tests/server_lifecycle.cpp, tests/process.cpp, tests/server_instance.cpp, tests/server_lobby.cpp, tests/server_games.cpp). Includes are written from src/, like in the client: #include "Common/Options.hpp". The next steps add their files to the folder of their mode: the lobby and the supervision of the instances in Master/, the game in Instance/, what both sides read in Common/.

items.title: Starting
items.text:
flowchart TB
    Main["main()"] --> Parse["parseOptions()"]
    Parse -- "invalid" --> Exit2["exit 2"]
    Parse -- "--help, --version" --> Show["shows it, exit 0"]
    Parse -- "master" --> Master["runMaster()<br/>loads the key, opens the port"]
    Parse -- "--instance" --> Instance["runInstance()<br/>reads the secret"]
    Master -- "fails" --> Exit1["exit 1"]
    Instance -- "fails" --> Exit1
    Master --> Run["runUntilStopped()"]
    Instance --> Run

The options are checked first; then each mode does everything that can fail before it starts running, so that a server that cannot work stops at once with the reason.

items.title: Master
items.text:
Option Default Meaning -p, --port <port> 4242 TCP port of the lobby; 0 lets the system choose --bind <ip> 0.0.0.0 Address to listen on: every interface by default, 127.0.0.1 for this machine only --game-ports <first>-<last> 4243–4299 UDP ports of the games, one per game: their number is the most games at once -k, --key <file> server.key Private key of the server (Generate the server keys) --check Loads the key and opens the port, then exits: checks a configuration without running it

The master loads its key (ServerIdentity::load()) and opens its port before anything else, and logs both:

INFO  master   Lobby on TCP 0.0.0.0:4242, games on UDP 4243-4299 (57 at most)
INFO  master   Server key 4026de0635ae89391bff98b7b9ddc0689fa8529f9804e4c4721eadce94d92dff
INFO  master   Master started: Ctrl+C to stop

The fingerprint is the one the clients pin: compare it with r-type_keygen --fingerprint server.pub when something looks wrong.

items.title: Instance
items.text:
The master starts each instance with these arguments (instances protocol), never by hand:

Option Meaning --instance The instance mode --id <id> Id of the game, from 1 --udp-port <port> UDP port of the game --master-port <port> Port where the master listens for its instances, on 127.0.0.1

It then writes the secret on the instance's standard input: 64 hexadecimal digits and a line feed. The instance reads it before anything else (readSecret()), and stops with code 1 without it. The secret proves to the master that the process connecting is the one it started; it is never an argument, since every user of the machine can read the arguments of a process (ps).

Standalone mode. r-type_server --instance --standalone --udp-port 4242 runs a game without a master, with public test keys, for development, the tests, the measures and the fuzzing. It only exists in debug builds (RTYPE_STANDALONE_INSTANCE): a released server refuses it. See below.

items.title: Common options
items.text:
Option Meaning --log-level <level> trace, debug, info, warning or error; wins over RTYPE_LOG_LEVEL (Logging) -h, --help Shows the usage --version Shows the version, the one of the project

The options of one mode are refused in the other (--key with --instance, --id without it), as are unknown options: a typo never goes unnoticed.

items.title: The lobby
items.text:
The master accepts the clients on its TCP port, over TLS with its key, and answers their requests (lobby protocol). Lobby (Master/Lobby.hpp) runs on the thread of the loop; the messages are those of libs/lobby (rtype/lobby/Messages.hpp), which the client uses too.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Handshake: TCP accepted, within the limits
    Handshake --> Unwelcomed: TLS secured
    Unwelcomed --> Lobby: HELLO / WELCOME
    Lobby --> InGame: CREATE_GAME or JOIN_GAME / GAME_JOINED
    InGame --> Lobby: LEAVE_GAME / LEFT_GAME, or LEFT_GAME (game over, crash, timeout)
    Handshake --> [*]: 10 s
    Unwelcomed --> [*]: no HELLO in 10 s
    Lobby --> [*]: closed, or 30 s without a frame
    InGame --> [*]: closed, or 30 s without a frame

Each connection is timed in each state; the client keeps it open with PING.

Request Before HELLO In the lobby In a game HELLO WELCOME with a new player id; INVALID_NAME; UNSUPPORTED_VERSION, then closed ALREADY_WELCOMED ALREADY_WELCOMED PING PONG PONG PONG LIST_GAMES HELLO_REQUIRED GAME_LIST GAME_LIST CREATE_GAME HELLO_REQUIRED GAME_JOINED once the game is ready; INVALID_NAME, SERVER_FULL, GAME_START_FAILED ALREADY_IN_GAME JOIN_GAME HELLO_REQUIRED GAME_JOINED; GAME_NOT_FOUND, GAME_FULL ALREADY_IN_GAME LEAVE_GAME HELLO_REQUIRED NOT_IN_GAME LEFT_GAME (REQUESTED) Any other type UNKNOWN_MESSAGE UNKNOWN_MESSAGE UNKNOWN_MESSAGE A malformed payload MALFORMED, then closed MALFORMED, then closed MALFORMED, then closed
  • One reply per request, in order: the requests of a connection are handled one after the other, so a client can send several without waiting. CREATE_GAME is answered once its game is ready, up to 10 seconds later: the requests sent meanwhile wait for its answer (32 at most, then the client is disconnected).
  • The state comes first: a second HELLO is ALREADY_WELCOMED whatever it holds, a LIST_GAMES before HELLO is HELLO_REQUIRED whatever its payload.
  • A player id is given by HELLO: never 0, never given twice by a master. Names do not have to be unique.
  • Leaving without asking: a game over, a crash or a client that timed out send LEFT_GAME with their reason, and the player is back in the lobby. A client that closed its UDP session itself (QUIT) is back in the lobby without a message: it knows. A lobby connection that closes takes its player out of its game.

Limits (LobbyLimits, the defaults of the protocol):

Limit Default When reached Connections 256 The next ones are closed at once, before any TLS work Connections per IP address 8 Same TLS handshake 10 s Closed HELLO after the handshake 10 s Closed: PING does not count Silence of a welcomed client 30 s Closed: any frame counts, PING is sent after 10 s of silence

On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, the lobby stops accepting and closes every connection with a TLS close_notify, then the loop stops 100 ms later. The logs show the players:

INFO  lobby    Pavel (1) joined the lobby from 192.168.1.20:51234
INFO  lobby    Pavel (1) left the lobby

items.title: The games
items.text:
Games (Master/Games.hpp) runs the games of the master, one instance each (ADR 0013, instances protocol).

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as Master
    participant I as Instance
    C->>M: CREATE_GAME (name, max players)
    Note over M: takes a free UDP port, draws a secret
    M->>I: starts r-type_server --instance, secret on its standard input
    I->>M: INSTANCE_HELLO (id, secret), on 127.0.0.1
    M->>I: CONFIGURE
    I->>M: READY (UDP port)
    M->>I: ADD_PLAYER (player, session, keys)
    M->>C: GAME_JOINED (game, UDP port, session, keys)
    C->>I: CONNECT, then the game

The creator is answered once the instance is ready; a player who joins later is added at once.

  • Its own executable: the master starts currentExecutable() with --instance --id --udp-port --master-port, and the --log-level it runs with: the instances log like it.
  • The instances connect back to a listener of the master on 127.0.0.1, on a port of the system. An instance has 10 seconds to present itself; an unknown id closes its connection, a wrong secret (compared in constant time, sameSecret()) also kills the instance it pretends to be.
  • A session per player: an id unique in its game, and two keys drawn by the master, given to the instance (ADD_PLAYER) before the player (GAME_JOINED), so that the game knows the session when the client connects.
  • One UDP port per game, from --game-ports: none free is SERVER_FULL. A port is given back once the process has exited.
What happens The players The instance The last player leaves, or its lobby connection closes — SHUTDOWN (EMPTY) No INSTANCE_HELLO or no READY within 10 s, or the program cannot start ERROR (GAME_START_FAILED) Killed GAME_OVER LEFT_GAME (GAME_OVER) Exits on its own It exits, or closes its connection, without GAME_OVER LEFT_GAME (GAME_CRASHED) Killed if still there PLAYER_DISCONNECTED (TIMED_OUT) LEFT_GAME (TIMED_OUT) — The master stops Their UDP sessions get DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) SHUTDOWN (MASTER_STOPPING)

The processes are checked every 50 ms (exitCode() never blocks). An instance that does not exit within 5 seconds of SHUTDOWN or GAME_OVER is killed. On Ctrl+C, the master closes its lobby, shuts every game down, and stops once every instance has exited:

INFO  games    Pavel creates game 1 "Bydo hunters" for 4 players: instance 48213 on UDP 4243
INFO  games    game 1 "Bydo hunters" ready on UDP 4243
INFO  games    Pavel (1) joins game 1 "Bydo hunters" (1/4)

items.title: With its master
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Master
    participant I as Instance
    participant C as Client
    Note over I: reads the secret
    I->>M: INSTANCE_HELLO (id, secret), on 127.0.0.1
    M->>I: CONFIGURE (name, max players)
    Note over I: opens its UDP port, starts the game thread
    I->>M: READY (UDP port)
    M->>I: ADD_PLAYER (player, session, keys, name)
    C->>I: CONNECT
    I->>C: ACCEPTED (slot, 60, tick), PLAYER_JOINED
    I->>M: PLAYER_CONNECTED
    loop every tick
        C->>I: INPUT
        I->>C: SNAPSHOT (every 2 ticks), ENTITIES_DESTROYED
    end
    M->>I: SHUTDOWN
    I->>C: DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN)
    Note over I: exits with 0

The instance presents itself, is configured, opens its port, then runs the game for the players the master gives it.

MasterLink holds the connection to the master (instances protocol). The master and its instances come from the same build, so anything outside the protocol is a failure: no CONFIGURE within 10 seconds, a player before CONFIGURE, CONFIGURE twice, a frame that does not decode. A failure, like the master closing the connection, stops the game with exit code 1: an instance never runs without its master.

items.title: Two threads
items.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Net["network thread (main): the event loop"]
        Link["MasterLink<br/>TCP to the master"]
        Host["GameHost<br/>UDP, SessionHost, players"]
    end
    subgraph Sim["game thread"]
        Game["GameThread<br/>Simulation, 60 ticks/s"]
    end
    Link --> Host
    Host -- "commands: add, remove, input" --> Game
    Game -- "loop.post(): each tick, the snapshot" --> Host

They share nothing but the commands, under a mutex, and the results, handed through loop.post() (ADR 0013).

  • GameThread owns the Simulation of libs/game and steps it every 1/60 s, whatever the network does. Behind by more than 250 ms (a machine that slept, a debugger), it goes on from now instead of running fast. The commands of the network thread apply at the start of the next tick. The inputs of each player wait in an InputBuffer for the tick they are stamped with (below), and the result of each tick goes back with the tick of the last input applied for each player.
  • GameHost is the game seen from the network (game protocol):
  • a player added gets the lowest free slot, and its ship when its client connects;
  • on CONNECT, the client receives ACCEPTED, then PLAYER_JOINED for each player connected, itself included; the others receive its PLAYER_JOINED;
  • the inputs of each INPUT go to the game, which applies each one at its tick;
  • every 2 ticks, each client receives the snapshot in parts, with its last input; every tick, the entities destroyed. They leave as soon as the tick is published, not at the next update of the sessions: up to a tick of delay less, and no jitter from it;
  • the game over goes to every client (GAME_OVER, with the last snapshot), then to the instance with the score of each player; nothing is published after it;
  • a session that closes takes the ship away; the others receive PLAYER_LEFT, and the master PLAYER_DISCONNECTED, unless it removed the player itself (REMOVE_PLAYER).
  • Its SessionHost is updated at 60 Hz by a Timer of the loop, not by the game thread: the heartbeats and resends go on even if the game stalls.

items.title: Inputs
items.text:
A client sends, once per tick, an INPUT with its last 8 inputs, each stamped with the tick at which the game should apply it (game protocol, 9.2). The game thread keeps them in one InputBuffer per player:

What happens What the game does An input for a tick to come, at most 60 ahead Kept until its tick, then applied An input for a tick already simulated, or more than 60 ahead Ignored The same tick received again (the next INPUT carries it too) The first one is kept A tick without its input: its datagram was lost or late The last input is applied again: the movement goes on 30 ticks without any input An empty input: the ship of a player who lost the connection stops

The 8 inputs of each INPUT are what makes a lost datagram harmless: the next one brings the missing ticks again. The client stamps its inputs a little ahead of the game, from the round-trip time it measures (The client online), so that they arrive before their tick.

items.title: Stopping an instance
items.text:
What happens The clients Exit code The game is over GAME_OVER, then DISCONNECT (GAME_OVER) once acknowledged, 2 s at most; the master gets the scores 0 SHUTDOWN from the master DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) 0 Ctrl+C, SIGTERM (or Process::stop() from the master) DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) 0 The master closes the connection, or breaks the protocol DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) 1 The UDP port cannot be opened — 1 A player added to a full game, or twice DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) 1 The simulation throws DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) 1

In each case the game thread stops first, then the sessions and the link close, and the loop stops 100 ms later, once the last datagrams are sent.

items.title: Standalone mode
items.text:
Without a master, nobody gives the clients a session and its keys: in standalone mode they are fixed, in rtype/game/Standalone.hpp, so that a client in development can join.

Slot Session Client key Server key 0 to 3 standalone::sessionId(slot): 1 to 4 standalone::clientKey(slot): every byte 0x10 + slot standalone::serverKey(slot): every byte 0x20 + slot

The four sessions wait for their clients; a session that closes, or never connects within 10 seconds, is given again, so that a client can always join. These keys are public: a released server refuses the standalone mode.

./build/bin/r-type_server --instance --standalone --udp-port 4242 --log-level debug

items.title: Stopping
items.text:
Both modes end in runUntilStopped(loop, shutdown), which runs the event loop on the main thread and handles the stop signals: Ctrl+C (SIGINT), SIGTERM (sent by kill, systemd or docker stop), and on Windows Ctrl+Break and the closing of the console.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Running
    Running --> Stopping: first signal: shutdown()
    Stopping --> Stopped: shutdown() is done, loop.stop()
    Stopping --> Forced: second signal, or 10 s
    Running --> Stopped: the work ends (game over)
    Stopped --> [*]: exit 0
    Forced --> [*]: exit 1

The first signal starts a proper stop; a second one, or the grace period, cuts it.

  1. The first signal calls shutdown, which ends the work properly and calls loop.stop() once done. An instance sends DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) to its players. The master closes the lobby, which disconnects its clients; with the games, it will also send SHUTDOWN to its instances and wait for them.
  2. A second signal stops at once: the person who pressed Ctrl+C twice does not want to wait.
  3. After 10 seconds (GracePeriod) without the loop stopped, the server stops at once too: a stop that hangs never blocks a restart.
INFO  server   SIGINT received: stopping (again to stop at once)
INFO  master   Master stopped

Under the hood, StopSignals (libs/network) receives the signals on the loop's thread, and a Timer counts the grace period (Networking). A signal handler of the C library could only set a flag: here the shutdown is ordinary code, which may close sockets and log.

items.title: Processes
items.text:
The master starts its instances with Process (Master/Process.hpp), which wraps reproc (ADR 0013). It is the only part of the server that knows the processes of the system, on Linux and Windows.

const std::vector<std::string> arguments = {"--instance", "--id", "7", "--udp-port", "4251", "--master-port", "5000"};
rtype::server::Process instance(rtype::server::currentExecutable(), arguments,
                                {.input = formatSecret(secret) + "\n", .stopGrace = std::chrono::seconds(5)});

instance.exitCode(); // its exit code once it has exited, nothing while it runs: never waits
instance.stop();     // asks it to stop, waits stopGrace, kills it if it still runs
  • Its own executable. currentExecutable() asks the system for the path of the program running (/proc/self/exe on Linux, GetModuleFileNameW() on Windows): argv[0] can be relative or a name found in the PATH, and the instance must be the same build as its master.
  • The arguments arrive unchanged: there is no shell, so a space, a quote or a ; is just a character. reproc does the quoting of the command line of Windows, where a backslash before a quote is a trap. An empty argument is refused (std::invalid_argument): reproc does not quote it, so Windows would lose it and shift the others.
  • The secret goes through the standard input, written before the program starts (input), which is then closed. Nothing can be written later: writing to an instance that has already died would raise SIGPIPE and stop the master.
  • Its output is the master's: the logs of the instances go to the same terminal, or the same journal.
  • Stopping comes in two steps. terminate() asks: SIGTERM on Linux, Ctrl+Break on Windows, which runUntilStopped() of the instance receives like Ctrl+C, so that it can tell its players. kill() stops at once. stop() does both: it asks, waits stopGrace, then kills. On Windows, Ctrl+Break needs a console: without one, stop() kills at once. A program that has only just started does not receive it yet either: stop() then kills it after stopGrace.
  • No program left behind: destroying a Process that still runs calls stop(), even when an exception goes through the master.
Exit code Meaning 0, 1, 2 The exit codes of r-type_server Process::Terminated (143) Stopped by terminate() without handling it: 128 + SIGTERM, as a shell shows it Process::Killed (137) Stopped by kill(): 128 + SIGKILL, the same value on Windows

exitCode() never blocks, so the master can check its instances from a Timer of its event loop; wait() and stop() block, for the tests and the end of the master. The supervision of the instances itself comes with the lobby.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Code When 0 Stopped properly: after a stop signal, after --help, --version or --check, or at the end of its game for an instance 1 Could not start (key missing or invalid, port in use, no secret), stopped on an unexpected error, or stop forced 2 Invalid arguments

The master reads the exit code of its instances: anything but 0 is a crash, which it reports to the players (instances protocol).

items.title: Tests
items.text:
• tests/server_options.cpp (tag [server]): the defaults, every option of both modes, every invalid combination, --help and --version first, the standalone mode refused in release, the exit codes of run(), a master without its key, an instance without a secret, and the secret itself.
  • tests/server_lifecycle.cpp (tag [server]): SIGINT and SIGTERM, sent to the test process itself, call the shutdown once; a second signal and the grace period force the stop; a server whose work ends stops properly.
  • tests/process.cpp (tag [process]): real programs started and stopped. A helper, tests/helpers/process_child.cpp, does what its arguments say: exits with a code, checks its standard input and its end, writes its arguments to a file, waits, or ignores the requests to stop. Before a request to stop, the tests wait for the file it creates once ready, since Windows drops a Ctrl+Break sent too early. The tests check the exit codes, arguments with spaces, quotes and backslashes, an empty argument refused, the input then its end, a program that does not exist, terminate(), kill(), stop() killing a program that ignores it, the destructor and the moves. They also start r-type_server --instance itself: with its secret and a master that never answers, it runs until asked to stop, then exits with 0; without it, it exits with 1.
  • tests/server_replication.cpp (tag [replication]): the InputBuffer: an input applied at its tick, the last one repeated then emptied after a silence, the ticks of a lost datagram filled by the next one, inputs too late, too far ahead or received twice ignored.
  • tests/server_instance.cpp (tag [instance]): the messages between the master and its instances (round trips, bytes, every malformed case, random bytes), the game thread (its rate, each input applied at its tick, whatever their order, nothing after stop()), the game over of GameHost (sent, reported with the scores, acknowledged, nothing after), every failure of MasterLink, and whole instances run by runInstance() on a thread of the test, with a fake master over TCP and real clients over UDP: two players who join, see each other and move, one removed by the master, one who quits, then SHUTDOWN; the master going away; a full game; a UDP port taken; and the standalone mode with its public keys, stopped by Ctrl+C.
  • tests/lobby_messages.cpp (tag [lobby]): the HELLO frame of the specification, the bytes of the other messages, round trips, the names checked apart, every malformed case, and random bytes.
  • tests/server_lobby.cpp (tag [lobby]): a Lobby on the loopback and real TLS clients pinning its key. HELLO, LIST_GAMES and PING; requests sent without waiting answered in order; the answers of each state; invalid names, another version, malformed requests; the limits per address and in all, a place freed taken again; the handshake, HELLO and silence timeouts, PING keeping a client; and closing the lobby.
  • tests/server_games.cpp (tag [games]): real instances of r-type_server started by Games, real lobby clients over TLS and game clients over UDP. A game created, listed, joined, full, left, and shut down with its last player; the requests after CREATE_GAME answered in order; SERVER_FULL; an instance that cannot start, exits at once or never gets ready, and its port given back; an impostor with an unknown id or a wrong secret; a crash reported as GAME_CRASHED; a silent client reported as TIMED_OUT; the master stopping its games; and the real binary run as a master, which starts the instance of a game created by a client.
  • The smoke tests of CTest run r-type_server --help, refuse an unknown argument, and run --check with a key made by r-type_keygen for the occasion.

items.title: Limits and next steps
items.text:
• The limits of the lobby are not options yet: LobbyLimits has the defaults of the protocol; options can come when a host needs others.
  • No waves yet: there are no Bydos in the game for now, so WAVE_STARTED is never sent.
  • The client draws the latest snapshot: drawing in the past between two snapshots (interpolation) and predicting the ship of the player come on the side of the client, and make the game online as smooth as offline.
  • No configuration file: everything is on the command line, which suits a service (systemd, Docker). A file can come if the options multiply.

items.title: Git workflow
items.text:
• main always builds and is protected: changes go through pull requests.
  • One branch per feature or fix, named after its purpose: feature/star-field, fix/udp-buffer-overflow, docs/protocol-header.
  • Every pull request is reviewed by at least one other team member and must pass the CI (Build, Format and, when relevant, Documentation).
  • Work is tracked in GitHub issues; reference the issue in the pull request (Closes #12).
  • Important milestones (deliveries, defenses) are tagged: v1.0.0, v2.0.0. Pushing a tag publishes a release automatically, see Releasing.

items.title: Commit messages
items.text:
Short summary line in English, in the imperative mood, followed by a blank line and details if needed:

Add UDP socket abstraction

Wraps BSD sockets and Winsock behind a single interface so that the
networking layer does not depend on the platform.

items.title: Coding conventions
items.text:
• C++20, compiled without warnings (-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic / /W4).
  • Formatted with clang-format using the repository's .clang-format. On pull requests, the format bot fixes unformatted code automatically. See Formatting.
  • New behaviour comes with tests, following the testing policy.
  • Public headers of the engine are documented with Doxygen comments, see Documenting C++ code.
  • Messages are written with a logger (rtype::log::Logger), not with std::cout or std::cerr, see Logging.

items.title: Repository administration
items.text: The one-time configuration of the repository (format bot, GitHub Pages, protection of main) is described in Repository setup.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: Any change visible to users or other developers comes with its documentation in the same pull request. See Writing documentation.

items.title: Writing documentation
items.text: The documentation is written in English, in Markdown files under docs/, and built with Zensical. The C++ API reference is generated by Doxygen from source comments. Both are published to GitHub Pages when main changes.

items.title: Adding a page
items.text:
1. Create a Markdown file in the right folder of docs/. Start from a template when one fits.

  2. Add it to the nav list in zensical.toml, where it should appear in the menu:

    { "Architecture" = [
  "architecture/index.md",
  "architecture/networking.md",   # new page
] },

  3. Open a pull request. The Documentation workflow builds the site in strict mode and fails if a link is broken or if a page is missing from nav.

Quick fixes

Every page has an Edit this page button that opens the file in the GitHub editor: no clone needed for a typo.

items.title: Previewing locally
items.text:
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate   # once
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt                 # once
zensical serve

The site is served on http://localhost:8000 and reloads on every save. The API reference is not part of this preview; to build the complete site like the CI does (requires doxygen):

git submodule update --init      # once: Doxygen theme (doxygen/doxygen-awesome-css)
python3 scripts/check_docs_nav.py
zensical build --clean --strict
doxygen doxygen/Doxyfile         # after Zensical, which cleans site/

The result is in site/.

items.title: Admonitions
items.text:
!!! warning "Title"

    Indented content.

Types: note, tip, info, warning, danger, question. Use ??? instead of !!! for a collapsible block.

items.title: Tabs
items.text:
=== "Linux"

    Linux instructions.

=== "Windows"

    Windows instructions.

items.title: Diagrams
items.text:
Diagrams are written as Mermaid code blocks, so they are reviewed like code:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Client -- inputs --> Server
    Server -- updates --> Client
```

items.title: Accessibility rules
items.text:
• Every image has an alternative text: ![Player ship sprite sheet](img/ship.png).
  • Every diagram is followed by a sentence that summarises what it shows.
  • Do not convey information by colour only.

items.title: Documenting C++ code
items.text:
Public classes and functions are documented with Doxygen comments in headers. They appear in the API reference at the next deployment, with no configuration to change.

/// Fixed-size UDP datagram received from the network.
class Packet {
public:
    /// Reads the payload as the given message type.
    /// @param offset Position of the first byte to read in the payload.
    /// @return The decoded message, or std::nullopt if the payload is too short.
    template <typename T>
    std::optional<T> read(std::size_t offset) const;
};
  • Use /// comments. The first sentence is the summary shown in lists.
  • Document every parameter (@param), the return value (@return) and errors (@throws) when relevant.
  • Explain what and why; the code already shows how.

items.title: Releasing
items.text: Releases are published automatically by the Release workflow when a version tag is pushed. Each release contains the client and the server for Linux and Windows, and release notes generated from the pull requests merged since the previous release.

items.title: Versioning
items.text:
Versions follow Semantic Versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

Release Example Typical use Final v1.0.0 Delivery of a project part, defense Prerelease v1.0.0-beta.1, v1.0.0-rc.1 Version to test before a delivery; marked as prerelease on GitHub

The version is defined once, in project(RType VERSION ...) of the root CMakeLists.txt, and the tag must match it: the workflow refuses a tag v1.2.0 if the project version is 1.1.0. A prerelease suffix is ignored for this check (v1.2.0-beta.1 matches 1.2.0).

items.title: Publishing a release
items.text:
1. Update the version. In a pull request, change VERSION in the root CMakeLists.txt, for example:

    project(RType
    VERSION 1.0.0

    Merge the pull request into main.

  2. Tag the merged commit and push the tag:

    git switch main
git pull
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "R-Type 1.0.0"
git push origin v1.0.0

  3. Follow the workflow in the Actions tab: Check version, then Build on Linux and Windows (tests included), then Publish release. The release appears in the Releases section of the repository.

items.title: Release contents
items.text:
File Content r-type-<version>-Linux-client.tar.gz r-type_client for Linux r-type-<version>-Linux-server.tar.gz r-type_server and r-type_keygen for Linux r-type-<version>-Windows-client.zip r-type_client.exe for Windows r-type-<version>-Windows-server.zip r-type_server.exe and r-type_keygen.exe for Windows SHA256SUMS.txt Checksums of the archives

To check a download:

sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS.txt

items.title: When something goes wrong
items.text:
The workflow fails at Check version

The tag does not match the version in CMakeLists.txt, or is not of the form vX.Y.Z. Delete the tag, fix the version through a pull request, then tag again:

git push origin --delete v1.0.0
git tag -d v1.0.0
The build or the tests fail

No release is created. Fix the problem through a pull request, then delete and recreate the tag on the new commit of main (same commands as above).

A release was published by mistake

Delete it from the Releases page (or with gh release delete v1.0.0), then delete the tag. Prefer publishing a new patch version over replacing the files of a published release.

items.title: Repository setup
items.text: One-time configuration of the GitHub repository, done by an administrator. Developers do not need any of this.

items.title: Format bot
items.text:
The Format workflow fixes unformatted C++ code in pull requests by itself: it runs clang-format, commits the result to the branch, and comments on the pull request. To push commits that trigger the other workflows (Build, Format), it uses its own identity, a GitHub App, instead of the default workflow token.

Without this setup, the workflow still runs but only checks the formatting and fails when files need to be reformatted.

items.title: 1. Create the GitHub App
items.text:
Open Settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App on the account that owns the repository, and fill in:

Field Value GitHub App name A unique name, for example rtype-format-bot (it appears as rtype-format-bot[bot] on commits) Homepage URL https://github.com/Akinator31/Rtype Webhook → Active Unchecked Repository permissions → Contents Read and write Repository permissions → Pull requests Read and write Where can this GitHub App be installed? Only on this account

Click Create GitHub App.

items.title: 2. Get its credentials
items.text:
On the page of the new app:

  1. Copy the Client ID (starts with Iv).
  2. In Private keys, click Generate a private key: a .pem file is downloaded.

items.title: 3. Install it on the repository
items.text: In the left menu of the app, Install App → Install next to the account → Only select repositories → Rtype → Install.

items.title: 4. Give the credentials to the workflow
items.text:
In the repository: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.

Tab Name Value Variables FORMAT_BOT_CLIENT_ID The Client ID Secrets FORMAT_BOT_PRIVATE_KEY The whole content of the .pem file, including the BEGIN and END lines

Then delete the .pem file from your computer: a new key can be generated at any time from the app page.

items.title: 5. Check
items.text:
Open a pull request with a badly formatted C++ file. The Format workflow should push a commit style: apply clang-format signed by the bot, comment on the pull request, and the Build workflow should run again on that commit.

The workflow still only checks the formatting

The bot is used only for pull requests opened from a branch of this repository (not from a fork), and only if the variable FORMAT_BOT_CLIENT_ID exists. Check its exact name in the Variables tab (not Secrets).

The push of the bot is rejected

Check that the app is installed on the repository (step 3) with Contents: Read and write. If the permissions were changed after installation, accept the new permissions in Settings → Applications → Installed GitHub Apps.

items.title: Documentation site
items.text:
Settings → Pages → Build and deployment → Source: select GitHub Actions. The Documentation workflow deploys the site on every change to main.

GitHub Pages on a private repository requires a paid plan (GitHub Pro, Team, or the GitHub Student Developer Pack).

items.title: Protection of main
items.text:
Recommended: Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New branch ruleset, targeting the default branch, with:

  • Require a pull request before merging, with at least one approval;
  • Require status checks to pass: Build (linux), Build (windows), clang-format;
  • Block force pushes.

Status checks can be selected only after they have run once, so add them after the first pull request. The Documentation checks are not required: that workflow only runs when the documentation or the code changes.

items.title: Page templates
items.text: Copy a template into a new file, fill it in, and add the page to the navigation.

For a task-oriented page: one goal, numbered steps.

## Prerequisites

items.title: Protocol message
items.text:
For a new message in the protocol specification: in Lobby (TCP), Game (UDP) or Master and instances. Take the next free type in the range of its direction, and add it to the right subsection. Changing an existing message increases the protocol version.

### MESSAGE_NAME (`0xNN`)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Direction** | Client → Game / Game → Client / Client → Master / ... |
| **Reliability** | Reliable / Unreliable (UDP messages only) |
| **Sent when** | Which event triggers it, and how often. |

| Offset | Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | | | |

**Receiver behaviour:** what the receiver does, and which values make the message invalid.

items.title: Testing policy
items.text: This page defines how R-Type is tested: which tools are used, what must be tested, how the code has to be designed to be testable, and which steps are still to be set up. The choice of tools is explained in ADR 0004.

items.title: Goals
items.text:
The subject sets requirements that are hard to prove without automated tests:

Requirement How we prove it Malformed packets must not crash the client or the server, nor consume excessive memory Unit tests for every rejection case, and fuzzing of the packet decoder The server is multithreaded and keeps running when a client crashes ThreadSanitizer and an integration test that kills a client Clients and servers on Linux and Windows play together Unit tests of the binary encoding, run on both platforms in CI Time flow does not depend on CPU speed Game logic tested with an injected, fixed time step

items.title: Tools
items.text: Purpose Tool Status Unit and integration tests Catch2 v3, fetched by CPM In place Test runner CTest In place Code formatting clang-format 23 (.clang-format, requirements-dev.txt), applied by the format bot In place Memory errors and undefined behaviour AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer Step 2 Packet decoder robustness libFuzzer (Clang) Step 2 Data races in the server ThreadSanitizer Step 3 Static analysis clang-tidy Step 3 Coverage report gcovr, published with this documentation Step 4 Performance measurements Catch2 benchmarks Step 4

items.title: Test levels
items.text: Unit tests Most of the tests. One behaviour per test, no network, no window, no sleeping. Targets: ECS, serialization, protocol messages (valid and invalid), game rules (movement, collisions, spawning). Integration tests The server and two to four headless "bot" clients in the same test, over UDP on 127.0.0.1: connection, propagation of a move, abrupt disconnection of a client. Fuzzing The packet decoder receives millions of random or mutated datagrams. Any crash, sanitizer report or excessive allocation is a bug. Smoke tests The binaries start and exit cleanly (smoke.* tests, registered with add_test in tests/CMakeLists.txt).

items.title: Designing testable code
items.text:
These rules are what make the tests above possible. They also match the decoupling expected from the engine.

  • The engine is a library linked by the client, the server and the tests. Tests never link the client or server executables.
  • Game logic does not depend on raylib: it runs without a window, in the server and in tests.
  • Time and randomness are injected: systems receive the elapsed time instead of reading a clock, and random generators take a seed. A test always replays the same way.
  • Networking is behind an interface: tests use a fake socket, which can also drop, duplicate or reorder packets on purpose.

items.title: Rules for contributions
items.text:
• A pull request that adds or changes behaviour comes with tests for it.
  • A bug fix comes with a test that fails without the fix.
  • Every pull request must pass the Build (both platforms, tests included) and Format workflows. Formatting is fixed by the format bot, see Formatting.
  • Tests are deterministic: no dependency on time, network outside 127.0.0.1, or execution order.

items.title: Writing a test
items.text:
Tests live in tests/. Add the file to rtype_tests in tests/CMakeLists.txt; each TEST_CASE then appears as a separate CTest test.

#include <catch2/catch_test_macros.hpp>

TEST_CASE("A packet shorter than the header is rejected", "[protocol]")
{
    const std::array<std::byte, 2> data{};
    REQUIRE_FALSE(decodePacket(data).has_value());
}
  • Name the test after the expected behaviour, as a sentence.
  • Tag it with its subsystem, for instance [ecs], [scenes], [engine], [render], [input], [audio], [log], [network], [platform], and later [protocol], [game]. Run one subsystem with ./build/bin/rtype_tests "[scenes]".
  • Use SECTIONs to share a setup between related checks.

items.title: Running the tests
items.text:
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --parallel
ctest --test-dir build -C Release --output-on-failure

Run a subset with Catch2 tags, or with a CTest name filter:

./build/bin/rtype_tests "[protocol]"
ctest --test-dir build -C Release -R smoke

Tests are built by default; configure with -DRTYPE_BUILD_TESTS=OFF to skip them.

items.title: Formatting
items.text:
Nothing to install: on pull requests, the Format workflow formats the code automatically. When a file needs it, the format bot pushes a style: apply clang-format commit to your branch and leaves a comment. Get its commit before pushing again:

git pull --rebase

To avoid this round trip, enable format on save in your editor: VS Code (C/C++ extension), CLion and Visual Studio read the repository's .clang-format without extra setup.

To format by hand with the exact version used by the CI:

pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
clang-format -i path/to/file.cpp

items.title: Continuous integration
items.text: Workflow Runs Checks Build Every push and pull request, Linux and Windows Compilation, all CTest tests, packaging Format Every pull request, and pushes to main that change C++ files Formats tracked C++ files; on pull requests the bot commits the fixes, elsewhere unformatted code fails the job

items.title: Roadmap
items.text: Steps still to set up, and what triggers each of them. Tick the box and move the tool to In place above when done.

items.title: Step 2 — when the protocol decoder and the ECS exist
items.text:
• CI job sanitizers: Debug build with Clang, -fsanitize=address,undefined, runs all tests (Linux).
  • Fuzz target tests/fuzz/packet_decoder.cpp (LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput) calling the packet decoder.
  • CI job fuzz: runs the fuzzer for a few minutes on pull requests that touch the network code, and longer every night; crashing inputs are kept as regression tests.
  • Unit tests for every message of the protocol, including each rejection case.

items.title: Step 3 — when the server runs several threads
items.text:
• CI job tsan: -fsanitize=thread build running the server tests.
  • Integration test: server and bot clients over 127.0.0.1, including a client killed mid-game.
  • clang-tidy with a small set of checks (bugprone-*, performance-*), extended progressively.

items.title: Step 4 — part 2 of the project
items.text:
• Coverage report (gcovr) published under /coverage/ of this site.
  • Catch2 benchmarks for serialization and ECS iteration.
  • Network condition simulation (loss, latency, reordering) in the fake socket, with measurements of bandwidth and responsiveness.

items.title: Technical decisions
items.text:
Each significant technical choice is recorded as an Architecture Decision Record (ADR): a short page explaining the context, the options that were compared, and the decision. Together, these records form the technical and comparative study of the project.

# Decision Status 0001 CPM.cmake as package manager Accepted 0002 raylib for the client Accepted 0003 Zensical and Doxygen for the documentation Accepted 0004 Catch2, sanitizers, fuzzing and clang-format for testing Accepted 0005 World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer Superseded by 0007 0006 Indexed vectors for the ECS component caches Accepted 0007 The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy Accepted 0008 Events switch systems on and off Accepted 0009 Named scenes in the engine Accepted 0010 A custom kinematic physics engine Accepted 0011 Asio as the networking library Accepted 0012 TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game Accepted 0013 One process per game Accepted 0014 Encryption of the client/server traffic Accepted 0015 One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session Accepted 0016 Full snapshots, explicit destructions and redundant inputs Proposed 0017 Asset preparation on a background thread Accepted 0018 Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons Accepted, partly superseded by 0019 0019 LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors Accepted

To record a new decision, copy the ADR template into a new file NNNN-short-title.md in this folder, add it to the navigation and to this table.

Changing a decision

Accepted records are not rewritten. When a decision changes, write a new record and set the status of the old one to Superseded by NNNN.

items.title: 0001 — CPM.cmake as package manager
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-01

items.title: Context
items.text: The project must build on Linux and Windows (MSVC) without relying on system-wide libraries, and third-party code must not be copied into the repository. A package manager has to fetch and build the dependencies (raylib for now, more later). The CI must not download every dependency again on each run.

items.title: Options
items.text: CPM.cmake vcpkg Conan Extra tool to install None (CMake script) vcpkg checkout + bootstrap Python + Conan client Integration CPMAddPackage() in CMakeLists Toolchain file + manifest Generated toolchain + profiles Builds dependencies From source, as part of the project From source, cached as binaries Prebuilt binaries when available CI caching Source cache directory Binary cache Binary cache / remote Learning curve Low Medium Medium to high

items.title: Decision
items.text: Use CPM.cmake. It only requires CMake, which every developer and CI runner already has, and dependencies are declared next to the targets that use them. Downloads are pinned by version and verified with a SHA-256 hash, and the source cache (CPM_SOURCE_CACHE) is kept between CI runs.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Dependencies are compiled from source on a clean build, which takes longer than downloading binaries. Acceptable for a small dependency set; to be reconsidered if heavy libraries are added.
  • cmake/CPM.cmake is the official bootstrap script: it downloads a pinned CPM version on configure.

items.title: 0002 — raylib for the client
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-01

items.title: Context
items.text: The client needs windowing, 2D rendering, input, and audio on Linux and Windows. Full game engines (Unity, Unreal, Godot) are forbidden: the library must stay low-level enough for the engine to be our own.

items.title: Options
items.text: raylib SFML SDL Scope Window, 2D/3D rendering, input, audio Window, 2D rendering, input, audio, network Window, input, audio; 2D renderer or GPU API API C, small and simple C++, object-oriented C, lower level Build CMake, no external dependency CMake, a few external dependencies CMake, no external dependency 3D / shaders Yes Limited Through the GPU API

items.title: Decision
items.text: Use raylib 6.0. It covers everything the client needs with a small API, builds from source with CMake and no further dependency on both platforms, and keeps 3D and shaders available for later features. Version 6.0 is the current release; 5.5 was tried first but its CMake configuration triggers deprecation warnings with CMake 4.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• raylib is a C library: rendering is wrapped behind our own engine interfaces so that game code does not depend on it directly.
  • Requires CMake ≥ 3.25.

items.title: 0003 — Zensical and Doxygen for the documentation
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-01
path: 0003 — Zensical and Doxygen for the documentation

items.title: Context
items.text: The documentation must be in English, browsable online with navigation and search, and go beyond generated API docs: architecture, protocol, decisions, tutorials. Adding a page must be easy for every team member, and documenting the engine API later must not require changing the tooling.
path: 0003 — Zensical and Doxygen for the documentation

items.title: Options
items.text: Zensical Material for MkDocs VitePress Docusaurus Sphinx Source format Markdown Markdown Markdown Markdown / MDX reStructuredText / MyST Look out of the box Very good Very good Good Good Plain (theme dependent) Toolchain Python Python Node Node (React) Python Maintenance Active (successor of Material) End of life on 2026-11-05 Active Active Active C++ API docs Via Doxygen Via Doxygen Via Doxygen Via Doxygen Breathe + Doxygen
path: 0003 — Zensical and Doxygen for the documentation

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• Zensical builds the documentation site from Markdown files in docs/. It is made by the authors of Material for MkDocs, which reaches end of life in November 2026, and reads the same configuration format.
  • Doxygen, with the doxygen-awesome-css theme, generates the C++ API reference from source comments and is published under /api/ on the same site.
  • Both are built by the Documentation workflow and deployed to GitHub Pages.
path: 0003 — Zensical and Doxygen for the documentation

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Zensical is still pre-1.0: its version is pinned in requirements-docs.txt and updated deliberately.
  • The navigation is listed explicitly in zensical.toml; scripts/check_docs_nav.py fails the CI when a page is missing from it.
  • Doxygen scans the whole repository, so new source folders appear in the API reference without any configuration change.
path: 0003 — Zensical and Doxygen for the documentation

items.title: 0004 — Testing tools
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-01

items.title: Context
items.text: The project needs automated tests on Linux and Windows (MSVC), run by the CI. Some subject requirements can only be demonstrated with dedicated tools: robustness against malformed packets, a multithreaded server that survives client crashes, and cross-platform binary compatibility. See the testing policy.

items.title: Test framework
items.text: Catch2 v3 GoogleTest doctest Test style TEST_CASE + SECTION, BDD macros Fixtures (TEST_F), xUnit style Close to Catch2 Mocking None built in GMock None built in Benchmarks Built in No (separate Google Benchmark) No CMake / CTest integration catch_discover_tests gtest_discover_tests Script provided MSVC support Yes Yes Yes Maintenance Active Active Slower

items.title: Other tools
items.text: Need Chosen Alternatives considered Robustness of the packet decoder libFuzzer AFL++ (more setup), hand-written random tests (much weaker) Memory and threading bugs ASan, UBSan, TSan Valgrind (slower, no data-race detection as precise as TSan) Formatting clang-format, pinned through pip Editor-specific settings (not enforceable) Applying the formatting Bot committing fixes on pull requests (GitHub App) Local pre-commit hook (requires an installation on every machine), check-only CI job (manual fix), pre-commit.ci (free for public repositories only)

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• Catch2 v3 for unit and integration tests, run through CTest on both platforms. Readable tests with sections, and built-in benchmarks for the measurements expected in part 2. Mocking is done with hand-written fakes behind interfaces, which also enforces the decoupling of the engine.
  • libFuzzer and the sanitizers on Linux (Clang) in CI, added when the code they target exists.
  • clang-format 23, pinned in requirements-dev.txt so that every developer and the CI format the same way. It is applied automatically on pull requests by a format bot, so no developer has to install anything; the bot is a GitHub App so that its commits trigger the other workflows.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Tests are built by default (RTYPE_BUILD_TESTS=ON); Catch2 is fetched by CPM like other dependencies.
  • No mocking library: interfaces must be designed so that a fake implementation is easy to write.
  • Fuzzing and sanitizers run on Linux only; Windows is covered by the regular test suite.
  • When the bot pushes a formatting commit, the author must git pull --rebase before pushing again. Formatting on save in the editor avoids it.
  • The repository administrator has to create the GitHub App once, see Repository setup.

items.title: 0005 — World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer
items.text: Status Superseded by 0007 Date 2026-10-06
path: 0005 — World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer

items.title: Context
items.text:
The client draws two different kinds of things:

  • The game world: ships, Bydos, missiles, obstacles, the star-field. Most of it comes from the server, which simulates the game with the ECS (libs/ecs); the client keeps a copy of these entities in its own ECS.
  • The interface: menus (home, connection, waiting room, options, game over) and the in-game HUD (score, lives, players).

We had to decide whether the interface is also made of ECS entities, or lives outside of the ECS. Constraints:

  • The ECS is shared with the server, which has no interface. It is developed by another team member and does not exist yet.
  • Menus exist before any game world: the home and connection screens are shown before the client is connected to a server.
  • Menus must be usable with a keyboard and a gamepad only, which requires a notion of focus (the selected button) and navigation between widgets. This is also needed for accessibility and for VR, where there is no mouse.
  • VR is planned with a "board" view: the world is drawn on a board floating in front of the player, and the interface on a separate floating panel. World and interface must be drawable separately.
path: 0005 — World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer

items.title: Options
items.text:
A. Everything in the ECS B. World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer C. Interface outside the ECS, including on entities Single way of describing what is drawn Yes No: entities for the world, widgets for the interface No Can start before the ECS exists No Yes Yes Menus without a game world Needs a "menu world" Natural Natural Widget hierarchy, focus, navigation The ECS must support parent/child relations Handled by the interface layer Handled by the interface layer Health bars and names following entities Natural Natural: they are drawn by the ECS The interface must track entities Impact on the ECS shared with the server Must support interface needs None None World and interface drawn separately (VR) Possible, with layers Natural: two passes Natural

Engines use both approaches: Unity and Unreal keep their interface systems apart from their game objects, while Bevy builds its interface with ECS entities.
path: 0005 — World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer

items.title: Decision
items.text:
Option B. The game world is made of ECS entities; the interface is a light layer of screens and widgets in the client, which does not know the ECS.

Element Where Ships, Bydos, missiles, obstacles, star-field ECS, drawn by the render system Interface attached to an entity: health bar above a ship, player name, damage numbers ECS, drawn by the render system, since it follows the entity and disappears with it Menus, options, connection and game over screens Interface layer HUD fixed on screen: score, lives, list of players Interface layer

Four rules keep the two parts from mixing:

  1. Only the Renderer draws. The ECS render system and the interface both draw through it; neither calls raylib.
  2. The order is fixed: in each frame, the world is drawn first, then the interface on top of it.
  3. The interface does not read the ECS. The game code gives it plain values (score, lives, player names). A change in the ECS does not change the interface.
  4. The ECS does not know the interface.
path: 0005 — World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The interface can be built now, in parallel with the ECS.
  • The ECS stays focused on the game: it does not need parent/child relations nor focus handling for widgets, and the server is not affected by interface needs.
  • A frame of the client is made of two passes, world then interface. In VR, the world pass is drawn on the board and the interface pass on a floating panel.
  • There are two ways of describing what is drawn: entities for the world, widgets for the interface. Developers must know where each element belongs; the table above is the reference.
  • The interface layer must stay light: a few widgets (button, text, text field), a stack of screens, and keyboard and gamepad navigation first. It is not meant to become a general-purpose interface framework.
  • To revisit if the ECS ends up supporting parent/child relations and the team wants a single model: the interface could then be moved to entities, screen by screen.
path: 0005 — World in the ECS, interface in a separate layer

items.title: 0006 — ECS component storage
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-06

items.title: Context
items.text:
The game engine is built around an Entity Component System (ECS): entities are only ids, components are plain data attached to them, and systems run the logic on the entities that have the components they need. The way components are stored decides how fast systems reach them, and how simple the engine is to write, debug and keep deterministic between the client and the server (prediction, reconciliation).

The expected load is a few hundred entities, with common components (position, velocity, sprite) and entities destroyed in the middle of a system update (a missile hits, an entity leaves the screen).

items.title: Storage of the components of one type
items.text:
Indexed vector Sparse set Hash map Structure vector<optional<T>>, index = entity id Dense array of components + sparse array of indices + entity array unordered_map<entity, T> Access to a component 1 memory access 2 memory accesses Hash + pointer chasing Iteration Visits every slot, skips empty ones Contiguous, only existing components Scattered nodes, poor locality Memory N × sizeof(optional<T>), wasted if the component is rare Compact if rare, larger than the vector if almost every entity has it Compact but one allocation per component Multi-component join Same index in every cache, trivial One sequential access + one random access One lookup per entity Destroying an entity while iterating Safe, the slot is reset Swap-and-pop breaks the forward iteration Invalidates iterators on rehash Order of iteration Entity id order, deterministic Depends on the add/remove history Depends on hash and rehash Code ~40 lines ~100 lines Short

The sparse set is to be preferred with tens of thousands of entities, components carried by less than about 10-20 % of them, large rare components, or many temporary tags. None of these applies yet.

items.title: Finding the cache of a type
items.text: A hash map type_index → cache is fine here: there are few types, and the lookup is done once per system, never per entity.

items.title: Per-system list of matching entities
items.text: Each system could keep the list of entities that have all its components, updated when a component is added or removed. It avoids testing every slot at each frame, but requires component signatures, keeping the lists in sync, and deferring the destruction of entities during an update. Not worth it at this scale.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
• Indexed vector for each component cache (ComponentCache<T>), behind a small interface (emplace, erase, has, get, size) so that a type can later move to a sparse set without touching the systems.
  • Hash map type_index → cache in ComponentCaches, with a type-erased base (ICache) to remove an entity from every cache when it is destroyed.
  • Systems keep a direct reference to each cache they use, obtained once in their constructor with use<T>(), which also records the component type in the system (componentTypes()). Their update() walks the entity ids and tests has() on its caches.
  • Entity ids are uint32_t, recycled through a free list so the caches stay bounded.
  • No per-system entity list for now.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• A component is reached with a direct memory access, and systems can destroy entities while iterating.
  • Iteration order is the entity id order, the same on the client and the server.
  • Memory is wasted for rare components and every system visits all slots up to the highest entity id.
  • Adding a component of an iterated type from inside a system may reallocate its cache and invalidate references; this must be avoided.
  • If profiling shows a problem, the per-system entity list or a sparse set for the faulty types can be added without changing the public interface of the caches. A new record would then supersede this one.

items.title: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-07 Supersedes 0005
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: Context
items.text:
ADR 0005 put the game world in the ECS and the interface (menus, HUD) in a separate library of screens and widgets. It was decided while the ECS did not exist, and it relied on three reasons: the interface could not wait for the ECS, an interface needs parent/child relations, and interface needs could weigh on an ECS shared with the server.

Since then:

  • The ECS is done (ADR 0006). It is generic: any type can be a component, so components of the interface can live in the client only, unseen by the server.
  • Writing the interface library showed that most of its code would only serve the interface: drawing texts, positions, and above all animations. A button bouncing when it gets the focus, an enemy flashing when hit and a bonus appearing are the same thing, and would be written twice.
  • The team decided that the HUD is drawn by the ECS.

The questions were where the interface lives, how screens and game phases (home, game, pause) are organised, and how entities attached to others (a dropdown and its options, the Force and the ship) are handled.
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: Options
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: Where the interface lives
items.text: A. Separate interface library (ADR 0005) B. Interface made of entities Code shared with the game Little: the library has its own drawing and no animations Drawing, positions, hierarchy, animations Animations Written in each widget One Tween component and system, for the interface and the game Separation from the world (VR panel) Natural: two separate parts A Layer component: world and interface are drawn in two passes Input priority over the game Returned by the library The scene at the top receives the input (Scenes)
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: Scenes
items.text: One ECS, entities tagged by scene One ECS per scene No scenes, a global state Entities of several scenes at once (transition, star-field shared by the menus and the game, pause over the game) Natural Two worlds to keep in sync Natural Cleaning a closed scene One generic function destroying its entities Free: the whole ECS is destroyed By hand, error-prone Systems Ask which scene receives the input or updates Registered per scene One switch growing with the game
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: Parent / child relations
items.text: Without a hierarchy, every attached entity (dropdown options, Force, turrets of a boss, health bar above a ship) must be moved, hidden and destroyed by hand. With one, it follows its parent. Entity ids are reused by the ECS, so a reference kept by a child could end up designating another entity: references need a generation counter.
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: Decision
items.text:
B, in one ECS with tagged scenes, and a hierarchy.

  • Everything the client draws is an entity: the world, the HUD and the menus. A Drawable component gives its Layer (World or Interface) and its order. The SceneRenderer draws the world layer, then the interface layer: the interface stays on top, and the two passes stay separate for VR.
  • Scenes (engine::Scenes, in libs/engine): every entity of a scene has a SceneMember; closing a scene destroys them all. Entities without it are persistent. Scenes form a stack: only the scene at the top receives the input, a scene can keep updating when covered (the network game under the pause menu), and an overlay keeps the scenes below visible.
  • Hierarchy (ecs::Parent, LocalPosition, Hidden): a child follows its parent, is hidden with it and is destroyed with it. References between entities are EntityRef, with a generation.
  • The ECS gives the elapsed time to every system, and runs deferred actions after its systems, so that a button can open a menu without changing the world while the systems go through it.
  • The interface library is removed. Its behaviour (focus, navigation with the keyboard, a gamepad or the mouse, text fields, values read through functions) is kept by components and systems of the client library libs/engine.
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Animations, drawing and positions are written once, for the game and the interface.
  • The ECS gains features used by the server too (hierarchy, entity references, elapsed time), and its systems now take the elapsed time: update(float elapsed).
  • The order of the systems matters and is documented: scenes first, then the interface (which reads the input before the game), then the game, then what turns the state into positions and sizes.
  • Every system working on entities of a scene must ask Scenes whether the entity receives the input or updates. Persistent entities are never forgotten in a closed scene, but must not hold references to entities of a scene without checking them with Ecs::isAlive().
  • Menus are built with MenuBuilder, which only creates entities: anything can be added afterwards, an icon or an animation.
path: 0007 — The whole client in the ECS, with scenes and a hierarchy

items.title: 0008 — Events switch systems on and off
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-09
path: 0008 — Events switch systems on and off

items.title: Context
items.text:
The engine (libs/engine) has named events: systems subscribe to an event, and something (the input, another system) triggers it. A first version made Event::trigger() call update() on every subscribed system, right away. Since systems take the elapsed time (ADR 0007), it had to pass a made-up update(0.0f), which showed deeper problems:

  • update(elapsed) meant two things: "a frame went by" when called by the ECS, "something happened" when called by an event. A system could not tell them apart, and 0 is also the elapsed time of a paused frame.
  • A system is built by Ecs::registerSystem, which gives it its component caches, so it also runs every frame: a subscribed system was updated twice. Disabling it in the ECS also stopped the event, which skips disabled systems too.
  • The triggered system ran in the middle of the system that triggered the event, out of the order of the frame (scenes first, the interface before the game, positions before drawing). A subscriber removed during a trigger changed the list being gone through.

The question was what triggering an event does to the subscribed systems, without changing the ECS, which stays limited to entities, components and systems.
path: 0008 — Events switch systems on and off

items.title: Options
items.text:
A. Trigger calls update(0) B. Typed event queues C. Trigger switches enabled Meaning of update(elapsed) Two meanings, made-up elapsed time One: a frame One: a frame When the system runs Inside the triggering system At its place in the frame At its place in the frame Systems run by an event only Impossible (updated twice) Run every frame, do nothing without events Yes: disabled until an event enables them Data carried by the event None Typed (Collision{a, b}) None: the data stays in components Code An event class A queue per event type, given to the systems that read it An event class and two lists in Engine Systems to write Unchanged Each reads its queues Unchanged: they do not know the events

B is the classic ECS answer when events carry data. Here an event wakes systems up, and what they need is already in components (a collision system adds a component, the damage system goes through the entities that have it), so C keeps the systems unaware of events, with less code.
path: 0008 — Events switch systems on and off

items.title: Decision
items.text:
C: triggering an event changes the enabled flag of the subscribed systems.

Each subscription gives a reaction and a duration:

Duration::Permanent Duration::Once Reaction::Enable enables the system enables it for the next update, then restores it Reaction::Disable disables the system disables it for the next update, then restores it Reaction::Toggle inverts the flag inverts it for the next update, then restores it

A trigger takes effect at the start of the next Engine::update, wherever it comes from (the input in the main loop, a system, a deferred action):

void Engine::update(float elapsed)
{
    applyPendingReactions(); // the triggers received since the last update
    _ecs.update(elapsed);
