    restoreOnceReactions();  // every system ran at most once: restore the "once" ones
}

Restoring at the end of the update in which the event is triggered would be wrong: a system registered before the one that triggers the event is already skipped for this frame, then restored before it ever runs. Waiting for the next update gives every trigger one frame of delay, whatever the order of the systems.

Two rules settle the conflicts:

  • The reactions are applied in the order of the triggers; the last one wins. Two Toggle in the same frame cancel each other.
  • A permanent reaction cancels a pending restore. It is an explicit decision and is not undone. A system hit by several Once reactions in the same update is restored to its state before the first one.
path: 0008 — Events switch systems on and off

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Systems keep a single update(float elapsed), run once per frame at their place, with the real elapsed time. They do not know about events.
  • A system run by an event only is registered disabled, and subscribed with Reaction::Enable, Duration::Once.
  • An event carries no data: what a woken system needs must be in components.
  • The frame must go through Engine::update instead of Ecs::update, or the reactions are never applied. The client still updates its Ecs directly and has to move to Engine.
  • The enabled flag of a subscribed system belongs to its events: changing it by hand during a frame where a Once reaction is pending is overwritten by the restore.
  • If events need to carry data later (network messages, collisions with their entities), typed queues (option B) can be added next to this mechanism; they do not replace it.
path: 0008 — Events switch systems on and off

items.title: 0009 — Named scenes in the engine
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-09

items.title: Context
items.text:
The Scenes system (ADR 0007) is a stack of open scenes, identified by the SceneId that open() returns. Whoever opens a scene also creates its entities, by hand, wherever it happens to be (the client's main, a menu button). Going from the home screen to the game means knowing every scene that is open, closing them, then building the game again.

The Engine owns the ECS and the events (ADR 0008), but not the scenes: the client registers Scenes itself, and must remember to register it first. Scenes also holds a reference to the whole Ecs, only to destroy the entities of the scenes it closes: the stack of scenes depends on the ECS. Events and scenes do not know each other, although a scene change is when systems most often need to be switched on and off (the game's systems outside the game).

items.title: Options
items.text: A. Engine only owns Scenes B. Named scenes in the engine Opening a scene open(), then create its entities by hand By name: the engine calls its build function Changing scene Close what is open, open the next one, by hand switchScene("game") When it happens Right away, even inside a system's loop At the start of the next Engine::update Link with events None "<name>:open" and "<name>:close"

items.title: Decision
items.text:
B: the engine registers Scenes first, and keeps a table of named scenes.

  • Scenes only keeps the stack, and no longer knows the Ecs: close() and clear() remove scenes from the stack and record their ids. At the start of each update, the engine takes these ids (takeClosedScenes()) and destroys the entities of those scenes, whoever closed them (a scene request, a menu button, Back). Until then, these entities are neither visible nor updated, since their scene is closed.

  • createScene(name, settings, build) declares a scene once. build(engine, id) is called each time it opens and creates its entities, each with a SceneMember.

  • switchScene(name) closes every open scene, then opens this one (home screen → game, game over → home screen). pushScene(name) opens one over the others (pause menu), popScene() closes the top one.
  • The requests take effect at the start of the next Engine::update, like a trigger: no entity is destroyed while a system goes through them, and a button can switch scene from its callback.
  • Each named scene has two events, "<name>:open" and "<name>:close", created with it. The engine triggers them when it opens or closes the scene; their reactions apply in the same update, before the systems run. A named scene closed without the engine (Scenes::close() from a menu button, Back) triggers its close event at the start of the next update.
void Engine::update(float elapsed)
{
    applySceneRequests();    // closes and opens scenes, triggers their events
    applyPendingReactions();
    _ecs.update(elapsed);
    restoreOnceReactions();
}

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Scenes are declared in one place, and a scene change is a single call, safe from anywhere.
  • Systems that belong to a scene subscribe to its events instead of checking which scene is open.
  • Scenes keeps working on its own: unnamed scenes (the menus of MenuBuilder) can still be opened with getScenes().open(), and are closed by switchScene and popScene like the others.
  • A switch has one frame of delay, like a trigger.
  • Scenes used without an Engine no longer destroys anything: the client and the tests go through the Engine. The entities of a closed scene live until the next update, hidden.

items.title: 0010 — A custom kinematic physics engine
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-11

items.title: Context
items.text:
The engine needs physics: entities that move, and the contacts between them (a missile hits a Bydo, a ship picks up a power-up, a ship runs into the walls of a level). The physics belongs to the engine, not to the R-Type: another game made with it must be able to use it with its own collision layers and its own reactions.

Requirements:

  • Kinematic only. A shoot'em up has no mass, rotation, friction, bounce or stacking: entities move at the speed they are given, and only the contacts matter, plus blocking against static obstacles.
  • In the ECS. Movement and collisions are components and systems, like the rest of the engine (ADR 0007), with no second world to keep in sync.
  • Without the engine library. The server simulates the game and has no window: the physics depends on libs/ecs only, never on raylib nor on libs/engine, where the scenes and the events live (ADR 0008, ADR 0009).
  • Independent of the frame rate. The same inputs give the same results at 30 or 144 frames per second, so that the server and the clients agree, the client can predict and be corrected, and tests are reproducible.
  • A few hundred colliders per update on the server (players, Bydos, missiles), within a fraction of a frame.
  • 3D assets are planned. The collision shapes are set by hand, independently of what is drawn: never the mesh of a model.

items.title: Options
items.text:
A. Box2D B. Jolt Physics C. Custom kinematic physics Dimensions 2D 3D Ours: 3D geometry, used in 2D with z = 0 What it brings Rigid bodies, joints, continuous collisions Rigid bodies, characters, constraints, multithreading Movement, overlaps, layers, blocking Used features Overlaps and filtering: a small part Same, an even smaller part All of them Data Its own b2World: positions copied from and to the components every step Its own PhysicsSystem, same copies The ECS components themselves Creating and destroying entities Mirrored in its world (bodies to create and destroy) Same Nothing to do Determinism Same binary and platform Cross-platform when built for it Same binary and platform; ours to control Dependency One more CPM package, in the server too A large one, in the server too None Code to write The synchronization with the ECS Same Integration, intersection tests, broad phase, tunneling: a few hundred lines

A and B solve problems the engine does not have (rigid body dynamics), and their main cost, a second world to keep in sync with the ECS, is paid on every entity. Their strength, stable stacking and joints, is not used.

items.title: Decision
items.text: C: a custom, kinematic physics library, libs/physics (rtype::physics), depending on rtype::ecs only.

items.title: What the engine provides, and what the game provides
items.text:
The physics provides components, systems and pure functions, and knows no game:

Provided by the physics Provided by the game Velocity, Acceleration, MaxSpeed The values Collider (shape, offset, trigger), Static, FastMoving The shapes and sizes, set by hand CollisionLayer, CollisionMask, as 32-bit masks, and canCollide() The names of the bits (Player, Enemy, …) ConfinedToBounds, DestroyOutOfBounds The zones MovementSystem, BoundsSystem, CollisionSystem Its own systems that react to the contacts (damage, pick-ups, score)

CollisionLayer and CollisionMask each hold a 32-bit mask. The game assigns meanings to the bits. canCollide(a, b) accepts a pair only when a's mask includes at least one of b's layer bits and b's mask includes at least one of a's layer bits. A missing layer or mask is treated as all bits set, so an entity with neither component accepts every layer. An explicit zero mask or layer matches nothing.

items.title: Shapes and geometry
items.text:
• Axis-aligned boxes first, spheres next, behind a std::variant in Collider. No rotated boxes, no polygons, no meshes.
  • The geometry is written in 3D (Vec3, Aabb, Sphere, Ray), as pure functions independent of the ECS. The game is played on a plane: Position stays {x, y} in the ECS, and the systems use z = 0. The same functions serve later for anything in 3D (picking with a ray, a 3D view) without a rewrite.

Aabb::halfSize contains the distances from its center to its faces. A shape stored in a Collider has its world center at {Position.x, Position.y, 0} + Collider::offset + shape.center. Intersections and point containment include touching boundaries, including zero-size shapes. A ray uses origin + direction * t for t >= 0; its direction need not be normalized, and a ray starting inside a shape hits at t = 0. Penetration returns a normal pointing from the first shape toward the second and a nonnegative depth; no overlap returns no result. For coplanar AABBs of zero z thickness, penetration chooses an x or y axis so the result can resolve a 2D collision.

items.title: Fixed time step
items.text:
The physics runs in fixed steps (1/60 s by default, set by the game), whatever the frame rate. A single system registered in the ECS, PhysicsStep, keeps an accumulator and runs the physics systems once per step, in this order:

void PhysicsStep::update(float elapsed)
{
    _accumulator += elapsed;
    for (int steps = 0; _accumulator >= _step && steps < _maxSteps; ++steps) {
        _movement.update(_step);  // Velocity and Acceleration → Position (LocalPosition for children)
        _bounds.update(_step);    // ConfinedToBounds, DestroyOutOfBounds
        _transform.update(_step); // Position of the children, from their parent
        _collisions.update(_step); // contacts, then blocking against Static colliders
    }
    _accumulator = std::min(_accumulator, _step); // late beyond _maxSteps: slow down instead of freezing
}
  • The game's systems that write velocities (input, AI) are registered before PhysicsStep, those that read contacts after it. They run once per frame, the physics zero, one or several times.
  • The cap on steps per frame avoids the "spiral of death": a machine too slow to keep up slows the game down instead of freezing it.
  • The remaining fraction of a step (alpha) is exposed, so that the drawing can interpolate between two steps.
  • Each physics system also derives from rtype::ecs::System and can be registered alone, for a test or a game that does not want a fixed step.

items.title: Collision events
items.text:
CollisionSystem exposes the frame's Collision events through collisions(). Each event contains two EntityRef values, a normal pointing from the first entity toward the second, and a penetration depth. Game systems registered after physics can read the list to apply damage, pickups, or scoring.

PhysicsStep clears the list at the start of every frame and collects contacts across its fixed steps. The same pair appears once per frame, including when it touches across several steps. A frame without a physics step has an empty list. A standalone CollisionSystem clears its list on each update() call. Game systems must use ecs.defer() to destroy an entity after reading the events; EntityRef remains recognizable as stale if an entity is later destroyed or its id reused.

items.title: Scenes
items.text: The physics does not know the scenes, which live in the engine. PhysicsStep takes an optional filter, std::function<bool(entity_t)>: the engine gives it scenes.updates(entity), so that the entities of a covered scene (the game under the pause menu) do not move. Without a filter, every entity is simulated, which is what the server and the tests do.

items.title: Collisions in a step
items.text:
1. Broad phase: a uniform grid, cells about the size of a typical collider; a naive version first, kept in the tests to check that the grid finds the same pairs.
  2. Filtering with canCollide(): both layers must accept each other.
  3. Narrow phase with the geometry functions, which also give the normal and the depth.
  4. Collision events added to the system's list.
  5. Resolution for two non-trigger colliders when one of them is Static: the moving entity is pushed out along the axis of least penetration, and its velocity along that axis is cancelled. Triggers are never resolved. Two mobile colliders and two static colliders produce events without physical separation. MovementSystem does not move an entity marked Static, even if it has a Velocity. When a mobile child is pushed, its LocalPosition and world Position are both updated.
  6. Fast AABB entities (FastMoving) expand their grid bounds over the displacement of the step. If the shapes do not overlap at the end of the step, a swept AABB test checks their relative movement and emits a contact with zero penetration at the first hit. A fast solid is stopped at the first static obstacle; a trigger only emits an event. Unmarked entities do not run swept narrow-phase tests. The sweep uses Velocity * elapsed for the preceding position, so teleports and position corrections need a separate collision check. Spheres continue to use overlap tests only.

items.title: Zone bounds
items.text:
BoundsSystem runs after movement and before the hierarchy transform. ConfinedToBounds keeps a whole collider inside its rectangle and cancels velocity directed out through a blocked edge. An entity without a collider is treated as a point. If a collider is too large to fit on one axis, its center is placed at the zone midpoint on that axis and its velocity on that axis is cancelled. A Static entity is not moved by confinement.

DestroyOutOfBounds removes an entity through ecs.defer() once its entire collider lies beyond the rectangle expanded by margin. Touching the expanded border is still inside. A child uses its current world position from its parent's position and its LocalPosition; confinement adjusts its local position so the following TransformSystem preserves the result. Zones must have finite ordered limits and the destruction margin must be finite and nonnegative.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Movement and collisions are ordinary components and systems: no second world, nothing to synchronize when an entity is created or destroyed, and the server links the physics without raylib.
  • The game decides everything that is specific to it (layers, shapes, reactions), so the physics can be reused by another game made with the engine.
  • The simulation does not depend on the frame rate, which the network prediction and the tests need.
  • The results are identical for the same binary on the same platform. Between Linux (GCC) and Windows (MSVC), floating-point results may differ slightly: the server is authoritative and corrects the clients, so this is acceptable, but exact cross-platform replays would need fixed-point numbers.
  • Everything is ours to write and test: intersection tests, grid, swept collisions. The work is split into the tasks of the "Physics Engine" issue.
  • No rigid body dynamics. If a game needs mass, rotation, joints or stacking, a library such as Jolt Physics would be considered then, in a new record that supersedes this one.

items.title: 0011 — Asio as the networking library
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-15

items.title: Context
items.text:
The client and the server talk over the network: UDP for the game, TCP for the lobby (ADR 0012). Something has to open the sockets, send and receive bytes, and tell the program when data arrives.

Requirements:

  • Linux and Windows, with the same code. Windows is built by the CI with MSVC, and cross-play between both is a goal of the subject.
  • Never wait for a client. The server keeps simulating the game frame after frame whatever the clients do, so receiving and sending must not block the simulation.
  • Encapsulated. The subject allows Asio or the system sockets, but system sockets must be wrapped in our own abstractions. Like raylib in the client (ADR 0002), the library must not appear in the public headers: the rest of the code only sees our classes.
  • Fetched by CPM (ADR 0001), nothing installed on the system.
  • The interesting part stays ours. Reliability over UDP, sessions, encryption of the datagrams and replication of the world are the topics of the Advanced Networking track: the library moves bytes, our code decides what they mean.

items.title: Options
items.text:
A. System sockets B. Asio (standalone) C. ENet D. GameNetworkingSockets What it is BSD sockets on Linux, Winsock on Windows C++ library for sockets, timers and asynchronous operations C library: reliable and unreliable channels over UDP Valve's library: reliability, encryption, fragmentation over UDP Linux and Windows Two APIs, differences to handle by hand (WSAStartup, error codes, SOCKET vs int, closesocket) Same code on both Yes Yes Waiting for data poll/select, or epoll / IOCP to write ourselves Event loop (io_context) with handlers, on epoll and IOCP Its own polling function Its own polling function TCP Yes Yes No No Timers (heartbeat, resend) To write Included (steady_timer) Internal only Internal only What is left for us Everything The protocol: reliability, sessions, encryption, replication Sessions and replication: reliability is done Replication only Dependency None Header-only, no dependency (no Boost) Small C library Large: protobuf, plus OpenSSL or libsodium Through CPM — Easy: headers only Easy Hard
  • A works, but the Linux/Windows differences and an efficient event loop are a lot of code that the game does not need to own, and that would have to be wrapped anyway.
  • C and D do the reliability (and, for D, the encryption) themselves. They would save time, but they remove the very work the networking track evaluates, and neither handles the TCP side.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
B: standalone Asio, fetched by CPM, wrapped in a new library libs/network (rtype::network).

  • Asio is a private dependency of libs/network. Its public headers expose our own types (Address, UdpSocket, TcpListener, TcpConnection), never asio:: types. The client and the server link rtype::network, never Asio.
  • The standalone version is used (ASIO_STANDALONE), not Boost.Asio: no Boost in the project.
  • Asio's TLS support (asio::ssl) is not used: it requires OpenSSL. The encryption uses Mbed TLS behind our own wrapper (ADR 0014), with Asio only moving the encrypted bytes.
  • libs/network knows nothing about R-Type: sockets, serialization, framing, reliability, sessions and encryption are generic. The R-Type messages live in a separate library shared by the client and the server.
  • Each program decides which thread runs the Asio event loop. The server never runs the game simulation on that thread (ADR 0013).
  • Messages go through the logging library (rtype::log::Logger, subsystem network), like the rest of the code.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• One code base for Linux and Windows. Asio provides the event loop, the timers and the error handling.
  • Asio's asynchronous style (handlers called by io_context::run()) has a learning cost. The wrapper keeps it inside libs/network and offers a simpler interface to the rest of the code.
  • Reliability, sessions and encryption of the datagrams are ours to write and test. The work is split into the issues of the "Server & networking" epic.
  • If the wrapper is respected, Asio could be replaced by system sockets later without touching the client or the server.

items.title: 0012 — TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-15
path: 0012 — TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game

items.title: Context
items.text:
The server hosts several games at once, and a player has to reach one before playing: connect to the server, choose a name, list the games, create or join one. Later come a chat, accounts and administration commands. Then, inside a game, the client sends its inputs and the server sends the state of the world many times per second.

These two kinds of traffic have opposite needs:

Outside a game (lobby) Inside a game Examples Connection, game list, create or join a game, chat, accounts Inputs, positions of the entities, spawns, deaths, shots Every message must arrive Yes, all of them Positions: no, the next one replaces a lost one. Spawns, deaths: yes Order Must be kept Each message carries its own tick Latency A few tens of milliseconds unnoticed Every millisecond is felt Size Sometimes large (a list of 50 games, a scoreboard) Small, many per second

What the subject requires:

  • The protocol is binary.
  • All in-game communications (entities, movements, events) MUST use UDP.
  • A second connection using TCP is tolerated for specific cases, with a strong justification.

See Networking concepts for the difference between a stream (TCP) and datagrams (UDP).
path: 0012 — TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game

items.title: Options
items.text: A. UDP only B. TCP only C. TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game Allowed by the subject Yes No: in-game traffic must be UDP Yes, with this justification Lobby messages Need our reliability, ordering and fragmentation layer over UDP Native Native Messages larger than a datagram Fragmentation to write Native Native for the lobby; the game only sends small messages In-game latency Good A lost packet delays everything after it (head-of-line blocking) Good Encryption One scheme to design for datagrams Standard TLS Standard TLS for the lobby; the keys of the datagrams are exchanged over it (ADR 0014) Client crash detection Timeout only Connection closed by the system Connection closed, and timeout for silent network failures Ports to open on the server One One One TCP port, plus UDP ports for the games Code One transport, but our reliability layer must also do ordering and fragmentation One transport Two transports, linked by a token
path: 0012 — TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game

items.title: Decision
items.text:
C: a TCP connection between the client and the master server for everything outside a game, and UDP between the client and its game for everything inside it.

Justification of the TCP connection:

  1. It carries no in-game traffic. Joining a game, the game list, the chat or the accounts happen outside the game simulation. Everything a game does goes through UDP, as the subject requires.
  2. These messages need TCP's guarantees. Every message must arrive, in order. Over UDP, the reliability layer would also have to keep the order and split large messages: it would be rewriting TCP, worse.
  3. Some messages are larger than a datagram. TCP splits and reassembles them without any work from us.
  4. TLS works on it. TLS 1.3 is the standard, audited way to encrypt a connection and to authenticate the server. It protects the keys of the datagrams and, later, the passwords of the accounts.
  5. A closed connection reveals a crashed client at once. When the process of a client dies, its system closes the connection, and the server knows immediately.

Rules:

  • Both protocols are binary, described in the protocol specification.
  • TCP is a stream: each message starts with its size, and the receiver reads exactly that many bytes. A size above the maximum closes the connection.
  • UDP keeps a reliability layer (sequence numbers and acknowledgements): in-game messages that must arrive (a player dies, a client leaves) are sent over UDP and resent until acknowledged.
  • A token links the two. When a player joins a game, the master gives the client, over TCP, the UDP address of the game and a secret token. The client sends this token in its first datagram, and the game knows which player it is.
  • The UDP heartbeat stays. A connection can stay open while the network is down (a cable unplugged, a router failure). The game sends and expects at least one datagram per second, and drops a player after a few seconds of silence.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as Master
    participant G as Game
    C->>M: TCP (TLS): hello, name
    C->>M: TCP (TLS): join game 3
    M->>G: player X, token T, keys
    M->>C: TCP (TLS): UDP port 4251, token T, keys
    C->>G: UDP: connect (T)
    G-->>C: UDP: world state
    C-->>G: UDP: inputs

The client talks to the master over TCP until it joins a game, then to the game over UDP with the token the master gave it.
path: 0012 — TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The lobby, the chat and the accounts reuse TCP's guarantees and TLS instead of rebuilding them.
  • Two transports to write and to test in libs/network, and a token to link a player's two connections.
  • The host opens one TCP port for the master and a range of UDP ports for the games (ADR 0013).
  • A client blocked by a firewall that lets TCP through but not UDP reaches the lobby and then fails to join a game: the client must report it clearly instead of waiting forever.
  • If a lobby message ever has to be sent during a game, it still goes through the TCP connection, which stays open during the game, as long as it does not concern the game simulation.
path: 0012 — TCP for the lobby, UDP for the game

items.title: 0013 — One process per game
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-15

items.title: Context
items.text:
The server hosts several games at once: players connect to it, see the games, and join different ones. Each game simulates its own world in an ECS, at a fixed rate, whatever its clients do.

Requirements:

  • The server is multithreaded: it never blocks waiting for a client message.
  • The server is robust: it keeps running "regardless of what's wrong might happen". A client that crashes is reported to the other players of its game.
  • The ECS is not thread-safe: a world must only be touched by one thread.
  • The subject names two binaries: r-type_server and r-type_client.
  • Linux and Windows.
  • Later: games on other machines than the lobby, if one machine is not enough.

items.title: Where the games run
items.text: A. One process, one thread per game B. One process per game A game crashes (bug, assertion, segmentation fault) The whole server dies, every game with it Only that game dies; the lobby sees it and tells its players Memory shared between games Possible, so concurrency bugs are possible Impossible: games only exchange messages with the lobby Games on other machines Needs a rewrite Start the process elsewhere, the messages are already network messages Communication with the lobby Queues in memory Local TCP connection, with our network library Ports One UDP port can serve every game One UDP port per game Start a game Create a thread Start a process (a few milliseconds) Debugging One process One process per game to attach to

items.title: How the games are started
items.text: B1. One binary, --instance mode B2. A second binary Versions The lobby and its games always come from the same build Both must be deployed together Subject Keeps the two names it requires A third binary to justify Package One file Two files Readability The two roles are separated in two folders Separated in two programs

items.title: How a process is started on Linux and Windows
items.text: Our own code reproc Boost.Process What it is posix_spawn on Linux, CreateProcess on Windows Small C/C++ library (MIT), CMake Part of Boost Standard input, waiting, killing To write for both systems, including Windows command-line quoting and pipes Included Included Dependency None Small, through CPM Boost

items.title: Decision
items.text: B1: a master process (the lobby) that starts one process per game, from the same binary run with --instance. Processes are started with reproc, wrapped in our own Process class.

items.title: The two modes of r-type_server
items.text:
int main(int argc, char **argv)
{
    const auto options = parseOptions(argc, argv);
    if (options.instance) {
        return runInstance(options); // one game
    }
    return runMaster(options);       // the lobby
}

The code of each mode lives in its own folder, apps/server/src/master/ and apps/server/src/instance/. What they share (options, the internal protocol) stays at the root of src/.

items.title: The life of a game
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Master
    participant G as Instance
    M->>G: start: r-type_server --instance --id 7 --udp-port 4251 --master-port 5000
    M->>G: standard input: secret
    G->>M: local TCP 127.0.0.1:5000: instance 7, secret
    M->>G: players, their tokens and keys, game rules
    Note over G: opens UDP 4251, runs the game
    G->>M: game over, scores
    Note over G: exits
    Note over M: frees port 4251

The master starts the instance, which proves who it is with the secret, receives its players, runs the game and reports the result before exiting.

  1. The master starts the instance with its own executable (found by the system, not by argv[0]), a game id, a UDP port and the port of the master's local listener.
  2. The master writes a random secret to the instance's standard input. Command-line arguments are visible to every user of the machine (ps), the standard input is not.
  3. The instance connects to the master on 127.0.0.1 and presents its id and the secret. The master's local listener only accepts connections from the machine itself, and drops any connection without the right secret.
  4. The master sends the players expected in the game, their tokens and encryption keys (ADR 0014), and the rules of the game. It sends new players the same way while the game runs.
  5. The instance opens its UDP port, accepts the players with their tokens, and runs the game.
  6. When the game is over or empty, the instance sends the result to the master and exits. The master frees the UDP port.

items.title: Ports
items.text:
• The master listens on one public TCP port (4242 by default) for the clients, and on one local port for its instances.
  • Each instance gets a UDP port from a range set in the configuration (for example 4243–4299). The size of the range is the maximum number of games. The host opens the public TCP port and the whole UDP range.
  • The client talks to its game directly, without going through the master: no extra hop, no extra latency.

items.title: Threads
items.text:
• Master: one thread runs the Asio event loop (client connections, local connections, timers). Process supervision goes through the same loop.
  • Instance: one network thread runs the Asio event loop (receives, decrypts, decodes; encodes, encrypts, sends), and one simulation thread runs the ECS at a fixed rate. They only share two thread-safe queues: the messages received, and the messages to send. The simulation never waits for the network.

items.title: Crashes
items.text: What dies Who sees it How What happens A client Its game No datagram for a few seconds The game removes the player and tells the other players A client The master The TCP connection is closed The master removes it from the lobby and tells its game A game The master The process has exited, and the local connection is closed The master frees the port and tells the players of that game The master Its games The local connection is closed Each game ends and exits: no orphan processes

items.title: Standalone mode, for tests
items.text: r-type_server --instance --standalone --udp-port 4242 runs a game without a master, accepting clients with a fixed test key. It only exists in debug builds. It serves the automated tests, the measurements and the fuzzing of the game's decoder.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• A bug in one game no longer stops the others. The master is small and has no game code, so it is less likely to crash.
  • Games only communicate through messages, so moving them to other machines later changes the address they connect to, not their code.
  • The master/instance protocol is a protocol of its own, binary like the others, documented in the protocol specification.
  • One more dependency (reproc), hidden behind Process.
  • The host opens a range of UDP ports instead of one. Docker publishes the same range.
  • Debugging a game means attaching to its process, or running it in standalone mode.
  • The engine's events and scenes live in libs/engine, which depends on raylib: neither mode can use them. If the server needs them, the parts without raylib move to a library the server can link, in a separate change.

items.title: 0014 — Encryption of the client/server traffic
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-15

items.title: Context
items.text:
The server is hosted on the Internet, and the clients reach it through networks we do not control. Whoever sits between them (a public Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an operator) must not be able to read or change the traffic, nor pretend to be the server.

The traffic is a TCP connection between the client and the master for the lobby, and UDP datagrams between the client and its game (ADR 0012). Both must be protected, with three properties:

Property Means Without it Confidentiality Nobody else can read the traffic Anyone on the path reads it, with Wireshark for instance Integrity Nobody can change it without being detected An attacker changes or forges messages Authentication of the server The client is sure it talks to our server Man-in-the-middle: the attacker sets up encryption with each side, decrypts, reads, re-encrypts

Encryption alone only gives the first one: if the client and the server simply agree on a key, an attacker in the middle agrees on one key with each of them, and both sides believe they are safe. The client must be able to check the identity of the server.

Other requirements:

  • In-game latency: no handshake per game, and a small cost per datagram (at most 1200 bytes, sent 20 to 60 times per second).
  • Lost and reordered datagrams: each datagram must be decryptable alone.
  • Documented: someone must be able to write a compatible client from the protocol specification, so only standard algorithms.
  • Linux and Windows, fetched by CPM, nothing installed on the system.
  • Never design our own cryptographic algorithms or handshakes. Only assemble standard, audited pieces.

See Networking concepts for the vocabulary.

items.title: How the traffic is protected
items.text: A. Nothing B. TLS on TCP, DTLS on UDP C. TLS on TCP, keys of the datagrams given over TLS D. QUIC for everything E. Our own handshake on UDP Lobby (TCP) In clear TLS 1.3 TLS 1.3 QUIC streams Same handshake Game (UDP) In clear A DTLS handshake per game, then encrypted records Each datagram encrypted with keys received over TLS, no handshake QUIC datagrams Our handshake, then encrypted datagrams Man-in-the-middle Possible Prevented by the server certificate Prevented: the keys never travel outside the authenticated TLS connection Prevented Depends on our design: the classic place for mistakes Cost when joining a game None A full handshake None None A handshake Fits our protocol — DTLS adds its own records, retransmission and reordering on top of ours Our header, our sequence numbers, one encrypted block Replaces our reliability layer and TCP: the work the networking track evaluates disappears Yes Precedent — WebRTC netcode.io (Glenn Fiedler), for action games HTTP/3 —

items.title: Which library
items.text: OpenSSL Mbed TLS wolfSSL BoringSSL libsodium / Monocypher TLS 1.3 Yes Yes Yes Yes No: cryptographic primitives only Encryption of single datagrams (AEAD) Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Built by CPM on Windows Hard: Perl and NASM, no CMake Easy: plain C, CMake Possible Possible Easy Licence Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 GPL (or commercial) Own, no stable API promised ISC / BSD With Asio asio::ssl, built on OpenSSL Small adapter Small adapter Small adapter —

items.title: Decision
items.text: C: TLS 1.3 on the TCP connection, with the server's public key pinned in the client; each UDP datagram encrypted and authenticated with ChaCha20-Poly1305, with per-player keys the master sends over TLS. The library is Mbed TLS, for both.

items.title: TCP: TLS 1.3, server key pinned
items.text:
• Only TLS 1.3 is accepted, no older version.
  • The server has a key pair (ECDSA P-256). The private key is a file on the server, given with --key, readable only by the server's user and never in the repository. The public key is shipped with the client, in a file next to the executable.
  • The client accepts the connection only if the key presented by the server is the pinned one (compared by its SHA-256 fingerprint). This is key pinning, the same idea as SSH's known_hosts: no certificate authority and no domain name are needed. An attacker cannot present our key, since proving ownership of it requires the private key.
  • Asio moves the bytes, Mbed TLS encrypts and decrypts them, behind our own TlsConnection class in libs/network (ADR 0011).

items.title: UDP: keys given by the master
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as Master
    participant G as Game
    C->>M: TLS: join game 3
    Note over M: draws session id S and two random keys
    M->>G: local link: player X, S, keys
    M->>C: TLS: UDP port, S, keys
    C->>G: UDP: header (S, packet number) + encrypted payload + tag
    G->>C: UDP: header (S, packet number) + encrypted payload + tag

The keys of the datagrams only travel inside the authenticated TLS connection and the master's local link, so an attacker on the path never sees them.

  1. When a player joins a game, the master draws a session id and two random 256-bit keys: one for the client-to-game direction, one for the game-to-client direction.
  2. It sends them to the game over its local link (ADR 0013), and to the client over TLS.
  3. Each datagram is made of:
    • a header in clear: protocol version, message type, session id, packet number (64 bits, starting at 0 in each direction, incremented on every datagram);
    • the payload, encrypted;
    • a 16-byte tag computed over the header and the payload.
  4. The algorithm is ChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439), an AEAD: it encrypts the payload and authenticates the payload and the header in one operation. The header is passed as associated data: it stays readable, but changing one bit of it makes the tag wrong.
  5. The nonce is the packet number, padded to 96 bits. A nonce must never be used twice with the same key: the number only grows, each direction has its own key, and new keys are drawn for every game the player joins. A sender that would wrap its counter closes the session instead.
  6. The receiver finds the keys with the session id, checks the packet number against a replay window (the highest number received and a bitmap of the 256 previous ones), then decrypts. A wrong tag, an unknown session or a number already seen: the datagram is dropped silently, and counted. The window is updated only after a successful decryption.
  7. Possessing the key is the proof of identity: the first datagram a game decrypts with a player's key comes from that player. The session id only selects the key and is not a secret.

ChaCha20-Poly1305 is chosen over AES-GCM because it is fast and runs in constant time in software on every processor, with or without AES instructions. It is the algorithm of WireGuard.

items.title: Master ↔ instance link
items.text: The link stays on the machine (127.0.0.1) and is not encrypted: no traffic leaves the machine. The instance proves who it is with the secret received on its standard input. If games ever run on other machines, this link gets TLS too, in a new record.

items.title: Keys in practice
items.text: Where What Server Private key file, given with --key. *.key files are ignored by git. Client Server public key next to the executable. Changing server means changing this file. Development A tool, r-type_keygen, generates a local key pair: see Generate the server keys. Standalone instance (debug builds only) A fixed test key, so that tests and fuzzing can talk to a game without a master.

items.title: What this does not protect
items.text:
• The sizes and the timing of the datagrams stay visible.
  • Flooding: handled separately, by limiting the number of clients and of datagrams per second and per address. A datagram with a wrong tag is rejected before any expensive work.
  • A modified client (cheating): the server is authoritative and only accepts inputs, never positions.
  • Who the player is: anyone with the client can connect. Accounts and passwords, protected by TLS, come later.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Nobody on the path can read, change, forge or replay the traffic, nor impersonate the server.
  • Joining a game costs no handshake; each datagram costs 16 bytes of tag and a negligible encryption time.
  • Forged datagrams without the key are rejected by the tag. This replaces the cookie handshake that would otherwise protect against spoofed source addresses.
  • Wireshark no longer shows the content: a debug build can log the decrypted messages at the trace level.
  • The specification describes the header, the nonce, the associated data and the replay window, so that another client can be written.
  • Mbed TLS is one more dependency, wrapped in libs/network. The latest release is used (4.2.0 when this record was written), not an LTS branch: every 4.x release keeps the same API, so following new releases is a version bump.
  • Mbed TLS 4 moved its cryptography to the PSA Crypto API and to a separate repository, TF-PSA-Crypto, included as a git submodule. CPM fetches the release archive (mbedtls-4.2.0.tar.bz2, with its SHA-256), which contains the submodules, not the archive GitHub generates from the tag, which does not.
  • Its security advisories are followed: a fix means bumping the pinned version and hash in CPM.
  • The private key must be protected on the host. If it leaks, a new key pair is generated and a new client configuration distributed.

items.title: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-16
path: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session

items.title: Context
items.text:
The client needs its game scene (issue #124). The main menu leads to it two ways:

  • Play: a game alone, offline, without a server.
  • Online: the lobby, then a game hosted by an instance of the server (ADR 0012, ADR 0013).

Both games must look and feel the same: same ships, same Bydos, same HUD, same pause menu. Only who decides what happens changes.

Requirements:

  • The server is authoritative online. The client sends its inputs and draws the world it receives; it never decides a collision, a death or a spawn.
  • The rules of the game are written once. The server instance simulates them, and the offline client must simulate the same ones: a Bydo must not behave differently offline.
  • The rules cannot live in libs/engine, which depends on raylib and is client-only, nor in libs/ecs, which stays pure (ADR 0006). The server links neither raylib nor the engine.
  • The simulation runs at a fixed tick (60 per second, the tick rate of ACCEPTED), like the physics (ADR 0010), whatever the frame rate of the client.
  • The pause differs: offline, the pause menu stops the game; online, the game goes on under it.
  • Later: prediction of the local ship online, and the game logic on its own thread (issue #118).
path: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session

items.title: Options
items.text:
A. Two game scenes B. One scene, rules in the client's world offline C. One scene, fed by a session D. One scene, a local server process offline Idea game_offline and game_online, each with its own systems Offline, the rules' systems run in the engine's ECS on the drawn entities; online, replication systems write them The scene draws snapshots and sends inputs; a local session simulates in the client process, a remote session talks to the server Offline, the client starts r-type_server --instance --standalone and connects to it over UDP on 127.0.0.1 Rules written once Yes, if both share a library Yes, shared library Yes, shared library Yes, it is the server Code of the scene (view, HUD, pause) Twice, or factored out by hand Once Once Once Paths of the world state in the client Two Two: the rules write the entities offline, the replication online One: snapshots in both modes One Replication tested offline No No Yes: an offline game goes through it Yes Authoritative state apart from the drawing Depends No: the rules see the drawing components, and could start depending on them Yes: the simulation has its own ECS, like on the server Yes Pause offline Easy The scene stops updating The local session stops stepping A message to the server process What offline needs at runtime Nothing Nothing Nothing The server binary next to the client, a free UDP port, encryption keys, a firewall that lets it through Logic on its own thread later To redo for each scene Hard: the rules share the world of the drawing The local session runs the simulation on a thread, like the instance Already another process Cost Duplicated code Nothing extra A copy of the world state per tick (a few hundred entities) A process, encryption and the network for a game alone

A duplicates what makes both games feel the same. B mixes the authoritative state with the drawn entities: offline and online then go through different code, and a replication bug only shows online. D works, but a game alone depends on a second binary, a port and a firewall, and the standalone mode only exists in debug builds (ADR 0013).
path: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session

items.title: Decision
items.text:
C: one game scene, fed by a GameSession. Offline, a LocalSession runs the simulation in the client process; online, a RemoteSession talks to the instance. The rules live in a new library, libs/game, shared by the server and the client.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Client["r-type_client"]
        direction TB
        Scene["Game scene<br/>view, HUD, pause<br/>(engine ECS)"]
        Session{{"GameSession"}}
        Local["LocalSession<br/>Simulation in the process"]
        Remote["RemoteSession<br/>UDP session"]
        Scene -- "PlayerInput" --> Session
        Session -- "Snapshot" --> Scene
        Session -.-> Local
        Session -.-> Remote
    end
    subgraph Instance["r-type_server --instance"]
        Sim["Simulation"]
    end
    Remote -- "inputs (UDP)" --> Instance
    Instance -- "world state (UDP)" --> Remote

The scene only exchanges inputs and snapshots with its session; offline the simulation runs in the client, online in the server instance.
path: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session

items.title: Who does what
items.text:
libs/game/                rtype::game, rules of the R-Type; depends on ecs, physics, log; no raylib
  Component/              Player, Bydo, Missile, Health, Score...: the authoritative state
  System/                 player control, shots, waves, damage, score...
  Input/PlayerInput       what one player does during one tick: direction, buttons
  Snapshot/Snapshot       the world at one tick: the state of each entity, the events of the tick
  Simulation/Simulation   owns an ECS and the systems; takes inputs, steps one tick, gives a snapshot

apps/server/src/instance/ Simulation + the UDP sessions of the players
apps/client/src/Game/
  GameSession             the interface below
  LocalSession            owns a Simulation
  RemoteSession           the UDP session with the instance (game protocol)
  GameScene               builds the scene: background, HUD; the pause menu over it
  GameSessionSystem       Controls → PlayerInput → session; snapshots → drawn entities

  • Simulation is the game. It owns its own Ecs, registers the rules' systems and the physics (PhysicsStep with the tick as its step), and knows neither the network nor the drawing. The instance and the LocalSession use the same class.

    rtype::game::Simulation simulation(rules);
simulation.addPlayer(0);
simulation.setInput(0, input);        // input of slot 0 for the next tick
simulation.step();                    // exactly one tick
const rtype::game::Snapshot &state = simulation.getSnapshot();

  • GameSession is all the scene knows. The names below are a sketch, to be settled with the code:

    class GameSession {
public:
    virtual ~GameSession() = default;
    /// The local player's input, sent with the next tick.
    virtual void sendInput(const game::PlayerInput &input) = 0;
    /// Steps the local simulation, or handles the datagrams received.
    virtual void update(float elapsed) = 0;
    /// The snapshots received since the last call, oldest first.
    [[nodiscard]] virtual std::vector<game::Snapshot> takeSnapshots() = 0;
    /// Offline, stops the game; online, the game goes on.
    virtual void setPaused(bool paused) = 0;
    [[nodiscard]] virtual bool isOver() const = 0;
};

    LocalSession::update accumulates elapsed and steps the simulation once per tick, like PhysicsStep. RemoteSession::update polls the network, decodes the game messages into the same Snapshot, and closes the session as the protocol says.

  • The game scene is the view. Its entities only carry what is drawn (Sprite, Model, Drawable, HUD texts) and a Replicated{id} linking each one to an entity of the snapshots. The GameSessionSystem turns the Controls of the engine into a PlayerInput, then applies the snapshots: it creates the drawn entity of a new id from its kind (player ship, Bydo, missile), moves the existing ones (interpolated between the last two snapshots), and destroys those that disappeared. Effects that change nothing in the game (explosions, star-field, sounds) are created by the client from the events of the snapshots.
path: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session

items.title: Choosing the mode
items.text:
The session is created before the scene opens, and the scene does not know which one it gets:

Offline Online Started from Play GAME_JOINED received in the online menu Session LocalSession, one player in slot 0 RemoteSession: UDP port, session id and keys from the master The scene opens At once On ACCEPTED; until then, "Connecting…" in the online menu Pause menu Pushed over the game, setPaused(true) Pushed over the game, the game goes on; the ship receives no input End isOver(): game over isOver(): game over, DISCONNECT, timeout Back to The main menu The online menu (the TCP connection to the lobby stays open)

The client owns the current session (one at a time) and gives it to the scene's build function and to the GameSessionSystem; it destroys the session when the game scene closes. The game scene keeps updatesWhenCovered, so the session is still updated under the pause menu.
path: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The rules are written and tested once, in libs/game, without a window or a network: the [game] tests step a Simulation with inputs and check its snapshots.
  • An offline game goes through the same snapshots, interpolation and drawn entities as an online game, with no latency: most replication bugs show offline.
  • The client has two worlds offline: the simulation's ECS and the engine's. The state of a few hundred entities is copied each tick, which is negligible.
  • The rules cannot use the engine (scenes, events, Controls): inputs reach them as PlayerInput, and their results leave as Snapshot. The ECS is not modified.
  • The game messages of the protocol (types 0x40–0xFF, "defined in a later version") must carry PlayerInput and Snapshot: full or delta snapshots, and how often they are sent, are the next decisions.
  • Prediction of the local ship online can reuse the movement of libs/game inside RemoteSession, without touching the scene.
  • LocalSession can later run its Simulation on its own thread with two queues, like the instance (issue #118), without touching the scene either.
  • Local co-op (two players on one machine) would be a LocalSession with two slots and two PlayerInputs.
path: 0015 — One game scene, fed by a local or a remote session

items.title: 0016 — Replication of the game world
items.text: Status Proposed Date 2026-10-17

items.title: Context
items.text:
The game instance runs the Simulation of libs/game at 60 ticks per second and is authoritative: clients send what their players do, never positions or results (ADR 0015, ADR 0013). The protocol already defines how to exchange messages over UDP, encrypted, reliable or not (game protocol). What travels inside is left open: ADR 0015 notes that "full or delta snapshots, and how often they are sent, are the next decisions".

Two flows must be decided:

  • Inputs, from each client to its game: what the player does at each tick.
  • The world, from the game to each client: the entities (ships, Bydos, missiles), the players' scores and lives, and what happens (an explosion, a new wave, the end of the game).

Requirements:

  • Losses and reordering are normal. A lost datagram must cost at most a little smoothness, never a wrong world on the client: an entity that stays on screen after being destroyed, an action never received.
  • One datagram is at most 1200 bytes (game protocol), of which about 1150 for the messages. A game holds tens to a few hundred entities: missiles are many and short-lived.
  • Latency matters more than bandwidth. Waiting for a resend (an RTT or more) is visible; a few tens of kilobytes per second per player are not a problem for a server or a home connection.
  • Simple to implement and to test, in the client and in the server, by a team new to networking. Another client must be writable from the specification alone.
  • Ready for later improvements: interpolation now, client-side prediction of the local ship later, compression if measurements show the need.

items.title: The world
items.text: A. Full snapshot every tick B. Full snapshots at a lower rate, explicit destructions C. Delta snapshots D. Reliable events only Idea The state of every entity, 60 times per second The state of every entity every 2 ticks (30 per second), split in parts if needed; destructions as reliable messages Only what changed since the last snapshot the client acknowledged (the Quake 3 model) "Spawned here", "moved there", reliable A lost datagram Nothing: the next one replaces it Nothing: the next one replaces it Nothing, the base is the last acknowledged one Everything waits for the resend Size per player ~16 bytes × entities × 60 / s Half of A Much smaller when few things change; but in a shoot'em up almost everything moves Small, but many messages Entities beyond one datagram Several datagrams per tick Several parts, each one usable alone Same, plus the base tracking — Destruction An entity missing from the snapshot A reliable message: a lost part does not look like a destruction Explicit in the delta Explicit Complexity Low Low High: a history of snapshots per client, acknowledgements, a base per client Medium, and laggy Smoothness on the client Interpolation between snapshots Interpolation, 100 ms behind Same as B Jerky on losses

items.title: Inputs
items.text: A. The current state, unreliable B. Tick-stamped, unreliable, sent again in the next datagrams C. Reliable Idea "These buttons are held now" "At tick T the buttons were…, at T−1…": the last 8 ticks in every datagram Each input as a reliable message A lost datagram The input of that moment is lost; a short tap may never arrive Recovered by the next datagram: 8 datagrams in a row must be lost to lose an input Waits for the resend: the ship reacts an RTT late Which tick an input belongs to Unknown: the server applies it when it arrives Known: the server applies it at the right tick, and can tell the client which input it applied last (needed for prediction) Known Size 1 byte 1 byte per tick: 8 bytes 1 byte, plus the reliability

items.title: Decision
items.text: World: B. Full snapshots every 2 ticks (30 per second), unreliable, split in independent parts when they do not fit in one datagram; entities destroyed with a reliable message. Inputs: B. One byte of buttons per tick, stamped with its tick, the last 8 ticks in every datagram.

items.title: Snapshots
items.text:
• A snapshot holds the tick, the players' scores and lives, and the state of each entity: id, kind, owner, position, velocity, health and flags, 16 bytes per entity in fixed point. A datagram carries up to 69 entities; beyond, the snapshot is split in up to 16 parts, each with the tick and the players.
  • Each entity state is complete: a part can be applied alone, a lost part only delays the update of its entities. The client creates an entity the first time it appears in a snapshot.
  • An entity is destroyed only by ENTITIES_DESTROYED, reliable, with the cause (killed, or removed when it leaves the game area). Missing from a snapshot means nothing, since its part may be lost. The game never reuses an entity id, so a late snapshot cannot be mistaken for a new entity.
  • The client keeps the last snapshots and draws the world 100 ms in the past, interpolating between the two snapshots around that time: three snapshots, so one lost snapshot goes unnoticed.

items.title: Inputs
items.text:
• An input is one byte per tick: up, down, left, right, fire. The client samples the virtual gamepad once per tick and sends INPUT with the last 8 inputs.
  • The game applies, at each tick, the input of that tick if it has it, otherwise the last one it has. Inputs of ticks already simulated are ignored; inputs too far ahead too.
  • Each snapshot tells the client the tick of its last input that the game applied: unused for now, it is what prediction needs later.

items.title: Events
items.text: Only what cannot be read from the next snapshot is a reliable message: a destruction (to draw an explosion and remove the entity), a new wave (for the HUD), and the end of the game. Scores and lives are in every snapshot: a lost snapshot is replaced, and the client never shows an old score after a newer one.

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The client and the server only build or read whole snapshots: no history per client, no base to agree on. A replication bug can be reproduced offline, since LocalSession produces the same Snapshot (ADR 0015).
  • Bandwidth, for 100 entities: 2 datagrams per snapshot (about 1.8 KB), 30 snapshots per second, so about 55 KB/s per client from the server, and about 4 KB/s from each client. Four players: about 220 KB/s for an instance.
  • The world is drawn 100 ms late, on top of the network latency. The local ship can be predicted later, from the inputs not applied yet, without changing the messages.
  • A game cannot hold more than 16 × 69 = 1104 entities in a snapshot: far beyond what a level needs. The game must keep its entities in the area that positions can encode (−4096 to 4096 units), and destroy those that leave it.
  • Delta compression is the next step if a level ever needs much more bandwidth: it changes the SNAPSHOT message only, and increases the protocol version.
  • Adding an entity kind or an event does not change the version: older clients skip what they do not know.

items.title: 0017 — Asset preparation on a background thread
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-19
path: 0017 — Asset preparation on a background thread

items.title: Context
items.text: The main menu loads several large models. Synchronous file reads and decoding delay the first rendered frame. Raylib creates textures, model buffers and font atlases using the window's graphics context; these operations must remain on the render thread. Audio objects must also be created and used on their owning thread.
path: 0017 — Asset preparation on a background thread

items.title: Decision
items.text:
The engine owns one lazily created FIFO worker queue for asset preparation. The client passes it to the render and audio resource managers; direct users of either manager get a private queue by default. The worker reads the file and, where raylib offers a CPU-only operation, decodes it. ResourceManager::finishPendingLoads() and AudioPlayer::finishPendingLoads() are called by their owning threads. They finalize at most one ready request per asset type on each call. A std::shared_future<Id> reports completion or an exception. The caller polls with wait_for(0) and may draw a placeholder or loading screen until it is ready; it must not block its own thread with get() while a request is pending.

Asset Worker Owning thread Texture Read file and decode image in CPU memory Upload texture and create mipmaps Font Read file, decode glyphs and build their atlas in CPU memory Upload atlas texture Model Read model bytes Parse with raylib and upload meshes, materials and textures Sound Read file and decode wave in CPU memory Create audio buffers and voices Music Read file Create the streaming decoder on the audio owner thread

Raylib 6.0 does not expose a CPU-only model loader or a separate model upload operation. Consequently, model parsing still takes time on the render thread after the background file read. This is a remaining limitation of this implementation, visible on unusually large models. No OpenGL call runs on a worker.

Requests for the same path and options share a future. The underlying ResourceCache serializes inserts and lookups and stores resources at stable addresses, so overlapping requests cannot create duplicate handles. A failed request reports its exception and is removed from the pending map, allowing a retry. Existing synchronous methods remain available and return the same cached handle when an asynchronous request has completed.

The client's startup requests its fonts, starfield and menu models before building the menu. It draws a loading screen using the built-in font until the requests are ready, then builds scenes with the existing synchronous APIs, which find the assets in the cache. Tests exercise worker/owner separation, deduplication, retries, the engine's shared worker, concurrent cache access and the audio path without a device.
path: 0017 — Asset preparation on a background thread

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• The loading screen responds while files are read and textures or sounds are decoded.
  • Finalization must be pumped each frame on the resource owner's thread.
  • The manager must be destroyed after its outstanding requests or the requests receive a broken-promise error.
  • Resources remain owned by the manager and are freed before the window or audio device closes.
path: 0017 — Asset preparation on a background thread

items.title: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons
items.text: Status Accepted; The binding and Where it lives superseded by 0019 Date 2026-10-20
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Context
items.text:
Enemies and weapons (and the projectile categories they fire) are described by data: the model of a ship, its health, speed and acceleration, its weapon; for a weapon, its projectile type, fire rate, range, ammunition capacity and reload time; for a projectile category, its behavior and its sounds. Creating one must not need a recompilation: a new enemy or a new weapon is a new file.

Requirements:

  • Data first. The files describe values. Nothing in them is needed to run the game outside of the simulation's rules.
  • Scripting later. Some behaviors (the movement pattern of an enemy or of a boss) are easier to write as code than as data. Adding them must not mean replacing the configuration format.
  • Without the engine library. The server simulates the game and has no window: the loader depends on libs/game only, never on raylib (ADR 0010 follows the same rule).
  • Deterministic. The server and the clients load the same files and must reach the same results, so that the prediction and the replication agree (ADR 0016).
  • Safe. A configuration file must not be able to touch the disk, the network or the clock.
  • Simple to build. One more CPM package at most (ADR 0001), building the same way on Linux and Windows, in the CI and on the students' machines.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Options
items.text:
A. JSON B. Lua C. Python Nature Data only Embedded language Full language Dependency A header-only parser Lua (a few hundred KB, plain C) CPython and pybind11, to install or ship Build and CI Nothing special Compiled with the project The version of Python, its shared library, packaging of the client Determinism Total: values Controlled: no clock and no unseeded random in the sandbox Hard to guarantee Safety No code runs Sandboxable: libraries removed from the state Hard to sandbox Expressiveness None: no computation, no condition Functions, computations, patterns Same, richer Scripting later Another mechanism to add Same language, same loader Same, but heavy Validation Schema and precise errors By hand, on the loaded tables By hand

JSON is the simplest and covers the data alone, but a behavior script would be a second mechanism added beside it. Python brings a large dependency to the server and to every client without bringing more than Lua. Lua is data when the file is a table and code when it needs to be, in a single mechanism.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Decision
items.text: B: Lua 5.4, embedded in libs/game, fetched by CPM.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Files
items.text:
A configuration file is a Lua chunk that returns a table:

return {
    id = "bydo_scout",
    model = "models/bydo_scout.glb",
    health = 30,
    speed = 4.0,
    acceleration = 12.0,
    weapon = "pulse_cannon",
}

The data stay plain tables: no function is needed to describe an enemy or a weapon. A file may later set a field to a function (a movement pattern) without any change to the others.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Sandbox
items.text: Each file is run in its own state, with only the base functions, table, string and math libraries. io, os, package, debug and load*/dofile/require are not available, and math.random is removed: a file cannot read the disk, the clock or an unseeded random value, so the same files give the same simulation on the server and on the clients. A script that runs for too long is stopped by an instruction count hook.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Validation
items.text: Lua does not check the shape of a table. The loader reads the returned table into plain C++ structures (EnemyDefinition, WeaponDefinition, ProjectileCategory) and checks the types, the required fields and the ranges. An error names the file and the field (bydo_scout.lua: health: expected a positive number), and a file that fails is rejected as a whole; the server does not start with a partial configuration.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: The binding
items.text: The loader reads fields of a few tables: it uses the plain Lua C API behind a small wrapper (a state that owns the lua_State, typed getters for a field), not a template binding library such as sol2. The project favors explicit code over metaprogramming, and reading tables does not need more. If scripted behaviors later call into the simulation, the binding can be reconsidered in a new record.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Where it lives
items.text: The loader and the definitions are in libs/game, so the server and the client share them. Lua is a PRIVATE dependency of that library. The simulation only sees the C++ definitions, never a Lua state.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Creating an enemy or a weapon is writing a file, without recompiling.
  • Scripting (movement patterns, boss phases) can be added later with the same loader and the same language.
  • A new dependency, built from source by CPM in the server too; it is small and written in plain C.
  • Validation is ours to write: no schema checks the files for free as with JSON. The cost is a few typed getters and the error messages.
  • The sandbox must be kept tight. Adding a standard library to the state (for instance os for the time) breaks the determinism and needs a new record.
  • Lua 5.4 is used rather than LuaJIT, which is stuck on the 5.1 language and less portable across the platforms of the CI.
  • The existing JSON setup is converted to Lua tables once; JSON is not kept as a second format.
path: 0018 — Lua for the configuration of enemies and weapons

items.title: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors
items.text: Status Accepted Date 2026-10-21
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: Context
items.text:
ADR 0018 chose Lua 5.4 to describe enemies, weapons and projectiles, read through the plain Lua C API behind a small wrapper in libs/game. It left one question open: when scripts call into the simulation, the binding is to be reconsidered.

That time has come. Some behaviors are code, not data: the movement pattern of an enemy, the phases of a boss, the timeline of a wave. A script needs to read and change the game (the position of its entity, its velocity, firing its weapon, a random number from the game's seed), and the simulation needs to call a script function at each tick and read back what it returns.

With the plain C API, each exposed type is a userdata with a metatable, an __index function, a check of every argument on the stack and a push of every result. That is a few dozen lines per type and per function, all written by hand and easy to get wrong (stack balance, type checks).

The requirements of ADR 0018 still apply: no raylib (the server runs the scripts), deterministic, sandboxed, one more CPM package at most per need, the same build on Linux and Windows. In addition:

  • Little binding code. Exposing a class or a function takes one line, not a hand-written metatable.
  • Calls both ways. C++ calls Lua functions and reads typed results; Lua calls C++ functions and methods.
  • Errors with a name. A failing script reports its file and its message, and never crashes the server.
  • Contained compile time. The binding headers stay out of the headers of the game.
  • Maintained. The library follows the Lua releases.
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: Options
items.text:
The runtime stays Lua 5.4 (ADR 0018): LuaJIT is stuck on the 5.1 language and hard to build with CPM on Windows, and Luau is another language, typed and sandboxed but not supported by most bindings and not the format chosen for the configuration files.

A. Plain C API + our wrapper B. sol2 (v3) C. LuaBridge3 Exposing a class A metatable and __index written by hand lua.new_usertype<T>("T", ...) beginClass<T>("T").addFunction(...) Calling a Lua function lua_getfield, pushes, lua_pcall, pops sol::protected_function luabridge::LuaRef, called like a function Lua versions All 5.1 to 5.4, LuaJIT 5.1 to 5.4, LuaJIT, Luau, Ravi Dependency None besides Lua Header-only, C++17 Header-only, C++17 Compile time None Heavy: deep templates in every translation unit that includes it Lighter Code in our repository Large and error-prone Small Small Maintenance Ours Rare releases Active Errors By hand around lua_pcall Exceptions or protected_function_result Exceptions (LuaException) or result checks

Option A is the most explicit, but the binding code grows with every type the scripts see, and that code is where the bugs would be. sol2 is the most complete and the best documented, at the price of a heavy compile time and few releases. LuaBridge3 covers what we need with a simpler API, compiles faster, and is maintained.
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: Decision
items.text:
C: LuaBridge3, in a new library libs/scripting, on the Lua 5.4 of ADR 0018.

This replaces the sections The binding and Where it lives of ADR 0018. Its file format, sandbox and validation are unchanged.
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: libs/scripting
items.text:
rtype::scripting owns what every use of Lua shares, without any game notion (like the ECS, it stays generic):

  • the build of Lua: the Lua 5.4 sources are fetched by CPM (DOWNLOAD_ONLY) and compiled as a static C library, without lua.c and luac.c; LuaBridge3 is fetched by CPM, header-only. Both are included as SYSTEM so that their warnings do not reach rtype_options;
  • a State that owns the lua_State, opens only the libraries of the sandbox of ADR 0018 (base, table, string, math without math.random), installs the instruction count hook, and loads a file into its own environment table, so that two scripts do not share their globals;
  • the conversion of a Lua error into a C++ error that names the file.

It depends on Lua and LuaBridge3 only: no raylib, no ECS, no engine. LuaBridge3 is part of its public interface, for the libraries that write bindings.
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: Bindings in libs/game
items.text:
libs/game links rtype::scripting PRIVATE. It writes the bindings of what the scripts may see, in its .cpp files only: no header of the game includes Lua or LuaBridge3, and the simulation's systems keep working on C++ types.

The scripts see a small API made for them (their entity's position and velocity, firing, the tick, a random number), not the ECS: the component caches are not exposed. The random number comes from GameContext::randomBetween, seeded by the rules, so a game still replays the same. The exact API is documented in docs/architecture/game.md when it is written.
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: States and lifetime
items.text:
• The configuration files keep a throwaway state each, as in ADR 0018: they are read once into C++ definitions.
  • The behavior scripts run in one State owned by the Simulation, created when the game starts and destroyed with it. The scripts run wherever the simulation runs: the server instances and the client offline. An online client never runs a script, it shows the snapshots (ADR 0016).
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: Errors
items.text: A script that fails to load rejects the configuration, as in ADR 0018: the server does not start. A script that fails during the game (an error or the instruction limit) is logged with its file and message, and that behavior is stopped for the rest of the game; the server keeps running.
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: Consequences
items.text:
• Exposing a function or a type to the scripts is one line in a binding file, instead of a hand-written metatable.
  • One more header-only dependency, LuaBridge3, beside Lua; both build from source with CPM on every platform.
  • The wrapper planned by ADR 0018 lives in libs/scripting, not in libs/game, and the configuration loader uses it like the behaviors do.
  • LuaBridge3 hides its templates behind a plain API; our code does not add metaprogramming. Compile time stays limited to the binding files, which are the only ones that include it.
  • The API of the scripts is a contract: renaming a bound function breaks the scripts. It is kept small and documented.
  • Every call into Lua costs a little more than a C++ call. With a few dozen enemies at a fixed tick this is negligible; if a profile says otherwise, the per-tick calls are the place to look, not the runtime.
  • Revisit this record if LuaBridge3 stops following the Lua releases, or if the scripts need a typed language (Teal or Luau).
path: 0019 — LuaBridge3 and a scripting library for Lua behaviors

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
This section gets you from a fresh clone to a running client and server.

  1. Build the project on Linux or Windows.
  2. Start the server, then one client per player.
./build/bin/r-type_server
./build/bin/r-type_client

Prebuilt binaries

Released versions of the client and the server, for Linux and Windows, are available on the Releases page. Every push also builds the project; its archives can be downloaded from the Artifacts section of the corresponding run in the Build workflow.

items.title: Building the project
items.text: The project is built with CMake. Third-party libraries are downloaded and built automatically by CPM.cmake during the first configure: nothing has to be installed system-wide besides a compiler and, on Linux, the X11/OpenGL development packages.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• CMake ≥ 3.25
  • A C++20 compiler: GCC or Clang on Linux, Microsoft Visual C++ (Visual Studio 2022) on Windows
  • Internet access for the first configure
Debian / UbuntuArch LinuxWindows 
sudo apt install build-essential cmake \
    libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libgl1-mesa-dev

sudo pacman -S base-devel cmake libx11 libxrandr libxinerama libxcursor libxi mesa

Install Visual Studio 2022 with the Desktop development with C++ workload, which includes CMake.

items.title: Configure and build
items.text:
LinuxWindows 
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build --parallel

Binaries are written to build/bin/.

From a Developer PowerShell for VS 2022:

cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build --config Release --parallel

Binaries are written to build\bin\Release\.

items.title: Running the tests
items.text:
ctest --test-dir build -C Release --output-on-failure

See the testing policy for how tests are organised and written.

items.title: Sharing downloaded dependencies
items.text:
By default, each build directory downloads its own copy of the dependencies. Point CPM to a shared cache to download them only once:

LinuxWindows 
export CPM_SOURCE_CACHE="$HOME/.cache/CPM"

setx CPM_SOURCE_CACHE "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\CPM"

The variable is read when a build directory is configured for the first time.

items.title: Packaging
items.text:
cd build
cpack -C Release

This produces one archive per program: r-type-<version>-Linux-client.tar.gz and r-type-<version>-Linux-server.tar.gz on Linux, .zip files on Windows. Published versions are built the same way, see Releasing.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
CMake reports a dependency path that no longer exists
