The dependency cache location is stored in the build directory when it is first configured. Delete the build directory (or build/CMakeCache.txt) and configure again.

Missing X11 headers on Linux

Install the development packages listed in Requirements; raylib needs them to create its window.

items.title: Guides
items.text:
Step-by-step guides for common tasks in the client and the server. They assume the project builds, see Build.

Guide What you will do Write a system Add a component and a system to the ECS, and test it. Draw a sprite Add an image to the assets, load it and show it with an entity. Add a menu Build a menu with widgets, open it and close it. Add a player action Add a new action, bind it to keys and buttons, and react to it. Add a network message Specify a message, encode and decode it, and test it. Generate the server keys Make the key pair the server proves its identity with, and put each key where it belongs. Run a server Check the configuration, open the ports, start the server and stop it. Play online Give the key of the server to the clients, connect, create and join a game.

For how the systems used here work, see Scenes and interface, Rendering, Input and Networking.

items.title: How to add a menu
items.text: This guide adds a menu to the client, for instance a Controls menu opened from the options. It is for anyone building the interface.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• The project builds: see Build.
  • You know how menus work: see Menus and Scenes.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Declare a function that opens the menu in apps/client/src/Menus.hpp, next to the others. It takes the MenuTargets: what the menus are built with and act on.

    /// Opens the controls menu: the keys of each action.
void openControlsMenu(const MenuTargets &targets);

  2. Build the menu in apps/client/src/Menus.cpp with a MenuBuilder. It opens a scene, and creates a background, a title and the widgets stacked at the centre.

    void openControlsMenu(const MenuTargets &targets)
{
    engine::MenuBuilder menu(targets.ecs, targets.scenes, targets.metrics, targets.style, "Controls");
    const engine::SceneId scene = menu.scene();

    menu.label("Choose an action to change its keys");
    menu.button("Shoot", [] { /* ... */ });
    menu.button("Back", [targets, scene] { targets.scenes.close(scene); });
}
    • Overlay or not: pass {.overlay = true} as the last argument of the MenuBuilder to keep the scene below visible, dimmed, like the pause menu over the game. Without it, the menu hides what is below, like the options.
    • Widgets: label, button, toggle, slider, choice and textField (see the table in Menus). Settings are given as functions that read and write them, never as copies.
    • Captures: the lambdas capture targets by copy (it only holds references) and the scene id. Never capture local variables by reference: the function returns long before the buttons are pressed.

  3. Open it from another menu, or from the game:

    options.button("Controls", [targets] { openControlsMenu(targets); });

    From the game code, open a menu only while the game scene receives the input (scenes.receivesInput(game)), as the pause menu is opened in main.cpp.

  4. Going back. Escape (or the right face button of a gamepad) closes the menu at the top and shows the one below. To do something else, for instance asking for confirmation before leaving the game, give an onBack to the scene: {.onBack = [targets] { openQuitConfirmation(targets); }}.

  5. Test it without a window, like tests/engine.cpp: build the menu with the FakeInput and fake text measures, press keys, and check what the widgets did.

items.title: Result
items.text: The menu opens over the others, can be used with the keyboard, a gamepad or the mouse, and its entities are destroyed when it closes. The focused widget bounces, like in every menu built with MenuBuilder.

items.title: How to add a network message
items.text: This guide adds a message to the protocol, from its specification to its tests, taking CREATE_GAME of the lobby as the example. It is for anyone who needs the client and the server to exchange something new.
path: How to add a network message

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• The project builds: see Build.
  • You have read the protocol conventions (types, byte order) and the serialization part of Networking.
path: How to add a network message

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Specify the message first, in the page of its protocol: lobby, game or master and instances. Copy the message template, take the next free type in the range of its direction, and describe every field with its type and its allowed values:

    #### CREATE_GAME (`0x03`)

| Offset | Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Name | `str8` | Name of the game, 1 to 32 bytes |
| 1 + n | Max players | `u8` | 1 to 4 |

    The specification is the reference: someone must be able to write a compatible program from it alone. Changing an existing message increases the protocol version.

  2. Write the message as a struct: its type, its fields, with the C++ types matching the specification.

    struct CreateGame {
    static constexpr std::uint8_t Type = 0x03;
    static constexpr std::size_t MaxNameLength = 32;
    static constexpr std::uint8_t MaxPlayers = 4;

    std::string name;
    std::uint8_t maxPlayers = MaxPlayers;
};

  3. Write encode(): the fields in the order of the specification, nothing else.

    void encode(const CreateGame &message, rtype::network::Writer &writer)
{
    writer.writeString(message.name);
    writer.writeU8(message.maxPlayers);
}

    The type byte and the size of the frame are added when the message is sent, not here.

  4. Write decode(): read every field in the same order, refuse the values the specification forbids with reader.fail(), and end with reader.finish(), which also refuses bytes left after the last field.

    std::optional<CreateGame> decode(rtype::network::Reader &reader)
{
    CreateGame message;
    message.name = reader.readString(1, CreateGame::MaxNameLength);
    message.maxPlayers = reader.readU8();
    if (message.maxPlayers < 1 || message.maxPlayers > CreateGame::MaxPlayers) {
        reader.fail();
    }
    if (!reader.finish()) {
        return std::nullopt;
    }
    return message;
}
    • Do not test the reader after each field: once a read fails, the following ones do nothing, and finish() reports the first problem.
    • Never size memory with a count read from the network (reserve(count)): for a list, loop while reader.ok().
    • Never throw, never log, never touch anything but the message: the caller logs the reason with toString(reader.error()), and the decoder stays a pure function that can be fuzzed.

  5. Test it in tests/, with the [network] tag. Test the round trip, the bytes of the specification, and every way the message can be refused:

    TEST_CASE("CREATE_GAME survives a round trip", "[network]")
{
    Writer writer;
    encode(CreateGame{.name = "Room", .maxPlayers = 2}, writer);
    Reader reader(writer.bytes());

    const auto message = decode(reader);
    REQUIRE(message);
    CHECK(message->name == "Room");
    CHECK(message->maxPlayers == 2);
}

TEST_CASE("A cut CREATE_GAME is refused at every length", "[network]")
{
    Writer writer;
    encode(CreateGame{.name = "Room", .maxPlayers = 2}, writer);
    for (std::size_t size = 0; size < writer.size(); ++size) {
        Reader reader(writer.bytes().first(size));
        CHECK_FALSE(decode(reader));
    }
}

TEST_CASE("CREATE_GAME with 5 players is refused", "[network]")
{
    Writer writer;
    writer.writeString("Room");
    writer.writeU8(5);
    Reader reader(writer.bytes());

    CHECK_FALSE(decode(reader));
    CHECK(reader.error() == ReadError::InvalidValue);
}

    Add a test for each other rejection: empty or too long name, invalid text, byte left at the end.
path: How to add a network message

items.title: Result
items.text:
./build/bin/rtype_tests "[network]" passes, and the specification describes the message.

On TCP, the message is sent as a frame with its type, and received whole (TCP framing):

Writer writer;
encode(CreateGame{.name = "Room", .maxPlayers = 2}, writer);
connection.send(CreateGame::Type, writer.bytes());

// On the other side, in the frame handler
if (type == CreateGame::Type) {
    Reader reader(payload);
    if (const auto message = decode(reader)) { /* handle it */ }
}

Dispatching the messages by their type is done by the lobby, and the datagram messages by the sessions, in the next steps of the "Server & networking" work.
path: How to add a network message

items.title: How to add a player action
items.text: This guide adds a new action to the player's controls, for instance a charged shot, binds it to keys and gamepad buttons, and reacts to it in the client. It is for anyone adding gameplay controls.
path: How to add a player action

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• The project builds: see Build.
  • You know how actions work: see Input.
path: How to add a player action

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Add the action to the Action enum in apps/client/src/Controls.hpp:

    enum class Action {
    MoveUp,
    MoveDown,
    MoveLeft,
    MoveRight,
    Shoot,
    ChargedShot,   // new
};

  2. Bind it in defaultControls(), in apps/client/src/Controls.cpp. Give it at least one keyboard key and one gamepad input, so that it can be played with both:

    controls.bind(Action::ChargedShot, Binding::key(Key::LeftShift));
controls.bind(Action::ChargedShot, Binding::gamepadButton(GamepadButton::FaceRight));

    Remember that keys are physical positions named after a QWERTY keyboard: Key::Q is the A key on AZERTY. Check that the new keys do not conflict with other actions.

  3. React to it in the client, after controls.update(devices, window.frameTime()). Choose the function matching the behaviour you want:

    if (controls.wasPressed(Action::ChargedShot)) {
    // start charging: true for one frame when the key goes down
}
if (controls.wasReleased(Action::ChargedShot)) {
    // fire: true for one frame when the key goes up
    const float charge = controls.heldDuration(Action::ChargedShot);   // seconds it was held
}

    Use isActive() for something that lasts while the input is held, wasRepeated() for something that repeats while it is held, and strength() for an analog value between 0 and 1.

  4. Update the documentation: add the action to the table of default controls in Input.

  5. Build and run the client:

    cmake --build build
./build/bin/r-type_client
path: How to add a player action

items.title: Result
items.text: The action reacts to every input bound to it. To test logic that depends on actions without a keyboard, use a fake InputSource as in tests/action_map.cpp.
path: How to add a player action

items.title: How to draw a sprite
items.text: This guide adds an image to the client's assets, loads it, and shows it with an entity. It is for anyone adding graphics to the client.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• The project builds: see Build.
  • The image is a PNG file. JPEG is not supported (see Supported formats).
  • Its licence allows using it in the project. Note its author and licence when adding it.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Add the file to apps/client/assets/, in the folder of its kind, for instance apps/client/assets/sprites/ship.png. Nothing has to be declared in CMake: the whole folder is copied next to the executable at every build.

  2. Load it once, after the ResourceManager is created and before the game loop. Loading returns a handle; keep it to give it to the entities.

    const TextureId shipTexture = resources.loadTexture("sprites/ship.png");   // relative to assets/

  3. Create an entity that shows it. Everything the client draws is an entity (ADR 0007): it needs a Position, a Drawable and a Sprite.

    const entity_t ship = ecs.createEntity();
ecs.addComponent<SceneMember>(ship, game);                    // destroyed with the game scene
ecs.addComponent<Position>(ship, 200.0f, 540.0f);             // centre of the sprite, in game units
ecs.addComponent<Drawable>(ship, Layer::World, 10);           // world layer, drawn over lower orders
ecs.addComponent<Sprite>(ship, shipTexture, Rectangle{0.0f, 0.0f, 32.0f, 32.0f}, 96.0f, 96.0f);
    • The Position is the centre of the sprite, in game units (1920x1080), not in window pixels.
    • The Rectangle is the part of the texture to show, in texture pixels: here the first 32x32 frame of a sprite sheet. The last two numbers are the size on screen, in game units: here three times bigger.
    • The Drawable sets the layer (World for the game, Interface for the HUD and menus) and the order: a higher order is drawn on top.

  4. Change it through its components, from a system or the game code:

    ecs.getComponent<Position>(ship).y -= 10.0f;                 // move it
ecs.getComponent<Sprite>(ship).source.x = 32.0f * frame;      // show another frame of the sprite sheet

    A Scale or an Opacity component changes its size or transparency, and a Tween animates them (see Animations).

  5. Build and run the client:

    cmake --build build
./build/bin/r-type_client

items.title: Result
items.text:
The SceneRenderer draws the sprite every frame, at the position of the entity. It stays at the same place relative to the game when the window is resized, and disappears when its scene closes.

If the client stops with r-type_client: Cannot load texture ..., the path is wrong, the file is missing from build/bin/assets/ (build again), or the format is not supported.

Drawing without an entity

The Renderer can also draw directly (renderer.drawTexture() between beginFrame() and endFrame()). Keep it for debugging tools: what is drawn this way is not part of a scene, nor of a layer, and is not drawn on the VR board.

items.title: How to generate the server keys
items.text:
This guide makes the key pair the server proves its identity with, and puts each key where it belongs. It is for anyone who runs a server, for development or for players.

The client only talks to a server that has the private key matching the public key it was given: another server, or an attacker between them, is refused (ADR 0014, TLS).
path: How to generate the server keys

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: • The project builds: see Build. The tool, r-type_keygen, is built with the server and packaged with it.
path: How to generate the server keys

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Generate the keys, in the directory of your choice (created if missing):

    LinuxWindows 
    ./build/bin/r-type_keygen --out keys

    .\build\bin\Release\r-type_keygen.exe --out keys

    Private key: keys/server.key  (keep it on the server only, never share it)
Public key:  keys/server.pub  (give it with the client)
Fingerprint: 5b61c7a9ce1a44bfc64fec2013a4a09b6b4d5a8db4129eff890a1462c7ea1f1c

    The tool does not replace keys that already exist: see Replacing the keys.

  2. Keep server.key on the server, which loads it with its --key option (Run a server). On Linux, the file is only readable by the user who made it (rw-------): run the server as that user. On Windows, the file gets the access rights of its directory, so put it in a directory only the server's account can read.

    Never commit it, never send it: anyone who has it can pretend to be the server. Git ignores *.key files.

  3. Give server.pub with the client, next to its executable. It is public: it can be committed, sent and published freely.

  4. Check the fingerprint if the public key went through someone else's hands. The fingerprint shown by the tool must be the same as the one of the file the clients have:

    r-type_keygen --fingerprint server.pub   # or server.key, which gives the same fingerprint

    Without the tool, OpenSSL gives the same value:

    openssl pkey -pubin -in server.pub -outform DER | sha256sum
path: How to generate the server keys

items.title: Result
items.text: The server has server.key, the clients have server.pub. When a client connects, the server proves in the TLS handshake that it has the private key, and the client checks that its public key is the pinned one. If they do not match, the client refuses the server, with NetworkError::UntrustedServer and an error in the logs naming both fingerprints.
path: How to generate the server keys

items.title: Replacing the keys
items.text:
Replace the keys only if they must change: every client keeps refusing the server until it gets the new server.pub.

r-type_keygen --out keys --force

If server.key leaked (committed, sent, copied to a machine you do not trust), replace the keys at once and give the new server.pub to every client: whoever has the old private key can pretend to be the server to the clients that still pin the old key. Removing the file from git is not enough, since it stays in the history.
path: How to generate the server keys

items.title: Reference
items.text:
r-type_keygen [--out <directory>] [--force]
r-type_keygen --fingerprint <file>
Option Effect -o, --out <directory> Where to write server.key and server.pub, created if missing. The current directory by default. -f, --force Replace the keys already there. Without it, nothing is written if either file exists. --fingerprint <file> Show the fingerprint of server.key or server.pub, and write nothing. -h, --help Show the usage. Exit code Meaning 0 Done 1 The keys could not be written (they exist, or the directory cannot be written) or read 2 Invalid arguments

Errors go to the logs, on the error output; set RTYPE_LOG_LEVEL=debug for more detail (Logging). The keys are ECDSA P-256 keys in PEM, which OpenSSL and other tools read.
path: How to generate the server keys

items.title: Play online
items.text: Run a server, give its key to the clients, and play the same game from several machines, or from several clients on one machine.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Make the keys of the server, once (Generate the server keys):

    ./build/bin/r-type_keygen --out keys

  2. Start the server with its private key (Run a server):

    ./build/bin/r-type_server --key keys/server.key

    For players on other machines, open the TCP port 4242 and the UDP ports 4243 to 4299.

  3. Give the public key to each client: copy keys/server.pub next to the executable of the client, as server.pub.

    cp keys/server.pub build/bin/server.pub

    On another machine, copy it next to its r-type_client. The key is public: it can be sent by any means.

  4. Connect. Start the client, choose Online, type the server and a name, then Connect:

    Field Example Meaning Server 127.0.0.1:4242 The address of the server and its port; the port is 4242 if omitted Name Pavel 1 to 16 characters, shown to the other players

  5. Play. In the lobby, Create a game, or Join one of the list (Refresh to see the new ones). A second client, on this machine or another, joins the same game: each player has a ship of its colour. Escape opens the pause menu, where Leave the game goes back to the list.

items.title: Result
items.text:
The players see each other's ships move. The server shows them in its logs:

INFO  lobby    Pavel (1) joined the lobby from 127.0.0.1:51234
INFO  games    Pavel creates game 1 "Pavel's game" for 4 players: instance 48213 on UDP 4243
INFO  games    game 1 "Pavel's game" ready on UDP 4243
INFO  instance Pavel (1) connected from 127.0.0.1:40102, slot 0
Toast in the client Fix server.pub is missing next to the client Copy the public key of the server next to the executable (step 3) Cannot reach ...: Connection refused The server does not run, or the address or the TCP port is wrong, or blocked This is not the expected server server.pub is not the key of this server: copy the right one The game cannot be reached: its UDP port may be blocked The lobby works but not the games: open the UDP range of the server The server cannot host another game Every game port is taken: wait for a game to end, or give the server more ports

items.title: How to run a server
items.text: This guide starts an R-Type server that players can reach, then stops it. It is for anyone who hosts a server, on their own machine for development or on a machine on the Internet.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• The project builds: see Build. The server is build/bin/r-type_server (build\bin\Release\r-type_server.exe on Windows), or the one of the server archive of a release.
  • The server keys: see Generate the server keys.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Check the configuration. --check loads the key and opens the port, then exits, without running the server:

    ./build/bin/r-type_server --key keys/server.key --check

    INFO  master   Lobby on TCP 0.0.0.0:4242, games on UDP 4243-4299 (57 at most)
INFO  master   Server key 5b61c7a9ce1a44bfc64fec2013a4a09b6b4d5a8db4129eff890a1462c7ea1f1c
INFO  master   Check passed: the server can start

    The server key must be the fingerprint of the server.pub the players have.

  2. Open the ports if players come from another machine: the TCP port of the lobby (4242), and the UDP range of the games (4243 to 4299), in the firewall of the machine and, at home, as port forwarding on the router. Without the UDP range, players reach the lobby but no game: their client gives up after 5 seconds.

    Linux (ufw)Windows 
    sudo ufw allow 4242/tcp
sudo ufw allow 4243:4299/udp

    New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "R-Type lobby" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 4242 -Action Allow
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "R-Type games" -Direction Inbound -Protocol UDP -LocalPort 4243-4299 -Action Allow

  3. Start the server:

    ./build/bin/r-type_server --key keys/server.key

    Other ports, fewer games, more logs:

    ./build/bin/r-type_server --key keys/server.key --port 5000 --game-ports 5001-5010 --log-level debug

  4. Stop it with Ctrl+C, or kill <pid> (SIGTERM), or systemctl stop / docker stop when it runs as a service. It stops properly, which may take a few seconds once games run; a second Ctrl+C stops it at once.

items.title: Result
items.text:
The server listens for the players until it is stopped, and exits with code 0. If it cannot start, it says why and exits with code 1:

Message Fix Cannot read the key server.key: No such file or directory Give the path with --key, or make the keys ... is not a key of the server The file is not an ECDSA P-256 private key: give server.key, not server.pub Cannot listen on 0.0.0.0:4242: Address already in use Another server runs on that port: stop it, or choose another with --port

Once it runs, the games it starts show in its logs. Players who create a game and get GAME_START_FAILED point to its instances: Cannot open UDP port means another program uses the game ports, choose others with --game-ports.

Every option is listed by r-type_server --help and in Server.

items.title: How to write a system
items.text:
This guide adds a component and a system to the ECS: a Velocity that moves entities every frame. It is for anyone writing gameplay, on the client or on the server.

Note

The physics already provides these, rtype::physics::Velocity and MovementSystem: use them in the game. The guide writes simpler ones to show how a system is built.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• The project builds: see Build.
  • You know the vocabulary: an entity is only an id, a component is plain data attached to an entity, a system runs the logic on the entities that have the components it needs. The whole API is described in ECS, and how components are stored in ADR 0006.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Write the component: a plain struct, with default values. No logic, no pointers to other entities (use an EntityRef, see below).

    struct Velocity {
    float x = 0.0f;   // game units per second
    float y = 0.0f;
};

    Put components used by the client and the server (positions, velocities, health) where both can include them; never in libs/engine, which depends on raylib and is not linked by the server.

  2. Write the system: derive from rtype::ecs::System, get the caches of the components it uses with use<T>() in the constructor, and keep the references.

    class MovementSystem : public rtype::ecs::System
{
    rtype::engine::Scenes &_scenes;
    rtype::ecs::ComponentCache<rtype::ecs::Position> &_positions;
    rtype::ecs::ComponentCache<Velocity> &_velocities;

public:
    MovementSystem(rtype::ecs::ComponentCaches &caches, rtype::engine::Scenes &scenes)
        : _scenes(scenes), _positions(use<rtype::ecs::Position>(caches)), _velocities(use<Velocity>(caches))
    {
    }

    void update(float elapsed) override
    {
        for (rtype::ecs::entity_t entity = 0; entity < _velocities.size(); ++entity) {
            if (!_velocities.has(entity) || !_positions.has(entity) || !_scenes.updates(entity)) {
                continue;
            }
            rtype::ecs::Position &position = _positions.get(entity);
            const Velocity &velocity = _velocities.get(entity);
            position.x += velocity.x * elapsed;
            position.y += velocity.y * elapsed;
        }
    }
};
    • Go through the ids of the rarest component (here Velocity), and check the others with has().
    • Multiply by elapsed: speeds are per second, so the game runs at the same speed at 30 or 144 frames per second. Never read a clock in a system.
    • Ask the scenes whether the entity updates (_scenes.updates(entity)): the entities of a menu covered by another one must not move. A system that reads the player's input checks _scenes.receivesInput(entity) instead.

  3. Register it, at the right place in the order of the systems (see The systems and their order). The arguments after the type are given to the constructor, after the caches:

    ecs.registerSystem<MovementSystem>(scenes);

    Game systems go after the InterfaceSystem and before the TransformSystem, so that children follow entities moved in this frame.

  4. Create entities that have the components:

    const entity_t missile = ecs.createEntity();
ecs.addComponent<SceneMember>(missile, game);         // destroyed with the game scene
ecs.addComponent<Position>(missile, 100.0f, 540.0f);
ecs.addComponent<Velocity>(missile, 1200.0f, 0.0f);

  5. Test it, without a window: create an Engine, register the system, run an update with a chosen elapsed time, and check the result. Add the test to tests/ (see Testing).

    TEST_CASE("A missile moves at its velocity", "[game]")
{
    Engine engine;
    Ecs &ecs = engine.getEcs();
    Scenes &scenes = engine.getScenes();
    ecs.registerSystem<MovementSystem>(scenes);
    const SceneId game = scenes.open();
    const entity_t missile = ecs.createEntity();
    ecs.addComponent<SceneMember>(missile, game);
    ecs.addComponent<Position>(missile, 100.0f, 540.0f);
    ecs.addComponent<Velocity>(missile, 1200.0f, 0.0f);

    engine.update(0.5f);

    REQUIRE(ecs.getComponent<Position>(missile).x == 700.0f);
}

items.title: Rules to keep in mind
items.text: Situation Do A component points to another entity (target, owner) Store an EntityRef (ecs.ref(entity)) and check it with ecs.isAlive(reference) before using it: ids are reused. An entity is attached to another one (the Force to the ship) Use the hierarchy: attach(), then move it with its LocalPosition. The system creates or destroys entities, or adds components of a type it goes through Wrap the change in ecs.defer(...): it runs after the systems, when no cache is being read. Destroying is safe while iterating, creating is not. The system needs data shared by every entity (score, wave number) Give it to the constructor by reference, like the Scenes above, rather than a global.

items.title: Result
items.text: Entities with a Position and a Velocity move every frame, and stop moving when their scene is covered by another one. The test runs in the CI with the other unit tests.

items.title: Network protocol
items.text: Status Version 1, specified, not yet implemented Version 1 Transport TCP with TLS 1.3 for the lobby, encrypted UDP for the games (ADR 0012, ADR 0014)

items.title: 1. Introduction
items.text:
This specification defines the binary protocol between r-type_client and r-type_server, and between the master server and its game instances. Anyone MUST be able to write a compatible client or server by reading it only.

It is split into four pages:

Page Content This page Conventions, overview, constants, error handling, security Lobby (TCP) The connection between a client and the master: TLS, framing, lobby messages Game (UDP) The datagrams between a client and its game: encryption, reliability, sessions, inputs and snapshots Master and instances The local connection between the master and the game processes it starts

Version 1 defines how to reach a game, how to exchange messages with it securely and reliably, and the messages of the game itself: the players' inputs, the snapshots of the world and the events (game, section 9).

The words used here are explained in Networking concepts.

items.title: 2. Conventions
items.text:
The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

  • All multi-byte integers are transmitted in network byte order (big-endian).
  • Sizes are given in bytes. Offsets start at 0.
  • Fields are written one after the other, with no padding.

items.title: 2.1 Types
items.text:
Type Size Description u8, u16, u32, u64 1, 2, 4, 8 Unsigned integers i16, i32 2, 4 Signed integers, two's complement bool 1 0 is false, 1 is true. Any other value is invalid. bytes[N] N N raw bytes str8 1 + n A u8 length n, then n bytes of UTF-8 text, without a terminating zero

A str8 is invalid if its bytes are not valid UTF-8, or if they contain a control character (0x00–0x1F or 0x7F). Each field of type str8 gives its allowed length range.

items.title: 2.2 Message tables
items.text:
Each message is described by a table of its fields. The offset is counted from the start of the message payload, after the header of the transport. Example of the layout of the bytes 00 01 05 50 61 76 65 6C:

Offset Field Type Value 0 Version u16 00 01: 1 2 Name str8 05 50 61 76 65 6C: "Pavel"

items.title: 3. Overview
items.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as Master
    participant G as Game instance
    C->>M: TCP 4242, TLS 1.3 handshake (server key pinned)
    C->>M: HELLO (version, name)
    M->>C: WELCOME (player id)
    C->>M: LIST_GAMES
    M->>C: GAME_LIST
    C->>M: JOIN_GAME (game id)
    M->>G: ADD_PLAYER (session id, keys)
    M->>C: GAME_JOINED (UDP port, session id, keys)
    C->>G: UDP: CONNECT
    G->>C: UDP: ACCEPTED (player slot)
    C-->>G: UDP: game messages
    G-->>C: UDP: game messages

The client authenticates the master with TLS, joins a game through it, and receives the UDP port and the keys of the game. It then talks to the game directly, over encrypted datagrams.

  1. The client opens a TCP connection to the master and runs a TLS 1.3 handshake. It checks that the server's public key is the pinned one (lobby, section 2).
  2. Inside TLS, the client and the master exchange framed lobby messages: the client says hello, lists the games, creates or joins one (lobby).
  3. When the client joins a game, the master draws a session id and two keys, gives them to the game process (instances), then to the client with the UDP port of the game.
  4. The client sends datagrams to that port, on the same IP address as the master. Each datagram is encrypted with the keys of the session. The first message is CONNECT; the game answers ACCEPTED (game).
  5. The TCP connection stays open while the client plays: the master uses it to tell the client when it leaves the game, or when the game ends or crashes.

items.title: 4. Versioning
items.text:
The protocol version is a u16, currently 1. It is sent by the client in HELLO, by the instance in INSTANCE_HELLO, and in the header of every datagram (as a u8).

  • A server MUST refuse a HELLO with another version, with the error UNSUPPORTED_VERSION, then close the connection.
  • A receiver MUST drop a datagram whose version is not the one of its session.
  • Any change to the layout or meaning of an existing message increases the version. Adding a new message type that older receivers can ignore does not.

items.title: 5. Constants
items.text: Name Value Description Master port 4242 (default) TCP port of the master, configurable Game ports 4243–4299 (default) UDP port range of the games, configurable Maximum TCP frame 16384 Largest TCP frame, size prefix included (lobby) Maximum datagram 1200 Largest UDP datagram, all fields included (game) Lobby ping interval 10 s A client sends PING if it sent nothing for this long Lobby timeout 30 s The master closes a connection silent for this long Game heartbeat interval 1 s Each side sends a datagram at least this often Game timeout 5 s A session silent for this long is closed Connect timeout 5 s A client without ACCEPTED after this long gives up Tick rate 60 per second Steps of the simulation (game) Game area 1920 × 1080 units The world the client shows; positions in eighths of a unit Snapshot interval 2 ticks 30 snapshots per second (game) Snapshot parts 16 at most Datagrams of one snapshot Inputs per INPUT 8 (recommended), 32 at most The inputs of the last ticks, sent again (game) Input lead 60 ticks The game ignores inputs further ahead Input hold 30 ticks Without inputs for this long, the game applies an empty input Interpolation delay 100 ms (recommended) How far in the past the client draws the world Players per game 1–4

items.title: 6. Error handling
items.text:
A receiver MUST NOT crash, block, or allocate memory according to a size read from the network beyond the limits of this specification, whatever it receives.

What is received TCP (lobby, instances) UDP (game) A frame or datagram larger than the maximum Close the connection Drop the datagram A datagram that fails authentication (wrong tag, unknown session, replayed packet number) — Drop it silently A message too short or too long for its type, or with an invalid value Answer ERROR (MALFORMED), then close Drop the whole datagram An unknown message type Answer ERROR (UNKNOWN_MESSAGE), keep the connection Skip the message, using its size A message that is valid but not allowed now (for instance JOIN_GAME before HELLO) Answer ERROR with the matching code, keep the connection Ignore the message

"Drop silently" means no answer is sent: answering an unauthenticated datagram could be used to flood a third party.

items.title: 7. Security considerations
items.text:
The decisions behind this section are in ADR 0014.

Threat Mitigation Eavesdropping TLS 1.3 on TCP; ChaCha20-Poly1305 on every datagram payload Tampering, forged messages TLS records are authenticated; each datagram carries a tag over its header and payload Man-in-the-middle, impersonating the server The client pins the server's public key (lobby, section 2); the datagram keys only travel inside TLS Replay of recorded datagrams Replay window on packet numbers (game, section 4) Spoofed source addresses A datagram without a valid tag is dropped before anything else Amplification The game never answers a datagram that failed authentication; TCP needs a handshake before any data Flooding, resource exhaustion Limits on connections, frames, datagrams and pending messages (table below) Malformed messages Strict validation of every field (section 6); the decoders are fuzzed Modified client (cheating) The server is authoritative: clients send inputs, never positions or results Stolen server private key Generate a new key pair and distribute a new client configuration

Limits a server MUST enforce, with configurable values:

Limit Default Lobby connections at the same time 256 Lobby connections per IP address 8 TLS handshake duration 10 s, then close Time to send HELLO after the handshake 10 s, then close Games at the same time Size of the game port range Datagrams per second and per source address, before decryption 200, the excess is dropped Reliable messages waiting for an acknowledgement, per session and direction 256, then the session is closed Inputs kept per player 60 ticks ahead, the others are ignored

What the protocol does not hide: the sizes and timing of the datagrams and frames, and the IP addresses of the players.

items.title: Game (UDP)
items.text: The datagrams between a client and its game: layout, encryption, reliability, session messages and game messages. Conventions and types are defined in the overview. The client receives the UDP port, the session id and the keys from the master, in GAME_JOINED.

items.title: 1. Layers of a datagram
items.text:
flowchart TB
    D["Datagram, at most 1200 bytes"]
    H["Header, in clear, 16 bytes<br/>magic, version, session id, packet number"]
    E["Encrypted body + 16-byte tag"]
    B["Body: acknowledgements + messages"]
    M["Messages: type, flags, id if reliable, size, payload"]
    D --> H
    D --> E
    E -- "decrypted with the session key" --> B
    B --> M

A datagram is a clear header followed by an encrypted body; once decrypted, the body carries the acknowledgements and the messages.

items.title: 2. Datagram layout
items.text:
Offset Field Type Description 0 Magic u16 0x5254 ("RT") 2 Version u8 Protocol version, 1 3 Reserved u8 0 4 Session id u32 Session given by the master, never 0 8 Packet number u64 Number of this datagram in its direction, from 1 16 Ciphertext The encrypted body, n bytes 16 + n Tag bytes[16] Authentication tag
  • A datagram is at least 32 bytes (empty body) and at most 1200 bytes, so the body is at most 1168 bytes.
  • The first 16 bytes are the header. They are sent in clear, but authenticated by the tag.

Example of a header: session 42, packet 1:

52 54                     magic "RT"
01                        version 1
00                        reserved
00 00 00 2A               session id: 42
00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01   packet number: 1

items.title: 3. Encryption
items.text:
The body is encrypted with AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 as defined in RFC 8439:

Input Value Key The client key for datagrams sent by the client, the server key for datagrams sent by the game (32 bytes each, from GAME_JOINED) Nonce 12 bytes: 00 00 00 00 followed by the packet number as a big-endian u64 Associated data The 16 bytes of the header Plaintext The body (section 5) Output The ciphertext (same size as the body) and the 16-byte tag

items.title: Packet numbers
items.text:
• Each side keeps its own packet number per session. It starts at 1 and increases by one for every datagram sent, resends included: a resent message travels in a new datagram with a new number.
  • A packet number MUST NEVER be used twice with the same key. If a sender would exceed 2^64 − 1, it closes the session instead.

items.title: Receiving a datagram
items.text:
A receiver processes a datagram in this order, and drops it silently at the first failed step:

  1. The size is between 32 and 1200 bytes.
  2. The magic is 0x5254, the version is 1, the reserved byte is 0.
  3. The session id is a known session.
  4. The source address has not sent more than 200 datagrams in the last second.
  5. The packet number is accepted by the replay window (section 4).
  6. The tag is valid, and decryption succeeds.
  7. The body is well formed (section 5).

Only then does the receiver mark the packet number in the replay window, record the time (for the timeout), apply the acknowledgements, and deliver the messages.

Peer address. The game learns the client's address (IP and port) from the first datagram that passes these steps. If a later datagram passes them from another address with a higher packet number, the game sends to the new address from then on: a home router may change the client's port.

items.title: 4. Replay window
items.text:
Each side remembers, per session:

  • H, the highest packet number accepted, 0 at the start;
  • a bitmap of the 256 packet numbers before H, marking those already accepted.

A packet number n is accepted if:

  • n > H, or
  • H − n ≤ 256, n ≠ H, and n is not marked.

Otherwise the datagram is a duplicate, a replay or too old, and is dropped. After a successful decryption, n is marked; if n > H, H becomes n and the bitmap shifts.

items.title: 5. Body
items.text:
Offset Field Type Description 0 Ack u64 Highest packet number received from the peer, 0 if none 8 Ack bits u32 Bit i (bit 0 is the least significant) set: packet Ack − 1 − i was received 12 Count u8 Number of messages that follow 13 Messages Count messages, one after the other

Each message:

Offset Field Type Description 0 Type u8 Message type 1 Flags u8 Bit 0: reliable. Other bits: 0. 2 Message id u16 Only if reliable (section 6) 2 or 4 Size u16 Size of the payload 4 or 6 Payload Size bytes
  • The body MUST end exactly after the last message. Extra bytes, a size going past the end, or a reserved flag set make the body malformed, and the whole datagram is dropped.
  • A body with no message is a heartbeat: it still carries the acknowledgements.
  • Message types 0x01–0x3F are the session messages of section 8. Types 0x40–0xFF are the game messages of section 9. A receiver skips a message of an unknown type, using its size.

items.title: 6. Reliability
items.text: A message is either unreliable (sent once, may be lost) or reliable (resent until acknowledged, delivered once, in order). The sender chooses per message; each message type below says which it is.

items.title: Acknowledgements
items.text: Every datagram acknowledges the packets received from the peer: Ack is the highest packet number received, and Ack bits mark the 32 before it. A packet is acknowledged as soon as one datagram from the peer marks it.

items.title: Sending reliable messages
items.text:
• Each reliable message gets a message id, per session and per direction, starting at 0 and increasing by one, wrapping from 65535 to 0.
  • The sender remembers which packets carried each reliable message. When one of them is acknowledged, the message is delivered and forgotten.
  • A reliable message not acknowledged after the resend delay SHOULD be added to the next datagram. The recommended delay is max(1.5 × RTT, 100 ms), where the RTT is measured from the acknowledgements, and taken as 100 ms until the first measure.
  • At most 256 reliable messages may wait for an acknowledgement. A sender that would exceed this closes the session: the peer no longer answers.

items.title: Receiving reliable messages
items.text:
The receiver keeps the next expected id E, 0 at the start. For a reliable message of id m, with d = (m − E) mod 65536:

Case Action d = 0 Deliver it, increase E, then deliver the buffered messages that follow without a gap 0 < d < 256 Buffer it, unless it is already buffered Otherwise Already delivered, or out of the window: ignore it

Reliable messages are therefore delivered exactly once and in order. Unreliable messages are delivered at most once (the replay window drops duplicate datagrams), in the order they arrive, which may differ from the order they were sent.

items.title: Round-trip time
items.text: The sender records when it sent each packet. When a packet is acknowledged for the first time, the elapsed time is a sample of the round-trip time. The RTT SHOULD be smoothed (rtt = 0.9 × rtt + 0.1 × sample); it is used for the resend delay and shown to the player as the ping.

items.title: 7. Session
items.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Connecting: GAME_JOINED received
    Connecting --> Connected: ACCEPTED
    Connecting --> Closed: 5 s without ACCEPTED
    Connected --> Closed: DISCONNECT, LEFT_GAME, or 5 s silent
    Closed --> [*]

The client state of a session: it connects, plays, and ends on a disconnection, a notification of the master, or a timeout.

  1. Connecting. The client sends CONNECT (reliable, so resent until acknowledged). The game, which received the session from the master, answers ACCEPTED, sends the client one PLAYER_JOINED per player already connected, and sends PLAYER_JOINED for the new player to the others.
  2. Connected. Both sides exchange messages. Each side sends at least one datagram per second, a heartbeat if it has nothing else to send. The client MUST NOT send game messages before ACCEPTED; the game ignores them.
  3. Closing. A side that closes the session sends DISCONNECT in three consecutive datagrams, then forgets the session. A side that receives no valid datagram for 5 seconds closes the session; it MAY skip DISCONNECT then, since the peer is probably gone.

If the client gets no ACCEPTED within 5 seconds, it gives up and tells the player that the game cannot be reached: a firewall probably blocks UDP. It sends LEAVE_GAME to the master.

When a session closes on the game's side, the game sends PLAYER_LEFT to the other players and, unless the master asked for it with REMOVE_PLAYER, tells the master with PLAYER_DISCONNECTED.

items.title: CONNECT (0x01)
items.text:
Direction Client → Game Reliability Reliable Sent when First message of the session.

No payload. The key proves who the client is: only the player who received it in GAME_JOINED can produce a valid tag.

Receiver behaviour: the game marks the session as connected, records the client's address, and answers ACCEPTED.

items.title: ACCEPTED (0x02)
items.text:
Direction Game → Client Reliability Reliable Sent when Reply to CONNECT. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player slot u8 0 to 3: the player's place in the game, which sets the colour of its ship 1 Tick rate u8 Ticks per second of the simulation, 60 2 Tick u32 Current tick of the game

Receiver behaviour: the client moves to the connected state. A slot above 3 or a tick rate of 0 makes the message malformed.

items.title: DISCONNECT (0x03)
items.text:
Direction Client → Game, Game → Client Reliability Unreliable, sent in three consecutive datagrams Sent when A side closes the session. Offset Field Type Description 0 Reason u8 See below Reason Value Meaning QUIT 0 The player left GAME_OVER 1 The game ended SHUTDOWN 2 The game process stops PROTOCOL_ERROR 3 The peer broke this specification (for instance, too many unacknowledged messages)

Receiver behaviour: the receiver closes the session. Unknown reasons are treated as QUIT.

items.title: PLAYER_JOINED (0x04)
items.text: Direction Game → Client Reliability Reliable Sent when A player connects to the game, and once per player already there when a client connects. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player slot u8 0 to 3 1 Player id u32 Id given by the master 5 Name str8 1 to 16 bytes

items.title: PLAYER_LEFT (0x05)
items.text:
Direction Game → Client Reliability Reliable Sent when A player's session closes. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player slot u8 0 to 3 1 Reason u8 See below Reason Value Meaning QUIT 0 The player left the game TIMED_OUT 1 Nothing received from the player for 5 seconds: its client crashed or lost the network LOBBY_CLOSED 2 The player's connection to the master closed

Receiver behaviour: the client removes the player and tells the local player, for instance "Pavel lost the connection" for TIMED_OUT. Unknown reasons are treated as QUIT.

items.title: 9. Game messages
items.text:
The messages of the game itself: the inputs of the players and the world they play in. How they were chosen is explained in ADR 0016. The game is authoritative: a client sends what its player does, and draws the world the game sends back.

Type Message Direction Reliability 0x40 INPUT Client → Game Unreliable, sent again in the next datagrams 0x80 SNAPSHOT Game → Client Unreliable, replaced by the next one 0x81 ENTITIES_DESTROYED Game → Client Reliable 0x82 WAVE_STARTED Game → Client Reliable 0x83 GAME_OVER Game → Client Reliable

Types 0x40–0x7F are sent by the client, 0x80–0xFF by the game. The client MUST NOT send game messages before ACCEPTED, and the game sends them only to connected sessions.

items.title: 9.1 The world
items.text:
Game area. The world is a fixed area of 1920 × 1080 units, the area the client shows whatever the size of its window. The origin is the top left corner, x goes to the right and y downwards. Entities may be outside the area, for instance a Bydo arriving from the right.

Positions and velocities are fixed-point numbers, in eighths of a unit:

Value Type Meaning Range Position i16 value / 8 units −4096 to 4095.875 Velocity i16 value / 8 units per second −4096 to 4095.875

The game MUST keep its entities in the range of the positions, and destroy those that leave it (cause REMOVED). Example: x = 200.0 is sent as 1600 (06 40), y = 540.5 as 4324 (10 E4), a velocity of −300 units per second as −2400 (F6 A0).

Ticks. The game simulates the world in ticks, 60 per second (the tick rate of ACCEPTED), numbered by a u32 from the start of the game.

Entities. Each entity has an id, a u32 drawn by the game: never 0, and never reused within a game, so that a late message about a destroyed entity cannot be mistaken for a new one. Its kind says what it is, hence what the client draws:

Kind Value Owner Health PLAYER_SHIP 0x01 Its player slot Hit points left PLAYER_SHOT 0x02 Slot of the player who fired 0 PLAYER_CHARGED_SHOT 0x03 Slot of the player who fired 0 BYDO_FLYER 0x10 None Hit points left BYDO_SHOOTER 0x11 None Hit points left BYDO_TANK 0x12 None Hit points left BYDO_BOSS 0x1F None Hit points left BYDO_SHOT 0x40 None 0
  • Ranges: 0x01–0x0F players and their shots, 0x10–0x3F Bydos, 0x40–0x5F Bydo shots, 0x60–0xFF reserved for later kinds (power-ups, the Force, obstacles). Kind 0x00 is invalid.
  • The owner is a player slot (0 to 3), or 0xFF for none.
  • A client MUST skip the entities of a kind it does not know: adding a kind does not change the protocol version (versioning).

items.title: 9.2 Inputs
items.text:
An input is the state of the player's controls during one tick, one byte:

Bit Control 0 Up 1 Down 2 Left 3 Right 4 Fire (held: the game decides what holding it does, for instance charging a shot) 5–7 Reserved: senders set them to 0, receivers ignore them

Up and down together, or left and right together, cancel each other.

Client. Once per tick, the client samples its controls and sends INPUT with the inputs of the last 8 ticks, newest first: a lost datagram loses no input, since the next ones carry it again. It stamps each input with the tick at which it expects the game to receive it, which it SHOULD estimate as:

tick of the latest snapshot received
  + (time since it was received + RTT) × tick rate
  + 2                                       margin, so that the input arrives before its tick

Game. For each player, the game keeps the inputs received for the ticks to come, at most 60 ticks ahead; it ignores inputs for ticks already simulated, and those further ahead. At each tick it applies the input of that tick, or, if it has none, the last input it applied: a lost input continues the previous movement. After 30 ticks without any input from a player, it applies an empty input (nothing pressed), so that a ship whose player lost the connection stops.

items.title: 9.3 Snapshots
items.text:
Sending. Every 2 ticks (30 times per second), after simulating the tick, the game sends each connected client a snapshot: the players' scores and lives, and the state of every entity. When the entities do not fit in one datagram, the snapshot is split in parts (at most 16), each in its own datagram, each with the tick and the players. With four players, a part holds up to 69 entities.

Receiving. The client keeps the tick L of the latest snapshot it applied, and for each part received:

  1. A part with a tick lower than L is late: it is ignored. Parts with the tick L are still applied.
  2. The players replace the scores and lives shown.
  3. Each entity of a known kind is created if its id is unknown, or updated otherwise. An entity missing from a snapshot is not destroyed: its part may have been lost.
  4. An entity is destroyed only by ENTITIES_DESTROYED. The client remembers the ids it destroyed, with the tick of their destruction, and ignores their states in snapshots older than that tick (a reliable message can arrive before an older unreliable one). It can forget an id once L reaches that tick.

Drawing. The client SHOULD draw the world 100 ms in the past, interpolating each entity between the two snapshots around that time: the movement stays smooth when a snapshot is lost. The velocity lets it extrapolate when no newer snapshot is there.

items.title: INPUT (0x40)
items.text:
Direction Client → Game Reliability Unreliable, sent once per tick, with the inputs of the last ticks Sent when Every tick, once connected. Offset Field Type Description 0 Tick u32 Tick of the first input, the newest 4 Count u8 Number of inputs, 1 to 32; 8 is recommended 5 Inputs bytes[Count] The input of Tick, then of Tick − 1, and so on (section 9.2)

Receiver behaviour: the game keeps the inputs as section 9.2 says. A count of 0 or above 32, or more inputs than Tick + 1, makes the message malformed.

items.title: SNAPSHOT (0x80)
items.text:
Direction Game → Client Reliability Unreliable Sent when Every 2 ticks, in one or more parts (section 9.3). Offset Field Type Description 0 Tick u32 Tick of the world described 4 Last input u32 Tick of the last input of this client that the game applied, 0 if none 8 Part u8 Number of this part, from 0 9 Parts u8 Number of parts of this snapshot, 1 to 16 10 Player count u8 0 to 4 11 Players Player count times the fields below 11 + 6p Entity count u8 Number of entities in this part 12 + 6p Entities Entity count times the fields below

Each player:

Offset Field Type Description 0 Slot u8 0 to 3 1 Lives u8 Lives left, 0 once out of the game 2 Score u32

Each entity, 16 bytes:

Offset Field Type Description 0 Id u32 Never 0 4 Kind u8 Section 9.1, never 0 5 Owner u8 Player slot, or 0xFF for none 6 X i16 Position, eighths of a unit 8 Y i16 10 Velocity X i16 Eighths of a unit per second 12 Velocity Y i16 14 Health u8 Hit points left, for health bars; 0 for kinds without 15 Flags u8 Bit 0: invulnerable (just respawned, drawn blinking). Bit 1: charging a shot. Bit 2: hit since the last snapshot. Bits 3–7: reserved, set to 0 and ignored

Receiver behaviour: the client applies the part as section 9.3 says. A part number not below the number of parts, a number of parts of 0 or above 16, more than 4 players, a slot above 3 or given twice, an entity id or kind of 0, or a size that does not match the counts makes the message malformed.

items.title: ENTITIES_DESTROYED (0x81)
items.text:
Direction Game → Client Reliability Reliable Sent when After a tick in which entities were destroyed: one message for all the entities of that tick, or several with the same tick when they do not fit in one datagram (228 entities at most per message). Offset Field Type Description 0 Tick u32 Tick of the destruction 4 Count u8 Number of entities, 1 to 255 5 Entities Count times the fields below

Each entity:

Offset Field Type Description 0 Id u32 Never 0 4 Cause u8 See below Cause Value Meaning REMOVED 0 Removed without effect: it left the game area, or its time was over KILLED 1 Destroyed in the game: the client draws an explosion

Receiver behaviour: the client removes the entities and remembers their ids (section 9.3). Unknown ids are remembered too: their first snapshot may still be on its way. Unknown causes are treated as REMOVED. A count of 0, an id of 0, or a size that does not match the count makes the message malformed.

items.title: WAVE_STARTED (0x82)
items.text:
Direction Game → Client Reliability Reliable Sent when A new wave of Bydos starts, and once to a client that connects during a wave. Offset Field Type Description 0 Wave u16 Number of the wave, from 1

Receiver behaviour: the client shows the number, for instance "Wave 3". A wave of 0 makes the message malformed.

items.title: GAME_OVER (0x83)
items.text:
Direction Game → Client Reliability Reliable Sent when The game ends. Offset Field Type Description 0 Outcome u8 See below Outcome Value Meaning DEFEAT 0 Every player lost all its lives VICTORY 1 The players finished the level

The game stops simulating, waits until every client acknowledged GAME_OVER (or 2 seconds at most), then closes the sessions with DISCONNECT (GAME_OVER).

Receiver behaviour: the client shows the outcome with the last scores it received. Unknown outcomes are treated as DEFEAT.

items.title: 10. Example
items.text:
A client sends its input at tick 1000: up and fire held for the last two ticks, up only the tick before. It has received the game's packets up to number 41, all of them. The decrypted body:

00 00 00 00 00 00 00 29   ack: packet 41
FF FF FF FF               ack bits: the 32 packets before were received
01                        count: 1 message
40                        type: INPUT
00                        flags: unreliable
00 08                     size: 8 bytes
00 00 03 E8                 tick: 1000
03                          count: 3 inputs
11                          tick 1000: up (bit 0) + fire (bit 4)
11                          tick 999: up + fire
01                          tick 998: up

The body is 25 bytes; once sealed (section 3), the datagram is 57 bytes.

The game answers with a snapshot of tick 1000, in one part: player 0 has 3 lives and 1500 points, and its ship (entity 7) is at (200, 540.5), going up at 300 units per second, invulnerable:

80                        type: SNAPSHOT
00                        flags: unreliable
00 22                     size: 34 bytes
00 00 03 E8                 tick: 1000
00 00 03 E6                 last input applied: tick 998
00                          part 0
01                          of 1 part
01                          1 player
00 03 00 00 05 DC             slot 0, 3 lives, score 1500
01                          1 entity
00 00 00 07                   id 7
01                            kind: PLAYER_SHIP
00                            owner: slot 0
06 40                         x: 1600 / 8 = 200
10 E4                         y: 4324 / 8 = 540.5
00 00                         velocity x: 0
F6 A0                         velocity y: −2400 / 8 = −300 units per second
03                            health: 3
01                            flags: invulnerable

items.title: Master and instances
items.text: The local connection between the master and the game processes it starts (ADR 0013). Clients never see this protocol. Conventions and types are defined in the overview.

items.title: 1. Starting an instance
items.text:
The master starts an instance with its own executable and these arguments:

r-type_server --instance --id <instance id> --udp-port <port> --master-port <port>
Argument Description --id Id of the instance, a u32 other than 0. It is also the game id shown to the clients. --udp-port UDP port the instance opens for its clients --master-port TCP port on which the master listens for its instances, on 127.0.0.1

The master then writes the secret to the instance's standard input: 32 random bytes, as 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters followed by a line feed (\n). The secret is never passed as an argument: the arguments of a process are visible to every user of the machine.

items.title: 2. Connection
items.text:
• The instance connects to 127.0.0.1 on the master port within 10 seconds, and sends INSTANCE_HELLO.
  • The master listens on 127.0.0.1 only. The connection is not encrypted: it never leaves the machine.
  • Frames use the same layout as the lobby (lobby, section 3), without TLS. Types 0x01–0x7F are sent by the instance, 0x80–0xFF by the master.
  • There is no error message. A side that receives an invalid frame, or a message it does not expect, closes the connection.
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as Master
    participant I as Instance
    M->>I: start process, secret on standard input
    I->>M: INSTANCE_HELLO (version, id, secret)
    M->>I: CONFIGURE (name, max players)
    Note over I: opens its UDP port
    I->>M: READY (UDP port)
    M->>I: ADD_PLAYER (player id, name, session id, keys)
    I->>M: PLAYER_CONNECTED (player id)
    Note over M,I: later, one of:
    M->>I: REMOVE_PLAYER (player id): the player left through the lobby
    I->>M: PLAYER_DISCONNECTED (player id): the player timed out
    I->>M: GAME_OVER (scores)
    Note over I: exits

The instance proves it was started by the master, receives its configuration, opens its port, then receives its players and reports their connections until the game is over.

items.title: 3. Life and death of an instance
items.text:
Event What happens No valid INSTANCE_HELLO within 10 s, wrong secret or id The master closes the connection and kills the process No READY within 10 s of the start The master kills the process and answers the client ERROR (GAME_START_FAILED) The UDP port cannot be opened The instance exits with a non-zero code; the master answers ERROR (GAME_START_FAILED) The game has no player left The master sends SHUTDOWN (EMPTY) The instance exits, or the connection closes, without GAME_OVER The master considers the game crashed: it sends LEFT_GAME (GAME_CRASHED) to its players and frees the port The connection to the master closes The instance sends DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) to its clients and exits

An instance exits with code 0 after GAME_OVER or SHUTDOWN, and with a non-zero code on any error.

items.title: INSTANCE_HELLO (0x01)
items.text:
Direction Instance → Master Sent when Once, first, right after connecting. Offset Field Type Description 0 Version u16 Protocol version, 1 2 Instance id u32 The --id argument 6 Secret bytes[32] The secret read on the standard input

Receiver behaviour: the master checks that it started an instance with this id, that this instance has not presented itself yet, and that the secret matches, comparing it in constant time. It then sends CONFIGURE.

items.title: READY (0x02)
items.text:
Direction Instance → Master Sent when Once, after CONFIGURE, when the UDP port is open. Offset Field Type Description 0 UDP port u16 The port opened, equal to --udp-port

Receiver behaviour: the game appears in GAME_LIST, and the master sends it the players waiting to join.

items.title: PLAYER_CONNECTED (0x03)
items.text: Direction Instance → Master Sent when A player's session receives CONNECT. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player id u32

items.title: PLAYER_DISCONNECTED (0x04)
items.text:
Direction Instance → Master Sent when A player's session closes on the game's side. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player id u32 4 Reason u8 QUIT (0) or TIMED_OUT (1)

Receiver behaviour: the master removes the player from the game. For TIMED_OUT, it sends the client LEFT_GAME (TIMED_OUT) if its lobby connection is still open.

items.title: GAME_OVER (0x05)
items.text:
Direction Instance → Master Sent when The game ends, just before the instance exits. Offset Field Type Description 0 Count u8 Number of entries that follow, at most 4 1 Scores Count entries: player id (u32), then score (u32)

Receiver behaviour: the master sends LEFT_GAME (GAME_OVER) to the players of the game and frees its port.

items.title: CONFIGURE (0x81)
items.text:
Direction Master → Instance Sent when Once, after a valid INSTANCE_HELLO. Offset Field Type Description 0 Name str8 Name of the game, 1 to 32 bytes 1 + n Max players u8 1 to 4

Receiver behaviour: the instance opens its UDP port and answers READY.

items.title: ADD_PLAYER (0x82)
items.text:
Direction Master → Instance Sent when A client creates or joins the game, before the master answers it GAME_JOINED. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player id u32 4 Session id u32 Unique in this instance, never 0 8 Client key bytes[32] 40 Server key bytes[32] 72 Name str8 1 to 16 bytes

Receiver behaviour: the instance expects a CONNECT on this session. If none arrives within 10 seconds, it forgets the session and sends PLAYER_DISCONNECTED (TIMED_OUT).

items.title: REMOVE_PLAYER (0x83)
items.text:
Direction Master → Instance Sent when A player sends LEAVE_GAME, or its lobby connection closes. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player id u32 4 Reason u8 LEFT (0): LEAVE_GAME; LOBBY_CLOSED (1): lobby connection closed

Receiver behaviour: the instance sends DISCONNECT (QUIT) to the player if connected, closes its session, and sends PLAYER_LEFT to the others with the reason QUIT or LOBBY_CLOSED. It does not answer PLAYER_DISCONNECTED: the master already knows.

items.title: SHUTDOWN (0x84)
items.text:
Direction Master → Instance Sent when The game has no player left, or the master stops. Offset Field Type Description 0 Reason u8 EMPTY (0) or MASTER_STOPPING (1)

Receiver behaviour: the instance sends DISCONNECT (SHUTDOWN) to its clients and exits with code 0.

items.title: Lobby (TCP)
items.text: The connection between a client and the master: TLS, framing, and the messages to list, create, join and leave games. Conventions and types are defined in the overview.

items.title: 1. Connection
items.text:
1. The client opens a TCP connection to the master, on port 4242 by default.
  2. The client and the master run a TLS 1.3 handshake (section 2).
  3. The client sends HELLO within 10 seconds. The master answers WELCOME.
  4. The client sends requests; the master answers each of them and may send notifications.
  5. The connection stays open while the client plays a game. Either side closes it with a TLS close_notify alert, then closes the TCP connection.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Handshake: TCP connected
    Handshake --> Unwelcomed: TLS established
    Unwelcomed --> Lobby: HELLO / WELCOME
    Lobby --> InGame: CREATE_GAME or JOIN_GAME / GAME_JOINED
    InGame --> Lobby: LEAVE_GAME or game over / LEFT_GAME
    Handshake --> [*]: failure or 10 s
    Unwelcomed --> [*]: no HELLO in 10 s
    Lobby --> [*]: closed or 30 s silent
    InGame --> [*]: closed or 30 s silent

A connection is welcomed with HELLO, then moves between the lobby and a game, and is closed on failure or silence.

State Messages accepted from the client Unwelcomed HELLO, PING Lobby LIST_GAMES, CREATE_GAME, JOIN_GAME, PING In game LIST_GAMES, LEAVE_GAME, PING

Any other message is answered with ERROR: HELLO_REQUIRED before HELLO, ALREADY_WELCOMED for a second HELLO, ALREADY_IN_GAME or NOT_IN_GAME otherwise.

items.title: 2. TLS
items.text:
• Only TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) is allowed. A peer MUST refuse older versions.
  • Cipher suites: the master MUST support TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 and TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256.
  • Key exchange groups: x25519 and secp256r1.
  • The master presents an X.509 certificate holding an ECDSA P-256 public key, signed with ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256. The certificate may be self-signed.
  • No client certificate, no early data (0-RTT), no session resumption: the master does not issue session tickets.

items.title: Key pinning
items.text:
The client knows in advance the fingerprint of the master's public key: the SHA-256 hash of the DER encoding of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo of the certificate, 32 bytes, written as 64 hexadecimal characters in the client's configuration.

  • The client MUST compute the fingerprint of the certificate the master presents, and abort the handshake if it differs from the pinned one. It reports the error to the player: the server is not the expected one.
  • The client MUST NOT rely on certificate authorities, host names or validity dates: the pinned key replaces them.

The fingerprint of a certificate, or of a public key in PEM, can be computed with OpenSSL:

openssl x509 -in server.crt -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER | sha256sum
openssl pkey -pubin -in server.pub -outform DER | sha256sum

items.title: 3. Framing
items.text:
TCP carries a stream of bytes with no boundaries. Inside TLS, each message is a frame:

Offset Field Type Description 0 Size u16 Number of bytes that follow this field: the type and the payload. From 1 to 16382. 2 Type u8 Message type 3 Payload Size − 1 bytes, layout given by the type
  • A frame is at most 16384 bytes, size field included. A receiver MUST close the connection when it reads a size of 0 or above 16382, without reading the rest.
  • Types 0x01–0x7F are sent by the client, types 0x80–0xFF by the master.

Example: HELLO with version 1 and the name "Pavel":

00 09   size: 9 bytes follow
01      type: HELLO
00 01   version: 1
05 50 61 76 65 6C   name: "Pavel"

items.title: 4. Requests, replies and notifications
items.text:
• Every request from the client gets exactly one reply: its own reply message, or ERROR.
  • The master answers requests in the order it received them. A client may send several requests without waiting, and match the replies in order.
  • The master may also send notifications at any time, between replies: LEFT_GAME when the game ends or crashes. A notification is never a reply.
Request Reply HELLO WELCOME LIST_GAMES GAME_LIST CREATE_GAME GAME_JOINED JOIN_GAME GAME_JOINED LEAVE_GAME LEFT_GAME PING PONG

items.title: HELLO (0x01)
items.text:
Direction Client → Master Sent when Once, first, right after the TLS handshake. Offset Field Type Description 0 Version u16 Protocol version, 1 2 Name str8 Name of the player, 1 to 16 bytes

Receiver behaviour: if the version is not supported, the master answers ERROR (UNSUPPORTED_VERSION) and closes the connection. If the name is empty, too long or invalid, it answers ERROR (INVALID_NAME). Otherwise it gives the player an id and answers WELCOME. Names do not have to be unique.

items.title: LIST_GAMES (0x02)
items.text:
Direction Client → Master Sent when The player opens or refreshes the list of games.

No payload.

Receiver behaviour: the master answers GAME_LIST.

items.title: CREATE_GAME (0x03)
items.text:
Direction Client → Master Sent when The player creates a game. Offset Field Type Description 0 Name str8 Name of the game, 1 to 32 bytes 1 + n Max players u8 1 to 4

Receiver behaviour: the master starts a game instance (instances), waits until it is ready, adds the player to it and answers GAME_JOINED. Errors: INVALID_NAME, MALFORMED (max players out of range), SERVER_FULL (no free game port), GAME_START_FAILED (the instance did not start within 10 seconds).

items.title: JOIN_GAME (0x04)
items.text:
Direction Client → Master Sent when The player chooses a game in the list. Offset Field Type Description 0 Game id u32 Id from GAME_LIST

Receiver behaviour: the master adds the player to the game and answers GAME_JOINED. Errors: GAME_NOT_FOUND, GAME_FULL. Players may join a game that has already started.

items.title: LEAVE_GAME (0x05)
items.text:
Direction Client → Master Sent when The player quits the game, before closing the UDP session.

No payload.

Receiver behaviour: the master removes the player from the game and answers LEFT_GAME with the reason REQUESTED.

items.title: PING (0x06)
items.text:
Direction Client → Master Sent when The client sent nothing for 10 seconds.

No payload.

Receiver behaviour: the master answers PONG. A master closes a connection on which it received nothing for 30 seconds.

items.title: WELCOME (0x81)
items.text: Direction Master → Client Sent when Reply to HELLO. Offset Field Type Description 0 Player id u32 Id of the player on this master, never 0

items.title: GAME_LIST (0x82)
items.text:
Direction Master → Client Sent when Reply to LIST_GAMES. Offset Field Type Description 0 Count u16 Number of games that follow, at most 256 2 Games Count entries, sorted by game id

Each entry:

Offset Field Type Description 0 Game id u32 Never 0 4 Name str8 1 to 32 bytes 5 + n Players u8 Players currently in the game 6 + n Max players u8 1 to 4

Receiver behaviour: a client MUST check that the entries fit exactly in the frame, and treat the frame as malformed otherwise.

items.title: GAME_JOINED (0x83)
items.text:
Direction Master → Client Sent when Reply to CREATE_GAME or JOIN_GAME. Offset Field Type Description 0 Game id u32 4 UDP port u16 Port of the game, on the same IP address as the master 6 Session id u32 Identifies the player's session in the game, never 0 10 Client key bytes[32] Key of the datagrams sent by the client 42 Server key bytes[32] Key of the datagrams sent by the game

Receiver behaviour: the client opens the UDP session described in Game (UDP). The keys are secret: a client MUST NOT write them to its logs.

items.title: LEFT_GAME (0x84)
items.text:
Direction Master → Client Sent when Reply to LEAVE_GAME, or notification when the player is no longer in the game. Offset Field Type Description 0 Game id u32 4 Reason u8 See below Reason Value Meaning REQUESTED 0 Reply to LEAVE_GAME GAME_OVER 1 The game ended normally GAME_CRASHED 2 The game process stopped unexpectedly TIMED_OUT 3 The game received nothing from the client for 5 seconds

Receiver behaviour: the client closes its UDP session and goes back to the lobby. For GAME_CRASHED, it tells the player that the game stopped.

items.title: PONG (0x85)
items.text:
Direction Master → Client Sent when Reply to PING.

No payload.

items.title: ERROR (0x86)
items.text:
Direction Master → Client Sent when Reply to a request that cannot be honoured. Offset Field Type Description 0 Request u8 Type of the request that failed, 0 if it could not be read 1 Code u16 See below Code Value Meaning Connection MALFORMED 1 Invalid frame or field Closed after the error UNKNOWN_MESSAGE 2 Unknown message type Kept UNSUPPORTED_VERSION 3 Protocol version not supported Closed after the error HELLO_REQUIRED 4 Request sent before HELLO Kept ALREADY_WELCOMED 5 Second HELLO Kept INVALID_NAME 6 Empty, too long, or invalid name Kept GAME_NOT_FOUND 7 No game with this id Kept GAME_FULL 8 The game has its maximum number of players Kept ALREADY_IN_GAME 9 CREATE_GAME or JOIN_GAME while in a game Kept NOT_IN_GAME 10 LEAVE_GAME while not in a game Kept SERVER_FULL 11 No more games can be created Kept GAME_START_FAILED 12 The game process did not start Kept

Receiver behaviour: the client shows a message matching the code. Unknown codes are shown as a generic error.

items.title: 6. When the connection closes
items.text:
• The client closes it, or it times out: the master removes the player from its game, if any. The game tells the other players (game, PLAYER_LEFT).
  • The master closes it: the client closes its UDP session, if any, and tells the player that the connection to the server is lost.
